articles.title: Zelensky Seeks Greater NATO Support as Starlink Restrictions Strain US Ties
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky opened his Brussels visit on Thursday, Oct. 15 by meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, urging allies for steady weapons deliveries as Russia continues increasing its strikes on Ukraine’s energy and civilian infrastructure nationwide.
The discussions centered on ballistic missile interceptors, ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets and new air defense packages from partners; all critically important as the country prepares for its fifth winter of war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“All of these are significant challenges, especially against the backdrop of restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine,” Zelensky said, “which is why it is very important that defense supplies from NATO partners continue.”
The President arrived in Brussels to attend the European Council summit.
His schedule also includes meetings with French President Emmanuel Macron, the prime ministers of Poland, Denmark and Belgium, and an audience with King Philippe of Belgium.
On Friday, Oct. 16 he is set to meet the presidents of the European Council and European Commission, as well as the prime ministers of Hungary, Finland and Sweden.
Russian strikes intensify after US ceasefire push
The meeting amid a week of escalating tensions with Washington.
Russia responded to the latest effort by US President Donald Trump to enforce a ceasefire by launching fresh waves of attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid, residential buildings and other critical infrastructure.
Brussels Drops ‘Urgency’ Language on Ukraine’s Next Accession Steps
According to Zelensky, Russian forces carried out several ballistic missile barrages in recent days while Shahed attack drones remained in Ukrainian airspace almost continuously, with close to 1,000 drones launched since the start of Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv on Oct. 11 on Truth Social media, claiming both sides had agreed, and called on Ukraine to stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Although neither side formally agreed and Ukrainian authorities appeared to find out about the truce by the news circulating online, Kyiv had refrained from striking Russia’s power infrastructure.
However, Russia increased its strikes significantly in recent days, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying on Oct. 14 that the truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.
His remarks came as Moscow’s latest strikes on Kyiv and Kharkiv’s power plants left at least 600,000 Ukrainian citizens without electricity.
Zelensky has since lifted Ukraine’s self-imposed pause on those strikes. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told The Financial Times.
Starlink and intelligence concerns
The pressure on Ukraine’s defenses is growing as Starlink satellite service faces restrictions in the country, making continued NATO supplies especially critical.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, the US aerospace giant Starlink and its owner Elon Musk tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour), disrupting Kyiv’s drone operations.
The move particularly crippled Ukraine’s key mid-range strike drones, used in strikes on Russian logistics.
It also disabled interceptor drones, used by Ukraine’s Defense Forces against Russian jet-powered Shaheds that are significantly harder to intercept due to their speed, reaching up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (250-370 miles per hour).
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” Zelensky said after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
Around the same time, Musk said on Oct. 14 that the US military – including Trump himself – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals, not SpaceX.
US intelligence officials told Ukraine’s embassy in Washington that information sharing would stop immediately if Kyiv kept striking Russian energy targets, The Washington Post reported on Oct. 14, citing a person familiar with the matter.
The source said sharing had not been fully cut off.
Zelensky confirmed the warning reached the military rather than him directly. “They said this to my generals, not to me.”
Trump, for his part, insisted cooperation continues and denied that the US cut off intelligence, although Ukrainian forces received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches toward Kyiv on two consecutive nights at the beginning of the week.
Concerns about intelligence sharing grew after media reports that US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had warned Ukrainian negotiators during talks in Miami on Oct. 9 that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing should Kyiv continue targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure.
While the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami hoping to reach a breakthrough and broker an end to Russia’s aggression, Trump abruptly announced that he signed a diesel deal with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The new license came only three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, appearing to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as networks close to the Kremlin leader.
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators signed a joint letter on Oct. 13, urging Trump to rescind his diesel agreement with Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.
They also joined Zelensky’s month-long appeals to utilize the sweeping sanctions.

articles.title: Ukraine Exhausts Patriot Interceptor Stocks, Leaving It Exposed to Russian Ballistic Missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine has depleted its stocks of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, stripping it of one of the very few tools capable of deterring Russian ballistic missiles, a source familiar with the situation said on Thursday, Oct. 15.
According to CNN’s exclusive, the shortfall was particularly felt during Russia’s latest large-scale attack overnight into Wednesday, Oct. 14, when most incoming ballistic missiles reached their targets. The strike hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy facilities in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring at least 25 in the capital.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the [interceptor] missiles,” the source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported shooting down four Russian ballistic missiles during that attack, which CNN said suggests Ukraine fired its last remaining Patriots.
Lockheed Martin in ‘deep’ production
Patriot interceptors are currently in short supply worldwide. Many of the countries have already depleted their stocks or are seeking to rebuild them amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
On July 20, Lockheed Martin introduced the PAC-3 ACE, a Patriot interceptor designed to deter air and missile threats at less than half the cost of the PAC-3 MSE variant. Initial production was expected to start within 36 months.
Current PAC-3 interceptors cost roughly $4 million per missile, and their high cost is compounded by the rate at which they are expended during sustained operations.
Brussels Drops ‘Urgency’ Language on Ukraine’s Next Accession Steps
The launch came as Ukraine already faced a critical shortage of ballistic missile defense.
For the country, the PAC-3 is currently among the very few weapons capable of intercepting Russia’s Iskander-M, a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
Ukraine’s reliance on the weapons deliveries became clear by July, when the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reportedly exhausted its stocks during two Russian barrages; on July 1-2 Russia launched 24 ballistic missiles, four of which were intercepted, and on July 5-6, Russia launched 23 ballistic missiles, none of which were intercepted.
Around the same time, Russia launched four Zircons on July 1-2 and six on July 5-6, none of which were intercepted either.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US as demand triples.
Dan Tenney, the company’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, told Kyiv Post that the company is investing up to $9 billion through 2030 to expand missile production, strengthen supply chains and bring new factories online.
Ukraine urges partners to boost deliveries amid US rift
For much of this year, Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its Western allies for faster deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
The weapons systems were on the agenda again on Thursday, Oct. 15, during President Volodymyr Zelensky’s meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels, where the Ukrainian president urged its allies for steady arms deliveries as Russia continues its terror on civilian infrastructure nationwide.
On Sept. 8, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from it’s own Bundeswehr stocks, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
During his meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, US President Donald Trump had made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriot missiles domestically.
Trump initially announced the license transfer during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey early July, but later backtracked on the promises, saying Washington must exercise caution when sharing sensitive military technology.
On Sept. 5-6, senior US envoys from Trump’s administration – Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff – traveled to Moscow in an effort to broker an end to the war, where they held three hours of discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin followed by an informal dinner. A day later, they headed to Kyiv for the first time during their tenure.
Although all three sides described the meeting as substantive and positive, no breakthrough was reached.
The diplomatic efforts appeared to be gaining momentum, until last week, when Kyiv-Washington ties took a sour turn.
While the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami hoping to negotiate an end to Russia’s aggression, Trump abruptly announced that he signed a diesel deal with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
Trump then declared an immediate energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv on Oct. 11 on Truth Social media, claiming both sides had agreed.
Although neither strikes formally agreed and Ukrainian authorities appeared to find out about the truce by the news circulating online, Kyiv had refrained from striking Russia’s power infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Russia increased its strikes significantly, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying on Oct. 14 that the truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.
Zelensky has since lifted Ukraine’s self-imposed pause on those strikes. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told The Financial Times.
Around the same time, overnight on Oct. 13-14 the US aerospace giant Starlink and its owner Elon Musk tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour), disrupting Kyiv’s drone operations.
The move crippled Ukraine’s key mid-range strike drones, used in strikes on Russian logistics, and interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” Zelensky said after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
Musk’s response was that the US military – including Trump himself – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals, not SpaceX.
Around the same time on Oct. 14, US intelligence officials told Ukraine’s embassy in Washington that information sharing would stop immediately if Kyiv kept striking Russian energy targets.
Zelensky confirmed the warning reached the military rather than him directly. “They said this to my generals, not to me.”
Trump, for his part, insisted cooperation continues and denied that the US cut off intelligence, although Ukrainian forces received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches toward Kyiv on two consecutive nights at the beginning of the week.

articles.title: Ukraine live: Romania probes possible drone attack on tanker
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Brussels Thursday to rally support at a meeting with NATO chief Mark Rutte the same day, and a summit with EU leaders to follow Friday. Earlier, Zelensky asked the United States not to stand with Moscow and called for "honesty" after Kyiv said it had been betrayed by Washington's intelligence-sharing gaps. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Putin says no significant damage from recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, Ifax reports
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had not caused significant damage, Interfax news agency reported.
Russia will respond to these strikes, Putin said.
UK sending Ukraine more Storm Shadow missiles, Bloomberg reports
Britain is sending Ukraine additional long-range Storm Shadow cruise missiles to help disrupt Russia's military operations and counter attacks on civilian infrastructure, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London on Wednesday, when Britain reaffirmed its support for Kyiv and announced further military assistance following a recent deterioration in Ukraine's ties with Washington.
Black Sea incidents are Russian attempt to destabilize NATO eastern flank, Romanian president says
Recent attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea are Russian attempts to destabilize the eastern flank and weaken support for Ukraine, Romanian President Nicusor Dan said after a meeting with NATO's Secretary General Mark Rutte.
Dan did not provide further details about recent ships struck in and just outside Romanian territorial waters, saying more information will come after ongoing investigations.
Russia's latest strikes show Moscow not ready for peace, French Foreign Ministry says
Russia's latest strikes on Ukraine make it very clear Moscow is not ready to take steps towards peace, France's foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said.
"Russia is clearly not prepared to take a step toward peace, as evidenced by the strikes in recent days that have killed more than 150 civilians since the beginning of last week," he told reporters.
NATO's chief Rutte meets with Bulgarian, Romanian leaders to discuss security in Black Sea
NATO's Secretary General Mark Rutte met on Thursday with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President Nicusor Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and the latest attacks on commercial shipping, he said in a post on X.
"NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed," Rutte said.
Two aerial drones hit ships in Romanian waters, president says
Two aerial drones hit two ships which caught fire in Romanian territorial waters overnight, President Nicusor Dan said at a European Union Summit in Brussels.
Russia's Rosatom says truce in place for Zaporizhzhia power supply repairs
Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom said a truce agreement, mediated by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was in place to allow repairs at a thermal power station supplying power to the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine.
Kremlin says Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil targets contradict US peace efforts
The Kremlin said that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts, after a Ukrainian drone struck a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia did not perceive that Ukraine had ever complied with an energy ceasefire announced last week by US President Donald Trump. Ukraine says it paused such strikes for three days but resumed them after Russia continued to attack its own energy sector.
UK defence chief urges Washington to back Kyiv amid growing row
Britain's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting urged the United States to support Ukraine amid a growing rift between the two countries, insisting it was in Washington's short- and long-term interest.
"There is enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine, the insight, the defense industrial relationship," Streeting said during an event hosted by the CSIS think tank in Washington.
"I think the US will find in the years and the decades to come that Ukraine will contribute a hell of a lot to American strength, both in terms of military power, but also its defense industrial base too," he said.
🎥 'We're done': Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries as 'only leverage' for peace talks
FRANCE 24's Delano D'Souza welcomes Peter Zalmayev, Founder and Director of the Eurasia Democracy Initiative, live from Kyiv.
As Zelensky declares Ukraine "done" with Trump's self-declared energy ceasefire and resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zalmayev warns: "When you talk about the energy ceasefire, it presupposes two to be able to tango and to dance this dance."
He challenges the legitimacy of Trump's unilateral announcement, made without agreement between Moscow and Kyiv, as Russia continues attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Yet he cautions that Zelensky may need tactical restraint to preserve vital US support.
🎥 Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data as missiles hit Kyiv
Russia frees Novaya Gazeta editor after raiding his house
Russian investigators released the chief editor of the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, Sergei Sokolov, on Thursday after questioning him and searching his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, his paper said.
Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed as a "foreign agent" by Moscow.
Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine in 2022, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile.
NATO chief says discussed with Zelensky 'importance of implementing an energy ceasefire'
NATO chief Mark Rutte said he discussed with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky the importance of enacting an energy truce with Russia and maintaining supplies of US weapons for Kyiv.
"We talked about the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as NATO allies' continuous support for Ukraine," Rutte posted online after meeting Zelensky in Brussels.
NATO to hold meeting to address drone attacks in the Black Sea, Romanian president says
Romanian president Nicusor Dan said NATO will hold a meeting on the increasing number of drone attacks on vessels in the Black Sea, believed to be spillover from Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"There will be a dedicated session of the North Atlantic Council to address the situation in the Black Sea," Dan said after a discussion with NATO chief Mark Rutte and a spate of such incidents off Romania and Bulgaria.
NATO officials said the issue would be put on the agenda at the regular meeting of alliance ambassadors in Brussels next week.
Romanian president says drone attacks on ships in Black Sea 'unacceptable'
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said drone attacks on vessels in the Black Sea were "unacceptable" and must stop, after two ships were struck off the country's coast, spillover from Russia's war with Ukraine.
"This is unacceptable and it has to stop. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake," Dan wrote on X after a meeting with NATO chief Mark Rutte to discuss a recent spate of such attacks.
Zelensky stresses 'win-win' cooperation with France after Le Pen comments
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in an interview stressed his country has a "win-win" defence cooperation with France, after Marine Le Pen said she would cut aid to Kyiv if elected French president.
Ukraine's experience with battlefield technology "is very important for the partners – UK, United States, France are among these partners", Zelensky told The Financial Times, adding: "Madame Le Pen is not deeply (familiar) with some details."
Of the defence tie-up with France, Zelensky said: "I think to my mind that it's win-win".
🎥 Elon Musk and Donald Trump: What their growing ties mean for Ukraine
The recent disruption of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine comes as Washington steps up pressure on Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The system plays a key role in Ukraine’s long-range drone operations, raising questions about the implications of the disruption and Elon Musk’s increasingly close ties with Donald Trump.
Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.

articles.title: North Korea fires two types of submarine-launched missiles
articles.body:
- North Korea said it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Oct. 14, without Kim Jong Un attending.
- South Korean experts believe the missiles came from Hero Kim Kun Ok, marking the submarine’s first public missile launch since 2023.
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the Korean Peninsula on Oct. 14, state media said, in what South Korean analysts believe was the first missile launch from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, the submarine Pyongyang unveiled three years ago as its first “tactical nuclear attack submarine.”
The Korean Central News Agency reported on Oct. 15 that the country’s Missile Administration carried out the launches. It did not give flight times, distances or missile names, but released photographs of a submarine and of missiles climbing away on trails of flame. Based on those images, South Korean experts concluded the launch platform was the 3,000-ton-class Hero Kim Kun Ok.
“The test-fire aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems and contributed to getting the Navy skilled in performing its strategic missions,” KCNA said.
Kim Jong Un did not attend. Senior Workers’ Party official Kim Jong Sik and Missile Administration chief Jang Chang Ha oversaw the launches together with navy underwater weapons engineers, KCNA said, adding that the test had no adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launches on Wednesday but said the next day that it had tracked the missiles from before launch through the end of their flights, using assets it declined to identify because of confidentiality arrangements with the United States. A JCS spokesperson said one missile was fired from a vertical launch tube and the other from a torpedo tube, Yonhap reported.
North Korea launched Hero Kim Kun Ok, hull number 841, on Sept. 6, 2023, with Kim Jong Un saying at the ceremony that arming the navy with nuclear weapons could not be delayed further. Despite its label, the boat is a diesel-electric submarine rebuilt from an old Soviet-designed Romeo-class hull; the “nuclear” designation refers to the nuclear-capable missiles it is meant to carry. Until this week, the submarine had not been publicly seen firing a weapon.
Some South Korean analysts told Korea JoongAng Daily that the two weapons may have been a longer-range Hwasal-2 and a shorter-range Pulhwasal-3-31, a missile with a reported range of up to 2,000 km (1,240 miles) that North Korea says can carry its Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead. At that range, the missile could reach all of South Korea and U.S. military bases in Japan. One analyst quoted by the newspaper said firing two missile types with different speeds and approach paths at staggered times would make them harder for air defenses to intercept.
Cruise missiles fly low, often around 100 meters (330 feet) above the surface, which makes them harder to spot on radar than ballistic missiles. Unlike ballistic missile launches, cruise missile tests are not banned under United Nations Security Council sanctions on North Korea.
The previous submarine-launched cruise missile test North Korea reported came in January 2024, when Pulhwasal-3-31 missiles were fired from the smaller 2,000-ton-class experimental submarine 8.24 Yongung with Kim Jong Un watching. Earlier this week, North Korea also fired tactical ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the same sea.

articles.title: Donald Trump claims ‘Iran war will end very soon’ as midterm rallies heat up – US politics live
articles.body:
Pentagon says Trump and Hegseth spoke about decision not to livestream execution ahead of announcement
The Pentagon has also now responded to Donald Trump’s decision to cancel the livestream of the execution of Nidal Hasan.
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said:
President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement.The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned.
While Donald Trump announced on Thursday he was cancelling Pete Hegseth’s recently announced plans to livestream the military execution of Nidal Hasan, because “many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die”. There were, however, some fans of Hegseth’s now-scotched idea: the rightwing religious figures who have long backed his career.
The de facto leader of Hegseth’s theocratic Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), Douglas Wilson, welcomed the announcement.
Wilson, the Idaho pastor who co-founded CREC, has promoted capital punishment as biblically authorized for decades. Last Friday he told Religion News that he prefers “public executions to those conducted in the recesses of a prison somewhere in the middle of the night”, adding that “executions in the scriptures were public”.
Wilson told the outlet that public executions can “turn into a circus”.
Wilson told the Guardian that “I support the execution of Hasan, and prefer public executions to private”, adding: “I prefer the older forms, like a firing squad, as opposed to attempts to ‘medicalize’ it, as with the recent botched execution by injection in Tennessee.”
He did stipulate that “the Pentagon has the responsibility to head off ghoulish behavior by some means”, but admitted: “That will be challenging with a live stream.”
Wilson wrote that he had not spoken to Hegseth nor anyone in his department about the issue.
Wilson and his religious allies are at odds with some other religious leaders, including Pope Leo and the archbishop to the US military, Timothy Broglio, both of whom have condemned Hegseth’s plans.
But CREC pastors, whose church in Washington DC Hegseth attends, have for years advocated the death penalty for many perceived moral infractions including adultery, abortion and homosexuality, and a podcaster from Hegseth’s former church has repeatedly called for executions to be public. Several have expressed hostility to Muslims and Islam, with one calling Allah a “demon God”.
Ilhan Omar’s office did not confirm to the Guardian whether the congresswoman’s phone has been seized, per reporting. But a spokesperson reiterated that the ongoing investigation is “politically motivated and an escalation of Trump’s personal vendetta” against the congresswoman.
“He [Trump] has lied about her family, about her immigration history, and about her love of this country. But the truth is that Trump’s push to strip her of her citizenship and deport her has no basis in the law and has no precedent,” the spokesperson added. “This isn’t a legitimate law enforcement action – it is an authoritarian move to silence an opponent right before an election where he and his party will be rejected by Americans in historic proportions.”
As more emerges about the raid by federal agents on Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s DC home, an unlikely defender has emerged in the form of Marjorie Taylor Greene.
The former Republican representative, now estranged from her party after falling out over the handling of the Epstein files and the Gaza war, took to social media to say that while she and Omar are not aligned on many issues, she questioned how the investigation would “bring gas down under $2, make health insurance freaking affordable, make a family’s weekly grocery bill make sense, and stop sending our beloved military off to fight for another fucking foreign war???”
Greene, who previously introduced a resolution in early 2024 to censure Omar over “treasonous” statements about US-Somali relations, said that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) probe was futile.
“People are so sick and tired of the bullshit,” she wrote on X. “When you dumb mf’ers at the WH actually release the Epstein files and lock up the pedophiles and rapists you all hang out with, then we will start paying attention.”
A reminder that federal authorities investigating Omar have reportedly seized her phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, a person briefed on the inquiry told the Associated Press. Markwayne Mullin previously suggested that agents are examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
We’re keeping an eye on the press conference between Pete Hegseth and his UK counterpart, Wes Streeting at the Pentagon. The pair are currently on the steps of the Department of Defense.
In the Rose Garden today, Donald Trump joked that “one of those beautiful robots” which they could make “look just like” the president could be sent out to campaign on his behalf.
“You wouldn’t know the difference. They make them pretty good. Send them out on the trail. I could sit home and watch them on television,” Trump said. “But, I love doing it.”
This comes as the president is in the middle of a midterm campaign blitz, to stump for everal Republican nominees across the country. After stops in Alaska, Arizona and Montana so far this week, the president will head to Georgia tomorrow, and Kentucky this weekend.
Trump will also head to Iowa on 22 October and 1 November, according to the chair of the Iowa Republicans.
Pentagon says Trump and Hegseth spoke about decision not to livestream execution ahead of announcement
The Pentagon has also now responded to Donald Trump’s decision to cancel the livestream of the execution of Nidal Hasan.
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said:
President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement.The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned.
UK defence secretary Wes Streeting emphasizes importance of standing with Ukraine as he speaks in Washington DC
Britain’s defence secretary Wes Streeting has stressed the importance of standing with Ukraine in its defence against Russia amid mounting fears over the United States’ commitment to Kyiv, the Press Association reports.
During his first visit to Washington in the role, Streeting warned that if Vladimir Putin’s aggression was rewarded, “the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent.”
Streeting is expected to meet his US counterpart PeteHegseth in a bid to strengthen ties that have been strained by issues including DonaldTrump’s stance on Kyiv and the widening US-Nato rift.
Streeting said today that the UK and US must strengthen their defence partnership to confront growing threats at a time when “it is not yet clear if this century will be defined by freedom or tyranny”.
Speaking at an event held by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies and the Royal United Services Institute, he said:
Britain and America have never been content to simply watch history unfold. At defining moments, we have helped determine its course.
The front line for freedom today can be found in Ukraine.
He continued:
Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent.
So standing with Ukraine is not a choice between our values and our self-interest. It is a recognition that ultimately they are inseparable.
Susan Collins, the US senator of Maine, has dismissed allegations that she traded federal contracts for campaign cash as “completely false” after it emerged the FBI examined the claims.
Asked by a reporter about an ethics complaint filed last week by a Maine attorney, the Republican – currently campaigning to retain her seat ahead of November’s US midterm elections – said the allegations were recycled from 2020 and had been rejected by the Department of Justice, the FBI and the Federal Election Commission.
“The allegations are completely false,” Collins said. She said the University of Maine, not the defense contractor Navatek, had asked her to back a research grant, and that she had never heard of the company. Its former chief executive, Martin Kao, she said, was “a crook” whom neither she, nor the university, knew about.
“We have a picture of his meeting with me and with other people in my office that is many months before he ever made a single contribution,” she added. “He spun this story up again in the hopes that the judge would be lenient, or the prosecutor would be.”
Earlier we brought you our colleague Andrew Roth’s report on the collapse of the White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Now CNN is reporting that Kyiv has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, leaving it more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has repeatedly warned for months that his country is running out of the US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. According to CNN's source, “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last [Russian] strike were not intercepted due to lack of the [interceptor] missiles.”
In a public statement on Wednesday, Zelenskyy pleaded for more stocks. “The American president has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor,” he said. “We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine.”
We’re getting some more reaction following Trump’s move to cancel the planned livestream of Nidal Hasan’s execution.
Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky who frequently spars with the president, said that “sanity prevails momentarily” in response to the news.
Meanwhile, one of Trump’s noted allies – far-right activist and conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer – said that broadcasting Hasan’s execution would have “really helped improve the morale of Americans in our country”.
“We need to feel a sense of national pride and have events that draw clear lines between those of us who support America, and those of us who empathize with America’s enemies,” she wrote on X, claiming that “a lot of people” were “looking forward” to the execution live stream.
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
An attack on two neutral ships in Romanian territorial waters at the mouth of the Danube River indicated that strikes against vulnerable commercial targets are set to expand.
On Wednesday Zelenskyy said he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked a gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”
Prior to the president’s announcement that the live stream of Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad will no longer go ahead, a new poll from the Washington Post and ABC News showed that 80% of Americans oppose a live online broadcast of the execution.
While the partisan breakdown shows that more Democrats (91%) oppose a live stream, 64% of Republicans still opposed the move.
Meanwhile, a majority of Americans, 53%, support executing Hasan by firing squad – while 42% are opposed.
Lawmakers from both parties welcome Trump's decision to cancel livestream of firing squad execution
Following the news that Donald Trump has canceled a plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, more lawmakers have welcomed the decision.
“Good. So sick to have ever considered this,” wrote Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, on X.
Meanwhile, Republican Senator John Curtis of Iowa, said “this is the right move, both for the loved ones of the victims and for the country.”
Curtis urged the administration to reconsider broadcasting the execution last week, warning that “cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment”, and is “not an effective deterrent”.
The president expressed private misgivings about the Pentagon’s move to broadcast the execution by firing squad, according to an Axios report published earlier this week, citing four people who had spoken with Trump.
A reminder that last week, Pete Hegseth told rightwing broadcaster Real America’s Voice that the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, scheduled for 3 December, would be available to watch online.
Hasan’s sentence is the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast.
Democrats and several Republicans said the decision to livestream the execution would align the US with authoritarian countries who make a public “spectacle” of executions and could run the risk of radicalizing people watching by turning Hasan into a martyr.
On Friday, vice-president JD Vance appeared to quell concerns that the execution would actually be live streamed. “First of all, I’ve seen these announcements. I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters, after he was asked about how he squares his Christian faith with the Pentagon’s decision to broadcast the execution. Vance also said that if the decision was made to livestream Hasan’s execution, he was “not going to be watching it”.
Trump says Nidal Hasan execution will not be live streamed
Donald Trump has said that the execution of Nidal Hasan, the US army doctor who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, would not be livestreamed.
The decision, issued via a post on Truth Social, comes after bipartisan backlash to defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement that Hasan’s execution by firing squad, would be broadcast online.
“Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote on Thursday. “He [Hasan] will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”
Today, a number of my colleagues who cover business, labor and consumer rights will be taking your questions about the impact of the economy of the upcoming midterms – now fewer than three weeks away.
Alongside his midterm stumping, Trump has devoted time to tout the his various renovation projects on the White House. On Truth Social the president shared pictures of the building’s South entrance and the new heliport – which he has frequently praised while speaking to reporters before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn.
“The exterior walls and ornamentation, both missing and in bad condition, has been fully restored to the Highest Level, giving the White House many decades of additional life! It had to be done, and I am very proud to be the President who did it!” Trump wrote. “Likewise, the Ballroom and Military Complex, is on time, and on budget, and will make an unbelievably beautiful addition, the first since the West Wing in 1901, to the White House.”
However, Trump is not the first president over the last century to undertake this kind of work. In 1942, Franklin D Roosevelt added a second-story to the East Wing. Prior to that he added an indoor therapy swimming pool in 1933, which would eventually become the press briefing room. Later, Harry Truman rebuilt the entire interior with a steel frame and added the Truman Balcony on the exterior of the White House.
The estimated cost of Trump’s ballroom has also ballooned. The Guardian previously reported the number sits around $400m, while the Washington Post has reported total costs could reach $600m.
In June, the administration also redirected $352m in federal funds, designated for the Secret Service, toward’s the project. The funds were drawn from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the president’s sweeping domestic policy legislation. However, the law stipulates the money may only be spent on Secret Service personnel, training facilities, technology and related costs, not construction.

articles.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.
Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.
“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”
Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.
That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.
“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.
Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.
As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.
Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.
Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”
The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.
The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.
Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

articles.title: Could Israeli technology aid Saudi Arabia's struggles to stop Houthi missile attacks? - analysis
articles.body:
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 8, 10, and 11 killed at least 16 people. The deadliest strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309 others. On October 13, another attack damaged an administrative building at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. Saudi forces have intercepted numerous incoming weapons, but others have reached their targets despite the billions of dollars the kingdom has spent on air defenses.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Why are missiles and drones still getting through, and could Israeli technology help Saudi Arabia stop them?
Israel has spent decades developing defenses against different types of aerial threats. Some have already been supplied to the United Arab Emirates. In May, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help defend the UAE against Iranian attacks.
There have also been reports of Saudi-Israeli discussions about sharing intelligence through American military channels. Neither government has confirmed such an arrangement, but it raises the possibility of cooperation that would have been politically difficult to imagine only a few years ago.
Why are Saudi defenses struggling?
Saudi Arabia operates American-made Patriot missile batteries and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), which is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude. The kingdom’s first THAAD battery became operational in July 2025, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
These systems provide substantial protection, but the Houthis have weapons designed to exploit different weaknesses.
Ballistic missiles climb high into the atmosphere before descending at high speed toward their targets. Cruise missiles fly more like pilotless aircraft, sometimes close enough to the ground to escape radar detection until late in their flight. Drones can be smaller, slower, and much less expensive than the missiles used to shoot them down.
A defender facing multiple weapon types at once must identify each threat, choose the right interceptor, and respond before the weapons reach their targets.
A 2020 study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, The Missile War in Yemen, documented the Houthis’ growing arsenal of missiles and drones, developed with Iranian assistance, and their repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
The Houthis have since improved their capabilities. Regional officials told the Associated Press that investigators believe drones were launched ahead of cruise and ballistic missiles during the recent attack on Riyadh’s airport. If confirmed, the sequence would suggest an attempt to stretch Saudi defenses by presenting several threats in quick succession.
The kingdom has faced similar problems before.
After the September 2019 attacks on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities, Washington Institute for Near East Policy researchers Michael Knights and Conor Hiney examined gaps in Saudi radar coverage and weaknesses in the coordination of its defenses.
The weapons appeared to approach from the north, while much of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture was oriented toward threats from the east. Low-flying missiles and drones could take advantage of radar blind spots created by terrain, the curvature of the Earth, and the limitations of individual sensors.
The researchers recommended better coordination among existing radars, command systems, and interceptors, rather than relying solely on additional missile batteries.
Saudi Arabia’s geography presents another problem. The kingdom covers nearly 2.15 million square kilometers, approximately 78 times the combined land area of Israel and the West Bank. Its cities, airports, refineries, oil fields, military bases, and ports are scattered across enormous distances.
Israel’s much smaller geographic area lets some defensive systems cover several population centers or installations. Saudi Arabia needs far more widely distributed equipment, even though large stretches of sparsely populated desert do not require the same protection as major cities or oil facilities.
Cost is another concern. An inexpensive drone can force defenders to fire an interceptor worth hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.
Dr. Sidharth Kaushal of Britain’s Royal United Services Institute discussed the depletion of Gulf interceptor stocks and the difficulty of replacing them quickly in an April 2026 BBC interview. The Financial Times reported this week that Saudi Arabia was struggling with interceptor shortages and ongoing gaps in radar coverage.
Interception does not always prevent casualties. On October 13, debris from intercepted cruise missiles injured four people and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to Saudi Civil Defense.
Which Israeli systems could help?
Israel’s air defenses rely on several systems that operate at different ranges and altitudes. Iron Dome is the best known, but other Israeli weapons may be better suited to some of the threats Saudi Arabia faces.
Iron Dome was developed to intercept short-range rockets. Its radar tracks incoming projectiles and calculates where they are likely to land, allowing the system to focus on threats to populated areas or key installations.
Upgrades have expanded its ability to engage drones and cruise missiles. Iron Dome batteries could protect individual Saudi sites, but their coverage is too limited to defend much of the kingdom’s territory.
David’s Sling, developed jointly by Israel and the United States, is designed to intercept cruise missiles, certain ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones. Tests conducted in February 2026 included improvements intended to address newer aerial threats.
Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 are intended mainly for ballistic missiles. Arrow 3 can intercept suitable targets outside the atmosphere, before they descend toward the ground. Israel has used Arrow-family defenses against missiles launched from Iran and Yemen.
Such systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ballistic-missile defenses, but they would not solve the problem of detecting and intercepting a small drone approaching an airport at low altitude.
Two less familiar Israeli products could be especially useful for defending individual installations.
Rafael’s mobile SPYDER system is designed to engage aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles. Israel Aerospace Industries manufactures Barak MX, which uses different interceptors against aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and some ballistic threats.
Either could potentially complement Saudi Arabia’s existing defenses around oil facilities, airports, or military bases, provided the equipment could be integrated into the kingdom’s command and radar networks.
Iron Beam offers a different approach. Instead of firing an interceptor missile, it uses a powerful laser to destroy certain short-range threats. Israel delivered its first operational system to the military in December 2025.
The attraction is partly financial: Firing a laser can cost far less than using a missile against a relatively inexpensive drone.
Its limitations are substantial, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Lasers need a clear line of sight, and dust, haze, clouds, and distance can reduce their effectiveness. They cannot replace longer-range defenses against ballistic missiles.
Israel also operates C-Dome, a naval adaptation of Iron Dome that could help protect ships and offshore installations.
Which systems would be most useful to Saudi Arabia would depend on the targets it wanted to protect, the weapons it expected to face, and the equipment it already possessed.
How has Israel helped defend the UAE?
The United Arab Emirates offers the clearest example of Israeli air defense technology being used by an Arab country.
After Houthi attacks on Abu Dhabi in early 2022, Israeli defense sources told Breaking Defense that an agreement to supply Rafael’s SPYDER system was nearing completion. The publication subsequently reported that an Israeli-made Barak air defense system had been deployed in the UAE, although the precise model was not identified.
The two countries had established diplomatic relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords, removing a major obstacle to military purchases.
Their cooperation reportedly expanded during the 2026 war involving Iran.
On May 12, Huckabee publicly confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help operate them in the Emirates, according to the defense publication Janes.
The Financial Times reported that Israel had supplied additional equipment, including a version of Iron Beam, surveillance technology, and real-time intelligence about Iranian missile launches.
Those details have not all been independently confirmed. An October study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies discussed the reported laser and surveillance deployments but did not independently verify that they took place. Janes also noted that Huckabee’s remarks did not confirm those specific transfers.
There is no public accounting of how many incoming weapons were intercepted by Israeli systems operating in the UAE.
Still, the deployment of Iron Dome batteries and personnel establishes that the Israeli-Emirati defense relationship has moved beyond ordinary equipment sales. That experience may offer lessons for Saudi Arabia, although Riyadh has not normalized relations with Israel.
Could Saudi Arabia obtain Israeli assistance without normalizing relations?
Intelligence sharing would probably be easier to arrange than a weapons sale.
Information about missile launches and flight paths could potentially be relayed through American military channels, giving Saudi crews more time to prepare an interception without requiring Israeli launchers or personnel on Saudi territory.
Regional arrangements already support this kind of cooperation. In January 2026, US Central Command announced the establishment of a multinational air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. It aims to improve information sharing, joint planning, and coordination among regional military partners.
Israeli media reports suggest that Saudi-Israeli intelligence cooperation may already be taking place.
In September, The Jerusalem Post reported, citing a regional diplomat, that the two countries had discussed intelligence assistance through US Central Command. Ynet and Israel Hayom also reported, citing diplomatic and security sources, that Israeli intelligence was reaching Saudi Arabia through American channels.
Neither government has publicly confirmed those accounts, and it is unclear what information, if any, is being shared.
The Media Line reported in September that senior military commanders from Israel, Saudi Arabia, and six other Middle Eastern countries had attended a US-organized security meeting in Germany. US Central Command confirmed the gathering, but it did not establish a formal military alliance.
Saudi political analyst Abdulaziz Alshaabani warned against assuming that such contacts would lead to open military cooperation.
“Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” Alshaabani told The Media Line.
Purchasing Israeli missile defenses would raise additional problems.
Israel would have to authorize the export, and Saudi Arabia would need arrangements for training, maintenance, software, spare parts, and replacement interceptors. Some Israeli systems would also require American approval because of US involvement in their development.
Germany’s purchase of Arrow 3, for example, required Washington’s consent.
Political considerations could be harder to overcome than the technical requirements.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly insisted that diplomatic relations with Israel depend on the establishment of a Palestinian state. Its Foreign Ministry reiterated in February 2025 that it would not normalize relations without an independent Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.
A publicly acknowledged purchase of Israeli weapons would be considerably more difficult for Riyadh to explain than intelligence cooperation conducted through American military channels.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly announced an agreement to purchase Israeli missile defense systems, nor has it officially confirmed that negotiations for such a deal are underway.
Would Israeli technology solve the problem?
Israeli missile defense systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s defenses, but acquiring and deploying them would take time.
Saudi Arabia would need its own launchers, radars, trained crews, and interceptor supplies. Iron Dome batteries stationed in Israel are too far away to protect Riyadh. Any new equipment would also have to operate alongside the kingdom’s existing Patriot and THAAD systems.
Israel has its own shortages to consider after prolonged fighting with Iran and the Houthis. Its military needs to replenish interceptor stocks, which could limit the equipment available for export.
Saudi Arabia is also seeking assistance from established defense partners, including the US, Britain, France, Turkey, and Pakistan. Those relationships offer alternatives without the political complications of buying weapons from Israel.
Protecting civilians remains important even when interception fails. Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent attacks after September 29, leaving residents without official alerts before the deadly airport strikes. Warnings later resumed, including alerts issued by Saudi Civil Defense for Riyadh and Al-Kharj on October 14.
For Saudi Arabia, earlier warning of incoming attacks may be more immediately useful than new missile batteries. Better intelligence could help its existing defenses respond sooner, while new equipment would require procurement, deployment, and training.
A Saudi purchase of Israeli missile defenses would be a much bigger step, requiring decisions in Riyadh, Jerusalem, and possibly Washington. In the meantime, Saudi forces must defend widely separated cities and installations against missiles and drones that can approach from different directions, often with little warning.

articles.title: Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
articles.body:
Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
October 15, 2026
North Korea announced that it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on Wednesday — a day after the state-run Korean Central News Agency reported that leader Kim Jong Un had visited a new defense industry museum, where he admired an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of hitting targets in the continental United States.
The visit came five days after South Korean President Lee Jae-myung observed the test launch of his country's first domestically developed hypersonic missile.
South Korea's breakthrough came after Pyongyang announced a test on October 3 of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that traveled 350 kilometers (220 miles) before striking its target.
"Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed the expectation and belief that all the nation's missile forces would remain faithful to their missions of defending the sovereignty and security of the republic in a responsible combat posture," the KCNA reported.
'Advanced conventional weapons'
Both North Korea and South Korea are primarily racing to develop hypersonic technology because it offers a step-up in offensive capabilities at a time of worsening tensions in the Indo-Pacific region.
Hypersonic missiles are weapons that can travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5) or over 6,100 kilometers per hour.
Their speed makes it far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy inbound missiles, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads. Their additional advantage over previous generations of missiles is their ability to suddenly change course, dip or weave in flight, making interception significantly more difficult.
"There has been an arms race on the Korean Peninsula for many years — and hypersonic weapons are just the latest manifestation of that," Chris Green, the senior Korean Peninsula adviser for the International Crisis Group, told DW.
Hypersonic weapons have become a "priority for the South" as the North has ramped up its capabilities and forged military and economic ties with Russia, Green said.
"And North Korea has nuclear weapons, but it would not be viable to use them," Green said, "as the threat has always been that doing so would mean that the US would turn the country to glass."
"For the North, it is unsurprising that the geopolitics of the region have encouraged them to pursue advanced conventional weapons as they try to have dominance on the peninsula," Green said.
Underestimating North Korea?
Though it is impossible to confirm with any certainty that the weapons North Korea says it has developed have the capabilities the government claims, Green said, it would be a mistake to underestimate Pyongyang.
"We do not know their capabilities, and it is possible this is all propaganda, but there is a long list of times the North's capabilities have been underestimated only to be shown that they can, in fact, do what they say," Green said.
Chun In-bum, a retired South Korean army general who is now a senior fellow with the National Institute for Deterrence Studies, shares that assessment.
"It's anybody's guess whether they're telling the truth on this, but any prudent military planner should always assume the worst," Chun said.
North Korea's mastery of the advanced technology required to operate hypersonic missiles appears to have been sudden, although it remains unclear how it acquired the capability.
"They probably obtained the technology through illegal means," Chun said. "They snoop around firms in the US, South Korea and Japan for this sort of information, but they also do it to their 'friends.'"
Wherever the data came from, the fact that North Korea's hypersonic missiles appear to have performed as required should be cause for deep concern.
"A greater offensive capability increases the overall danger posed by the North, and if they have weapons that are harder to shoot down, then it is possible there are greater temptations to use them," Chun said.
"I'm speculating, of course," Chun said, "but I'm sure that we are looking at ways to neutralize this particular threat — but, as I understand it, there is no good answer right now."
No game changer
Green said the viable systems developed by both sides could cancel each other out as a potent battlefield advantage.
"I do not think this changes the balance of power," Green said. "The North still has its nuclear deterrent and this 'porcupine strategy' of being sharp and prickly in order to keep everyone else at arm's length," he added. "And it's not a game changer south of the Demilitarized Zone either."
"It is clear, however, that if the North continues to develop its offensive systems and is able to deploy them in huge numbers," Green said, "then there will have to be a conversation about greater missile defense — not only in the South, but also in Japan, and that will then raise some very difficult questions."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

articles.title: Musk Says US Government Controls Ukraine’s Starshield Limits as Zelensky Accuses Russia of Exploiting Outage
articles.body:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday, Oct. 14, that the US military – including US President Donald Trump himself, not SpaceX – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals.
His remarks came after restrictions imposed overnight on Oct. 13-14 disrupted Kyiv’s drone operations, particularly interceptor drones – among Ukraine’s few effective tools against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which are significantly harder to intercept due to their speed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement on Wednesday, after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
Speaking during an interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored,” released on Wednesday, Zelensky said he feels betrayed by Trump and warned that SpaceX’s new Starlink restrictions will cost lives. “I’m sure they knew what they did,” he said regarding the outage.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink’s connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) is being restored. “Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense,” he said in a post on X, thanking Musk for his “continued support.”
General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
According to the latest estimates by Zelensky, Russia launched 124 drones overnight and another 145 during the day, with more than 40 Shaheds still in Ukraine’s airspace as he wrote.
UK fast-tracks missiles against jet-powered drones
Zelensky said he and Burnham agreed to speed up deliveries of British air defense systems to counter the jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than older Shahed models.
Earlier on Wednesday, The British government said it would accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), under a £45 million (approximately $60 million) surface-to-air missile package, bringing forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet Ukraine’s urgent winter needs.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe” Burnham said ahead of the meeting.
He has also tasked ministers with preparing new sanctions and further military and financial aid.
According to the BBC, Burnham greeted Zelensky at Downing Street with a military ceremonial guard – the first such honor for a foreign leader.
The visit followed a massive overnight strike in which Russia fired at least 39 missiles and 128 drones, cutting power to at least 600,000 people, according to Zelensky earlier in the day.
Questions over US intelligence sharing
The recent strains with Washington deepened after Ukraine received no early warning from Western partners about incoming Russian ballistic missiles for two nights in a row.
Zelensky said Kyiv’s systems detected the missiles only as they approached the capital.
Although NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said they had seen no sign that sharing had stopped, recent reports by other senior Ukrainian authorities appeared to suggest otherwise.
The lapse followed reports that Washington had threatened to cut intelligence sharing for Kyiv during roughly eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9.
Reportedly, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukraine’s delegation that it could lose access to US intelligence if it kept striking Russian oil refineries.
Several US media separately reported that Trump’s administration also warned it could suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism that enables European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, the main channel for buying Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied the claims, saying that no change has been made.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin that eased US sanctions on Russian fuel, which 12 senators from both parties called “a betrayal of Ukraine” in a joint letter, urging the US President to rescind the diesel deal and enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US President then announced an energy truce on Oct. 11 that neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed, insisting the two sides agreed “because I said, ‘You agree.’”
Although Ukraine abided by the abrupt ceasefire announcement, Russia continued striking Ukraine nationwide. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.
