articles.title: Britain is providing Ukraine with a new batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles — media
articles.body:
Britain is providing Ukraine with a new batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles — media
Kyiv • UNN
London is providing Kyiv with additional Storm Shadows to counter Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure. The number of missiles has not been disclosed.
The United Kingdom is providing Ukraine with an additional batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles to help it disrupt Russian military operations targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter. People familiar with the situation said, reports UNN, citing Bloomberg.
According to sources who agreed to provide the information on condition of anonymity, the supply of these British-made cruise missiles was discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday. The weapons shipment had not previously been announced publicly.
The United Kingdom and other allies of Ukraine are stepping up support for the war-torn country. This is happening as U.S. President Donald Trump announced last week that he had reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin on placing Russian diesel fuel on the global market. On Wednesday, in an interview on the program "Piers Morgan Uncensored," Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by events in recent days — in particular, the diesel-fuel agreement, Trump’s announcement of an "energy ceasefire," as well as problems with Ukrainian troops’ access to SpaceX satellite technology.
The publication notes that the United Kingdom has been supplying Ukraine with Storm Shadow missiles since 2023, although their use was initially restricted to the combat zone within Ukrainian territory. At the end of 2024, Ukrainian forces expanded the geography of their use, striking military facilities on Russian territory with British cruise missiles for the first time.
According to the sources, the United Kingdom considers Ukraine’s use of long-range weapons against Russian facilities involved in attacks on civilians and infrastructure to be defensive actions. In recent weeks, Russia has increased production of jet-powered drones and missiles to intensify attacks on Ukraine, so it is important for Kyiv to have the ability to counter these actions, the sources said.
The Trump administration urged Kyiv to stop drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, but the strikes resumed on Thursday — in response to ongoing Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities. As evidence of differences between the positions of the British and U.S. governments, the sources said that, in London’s view, Ukraine should not stop striking Russia until Moscow itself abandons such actions.
The media outlet notes that the British government declined to comment. It does not disclose exactly how many Storm Shadow missiles have been supplied to Ukraine during the war and does not report on each individual delivery. Storm Shadow missiles, produced by MBDA, have proven highly effective at penetrating Russia’s air-defense system and striking military and industrial facilities. These highly precise air-launched missiles have a range of more than 250 kilometers (155 miles); they are difficult to defend against because they fly at high speed while following the contours of the terrain.
In August, Burnham announced that the United Kingdom would provide Kyiv with technical documentation for long-range missiles so that Ukraine could establish their production on its own territory, although implementing the project will likely take some time.
In addition, Britain is developing low-cost long-range strike systems for Ukraine that will not depend on the supply of components or data from the United States.

articles.title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
articles.body:
In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

articles.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
articles.body:
The development – and its dire consequences for Ukraine – has put the spotlight on Starlink -SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a powerful military version developed by Elon Musk’s company for the Pentagon.
Here’s what we know about the two SpaceX systems, how they are controlled and why Zelenskyy has framed the shift as a betrayal by Donald Trump and the US.
What has happened to Ukraine’s connection?
On Tuesday night, Ukraine’s military reported the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working on terminals moving at speeds greater than 100mph (160km/h).
Kyiv installs SpaceX Starlink receptors in many of its drones as part of an onboard guidance system. Kyiv said the change was imposed without any explanation from the US.
How does the restriction affect Ukraine?
The restriction had two immediate consequences: It effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and it hampered air defence systems that stop Russian drones bombarding Kyiv.
Ukraine uses Starlink systems to direct many mid-range drones towards their targets – a critical frontline offensive capability. Russian Shaheds fly at speeds close to 200mph, so the new restriction means Ukrainian interceptor drones have no chance to chase them down.
Starlink is not used for long-range Ukrainian missions that have successfully targeted Russian oil refineries in recent months.
A Ukrainian air defence unit intercepts a Shahed drone during an attack on Kyiv. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon. Starshield’s service is separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, but the distinction is sometimes blurry.
Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action, SpaceX says, only defensive activities or for use by civilian clients.
Starshield, however, allows those capabilities and uses enhanced encryption to transmit sensitive information. In addition, Starshield provides users with the ability to integrate sensors on object like drones. Starshield’s secure communications rely on Starlink, the vast network of 11,000 satellites that Musk and SpaceX have sent into space since 2019.
Who made the decision to restrict access, Musk or the Pentagon?
Musk said the Ukrainian military was linked to Starshield, because Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons. He added that any Starshield disruptions being experienced by Ukraine would be the responsibility of the US government, not SpaceX. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Donald Trump.
A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink satellite at his positions at the frontline. Photograph: Reuters
The White House has not confirmed or denied Musk’s assertion. But the Trump administration has been pressuring Ukraine to limit its strikes on energy targets inside Russia.
What has the reaction been?
Zelenskyy said he felt personally betrayed by Trump, in an interview with Piers Morgan, saying Kyiv was “losing a strong partner”. As for what it meant for Ukraine and its people, Zelenskyy said: “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
In the US, Democrats denounced the Trump administration. “Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing the restrictions as “unconscionable”.
Republican senator Tom Tillis voiced his concern on X: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a gray area for the US government or for American corporations.”

articles.title: Russia launches nearly 1,000 UAVs against Ukraine over past 24 hours – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Since the start of the past 24 hours, Russia has launched nearly 1,000 attack drones against Ukraine; these attacks are taking place amid restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine and underscore the need for continued defense supplies from NATO partners, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said following a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels.
"Unfortunately, Russia has responded to yet another attempt by the U.S. president to reduce the intensity of the strikes with new waves of attacks against our energy sector, residential buildings, and other infrastructure. Over the past few days, there have been several waves of ballistic missile strikes, and Shahed drones have been constantly flying in our skies. From the start of the day yesterday until now, the Russians have launched nearly 1,000 drones," Zelenskyy said on his Telegram channel on Thursday.
"All of this poses significant challenges, especially given the restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine, and therefore it is very important that defense supplies from our NATO partners continue," he added.
According to him, this applies particularly to ballistic missile interceptors and ammunition for the F-16. The president said work is underway on new air defense packages.
"Literally every day and every hour, new packages can save the lives of Ukrainian men and women. We discussed this and other important issues during the meeting. Thank you, Mark, for your support and willingness to help," the president said.

articles.title: Why Data Centers Have Become Military Targets
articles.body:
When the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran earlier this year, Tehran responded by striking energy infrastructure across the Gulf. The result was a severe shock to global energy markets that continues to this day. Less publicized at the time were its strikes on another kind of infrastructure: data centers.
Similar attacks have since taken place in Russia and Ukraine, where both sides have been trading tit-for-tat strikes on data centers.
Experts say these attacks represent a new front in warfare, in which facilities powering the technology behind many critical industries have become military targets.
The AI boom has led to a surge in demand for computing power, data storage and cloud services, making the data centers that provide them a crucial part of modern infrastructure. A mass of data center construction is currently underway in the U.S., and tech companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars a year to meet AI demand. Telecommunications companies, banks, hospitals and energy suppliers all rely on them.
“Data centers are now on the critical path for modern digital infrastructure,” Kirk Cameron, founding director of the Institute for Advanced Computing at Virginia Tech, tells TIME. “The loss of key data centers could collapse economies, disrupt public and private transportation with loss of GPS, and affect government essential services for health, emergency dispatch, and power grids.”
Military use of AI for targeting and information processing has made data centers crucial to fighting a war. Ukraine uses AI for an array of battlefield functions such as drone targeting, battle planning, and missile analyzing Russian missile attacks. U.S. tech companies such as Palantir now work closely with Ukraine’s military to develop new AI-powered weaponry, taking advantage of the ability to immediately test their technology on the battlefield. The U.S. military also uses Palantir’s Maven system to help identify targets for strikes.
“Data centers are competitive advantages in warfare,” Cameron says. “Knocking out capabilities means potentially crippling combat operations for an adversary. It’s also a form of economic warfare and could lead to longer-term competitive challenges for the target.”
Where have data centers been attacked?
The first wave of attacks on data centers was carried out in March this year by Iran, when it launched strikes on two Amazon facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and another in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby drone strike.
Those facilities have been mostly offline ever since; Amazon said on Sept. 15 that it had been “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in those two regions.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers in late September disrupted television broadcasts and internet access. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it was striking data centers because they “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Ukraine’s response began on Oct. 8, and it has since carried out drone strikes on three data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, often called Russia’s version of Google. The first site hit, in Sasovo, houses two of the three supercomputers Yandex uses to develop its AI models, Meduza reported, and the outage disrupted several companies relying on Yandex’s cloud services, including Russian Railways, MegaFon, T-Bank, and several media outlets.
Following the first strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the retaliation: "We always respond in kind. You all know that they are hitting and hitting our data centers; we responded to them.”
How have tech companies responded?
The spate of attacks over the last year has already caused tech companies to rethink how and where they build data centers.
The United Arab Emirates is reportedly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project following the Iranian strikes. The original plan envisioned a 10-square-mile campus in Abu Dhabi, to be built in partnership with American tech companies like Oracle, Nvidia, and Cisco. Now the data centers will likely be spread out across the UAE, according to officials who spoke to Reuters.
Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, believes that data centers have become a new frontline in warfare—and that may require new strategies.
“If you’re Russia and you attack a Microsoft data center, is that an attack on Ukraine? Is that an attack on Microsoft? Is that an attack on a U.S. company and, by extension, the U.S.?” she asks.
The U.S. has largely followed a policy that attacks on American companies do not constitute an attack on the United States, but Harding says the government may need to decide on a new approach “that creates deterrence not just to protect life and health, but also data.”
And while the threat to data centers in the U.S. may be relatively low compared to the Gulf and Ukraine or Russia, tech companies will also have to think more about the security of their facilities when building, while trying to keep pace with massive demand.
“The knock-on effect is that the companies that own the data centers are realizing they can't protect them, and that kind of calls into question the cloud model in general,” Harding says. “They're having to make big adjustments. You could see a time in the future where Amazon starts losing business to Microsoft because Microsoft does a better job of hiding where their data centers are.”

articles.title: Western Europe is giving its spies teeth
articles.body:
Western Europe is giving its spies teeth
Something fundamental has changed in Europe over the past months. Governments across the continent have begun expanding the powers of intelligence agencies at a pace that would have been difficult to imagine only a few years ago.
Germany is preparing to give its foreign intelligence service a far more operational role. The Netherlands is expanding the ability of its intelligence agencies to act proactively against hostile actors. Austria is broadening its definition of espionage. Sweden is rebuilding its foreign intelligence architecture.
Taken together, these amount to a European securitization drive: more activities are being redefined as security problems, more institutions are being brought inside the security apparatus, and intelligence services are being transformed from organizations that primarily collect information into agencies which are increasingly expected to act.
Western Europe’s security establishment has been shaken by two developments: the continuing perception of a more assertive and dangerous international environment, and growing political uncertainty surrounding America’s role in European security under President Donald Trump.
Trump changed the conversation
The psychological shock came in March 2025, when the Trump administration temporarily halted US military and battlefield intelligence sharing with Vladimir Zelensky’s Ukraine.
For decades, European security planning had rested on an assumption that American intelligence capabilities would be available when the strategic stakes became serious. Suddenly, they could not be certain to rely on that anymore.
Later in 2025, the Netherlands reportedly stopped sharing certain information with US counterparts amid concerns over political interference and “human rights” considerations. Again, the immediate dispute was just one glimpse of the realization dawning on Washington’s European partners: intelligence cooperation is ultimately political, and political relationships can change.
The Europeans now had to confront a question they had largely been avoiding. What happens when an ally possessing the world’s most powerful intelligence apparatus can no longer be assumed to have the same political priorities?
The obvious answer is to build more European capacity. This does not mean that Europe is preparing to replace the US, or that trans-Atlantic intelligence cooperation is disappearing. But the European governments want to make sure their spies can still operate, even when Washington’s political priorities are different from theirs.
Germany: From spying to sabotage
Friedrich Merz’s Germany is perhaps the best example of how far the transformation could go. Berlin is pursuing the largest overhaul of the country’s intelligence system since World War II.
Under reforms expected to take effect in January, the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, would receive substantially greater latitude to conduct offensive activities. In a state of tension or military defense, the service could conduct acts of sabotage abroad.
That’s a major conceptual departure for an organization traditionally associated primarily with foreign intelligence collection.
The reforms would also expand the technological reach of German intelligence. The BND and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) would gain a greater ability to process large datasets with artificial intelligence and cross-reference biometric information with internet data. Telecommunications content collected for strategic intelligence purposes could be retained for up to six months, while communications data such as IP addresses could be retained for up to twelve months.
An intelligence agency that can collect more information is more powerful. An agency that can manipulate data, delete data, conduct offensive cyber operations or sabotage targets abroad becomes an instrument capable of exercising power, rather than simply informing those who exercise it.
In continental Europe, where historical experience has made the concentration of coercive authority particularly sensitive, that is a very big difference.
Austria is expanding what counts as espionage
The Austrian government is approaching the matter from a different angle. It has announced plans to strengthen its legal framework against espionage. Under the existing system, foreign intelligence activity could escape criminal liability when it was directed against entities other than Austria itself.
Under the proposed changes, espionage directed against international organizations headquartered in Austria could become a criminal offense. The list includes institutions such as the International Atomic Energy Agency, the United Nations Office at Vienna, the OSCE and various EU bodies.
The definition of harm is also being revised to include activities that have the potential to damage Austria’s security and international standing or economic interests, rather than only when actual damage can be demonstrated. The law would also target the recruitment of individuals by foreign intelligence services, including so-called low-level agents.
This is another important feature of Europe’s new security politics: the security perimeter is expanding.
The Netherlands wants intelligence to act first
In August 2026, the Dutch government proposed changes to national security legislation that would broaden the powers of the General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD), and the Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD).
The proposed rules would allow the services to undertake certain proactive operations without obtaining prior permission and would facilitate greater intelligence sharing with the armed forces, other government bodies and private companies.
The government has explicitly identified China, Iran and Russia among the actors it regards as “obvious adversaries.”
It also increases private sector integration with the national security system. Technology companies, telecommunications firms and operators of critical infrastructure increasingly possess information that governments need, so the distinction between the intelligence community and the private economy is getting erased.
Sweden is rebuilding for the post-neutrality era
Sweden is undergoing its own institutional transformation.
On January 1, 2027, a new Swedish Foreign Intelligence Service, UND, is scheduled to begin operations, separating civilian foreign intelligence from military intelligence. The Swedish government argues that the division will clarify responsibilities and improve the country’s ability to assess a broader range of security threats.
Sweden’s accession to NATO fundamentally altered the country’s strategic environment, and the transformation of its intelligence architecture is a logical consequence.
Membership in NATO requires more than just military interoperability – a state needs to understand threats, produce intelligence, protect sensitive information and contribute intelligence to allies. Sweden is doing something which has become increasingly common across Europe: rebuilding national security institutions for a world in which strategic uncertainty is the baseline rather than the exception.
Brussels cannot build a European CIA – but it is building something
The irony is that the EU as a bloc remains remarkably weak when it comes to intelligence. National security is still firmly controlled by member states. Brussels can coordinate and analyze, but it does not command a conventional European intelligence service.
For decades, this was reinforced by national distrust. The EU’s most capable intelligence services preferred small circles of trusted partners. The Club de Berne, the continent’s best-known intelligence cooperation forum, has no permanent headquarters or secretariat and traditionally meets only periodically.
The situation is beginning to change. Former Finnish President Sauli Niinistö proposed in 2024 that the EU should consider a fully fledged intelligence cooperation capability, effectively a European counterpart to the CIA, capable of serving both strategic and operational needs.
Politically, that remains unrealistic. Few member states are prepared to surrender control over their most sensitive intelligence capabilities to Brussels. But that does not mean European intelligence cooperation is standing still.
Intelligence liaison officers are increasingly present in EU member states’ permanent representations in Brussels. The European External Action Service is strengthening its intelligence-analysis capacity. The EU Intelligence and Situation Centre, INTCEN, is being developed as an increasingly important channel for classified information.
INTCEN does not conduct espionage itself. It relies on intelligence supplied voluntarily by national services and turns it into strategic assessments for European decision-makers.
That model may ultimately prove more realistic than a European CIA. Rather than one giant EU intelligence service, Europe is likely to develop smaller circles of national agencies sharing sensitive information, surrounded by stronger EU-level coordination and analytical institutions.
The real question is who controls the new power
There is a danger hidden inside this whole big transformation. Western European intelligence systems are historically diverse. They developed under different constitutional traditions, experiences of war, and conceptions of the relationship between intelligence and executive authority.
Intelligence services have traditionally been expected to support executive power, not become executive power themselves.
Giving intelligence agencies the ability to conduct offensive cyber operations, manipulate information, disrupt hostile networks or conduct sabotage may be justified under carefully defined circumstances. But every new capability raises the same questions: Who authorizes it? Who supervises it? Who can challenge it? What happens when a government wants to revise the perception of external threats?
Europe is becoming a security state
Western Europe has legitimate reasons to strengthen its capacity to detect and disrupt threats. The strategic environment is more competitive. Cyber operations have become routine instruments of statecraft. Intelligence warfare increasingly targets companies, infrastructure, political institutions and individuals rather than simply military installations.
But the transformation should be watched closely. Europe’s intelligence revolution is happening through dozens of apparently technical decisions: a longer data-retention period here, a broader definition of espionage there, new cyber authorities somewhere else, closer cooperation with private companies, a new intelligence office in Brussels.
There is no single European ‘Intelligence Act,’ but there does not need to be one. The security state can expand incrementally – which may be exactly what is happening now.
The strategic shock created by the Ukraine war and uncertainty over America’s future role has accelerated a process that was already underway. European governments are concluding that they need more independent intelligence capacity, more operational flexibility and tighter cooperation among themselves.
The likely result will not be a European CIA. It will be something more distinctly European: powerful national intelligence services operating in increasingly dense networks, supported by a stronger Brussels-based analytical and coordinating layer.
The continent is giving its spies teeth. The next question is whether it will also build strong enough institutions to decide when – and against whom – they may bite.

articles.title: Ukraine to Resume Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries – Zelensky
articles.body:
Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after a three-day pause urged by the United States.
The Financial Times reports.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine is no longer restricted from carrying out such attacks.
According to him, Ukraine refrained from attacking Russian energy infrastructure for three days at Washington’s request. Meanwhile, Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy facilities.
Zelensky also noted that Russian attacks had killed more than 100 civilians over the past week.
The President of Ukraine said that U.S. officials had warned the Ukrainian military that intelligence sharing could be suspended if Ukraine did not halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Later, the U.S. side attributed the problems with information sharing to technical glitches.
Zelensky also linked restrictions on Starlink services to pressure on Ukraine. According to him, disruptions to satellite communications complicated frontline operations and strikes on Russian military targets at medium range.
The President said Ukraine could agree to another pause in strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, even if Russia continued attacking Ukrainian facilities.
However, Kyiv would demand additional interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems from the United States in exchange for agreeing to such a pause.
Militarnyi previously reported that despite the energy truce announced by the U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes against energy facilities in Kyiv, including the CHPP-4 thermal power plant, during the night of October 14.
In addition, on the night of October 14, SpaceX restricted the operating speed of Starlink terminals while in motion, affecting the work of Ukrainian strike drones and interceptor drones.

articles.title: US has warned Ukraine data sharing will cease in event of new strikes on Russia – The Washington Post
articles.body:
US has warned Ukraine data sharing will cease in event of new strikes on Russia – The Washington Post
US intelligence officials warned the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington that the US would immediately halt all intelligence sharing in the event of new strikes against Russian energy facilities.
Source: The Washington Post, citing an informed source
Details: According to the WP's interlocutor, the warnings from the US were sweeping.
"The warnings were so widespread that anyone with a Ukrainian-sounding last name got a call," the source noted.
On Tuesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian generals had received threats from Donald Trump's administration regarding a halt to intelligence sharing.
Trump himself claimed on Tuesday 13 October that information sharing would continue.
"We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end," the US president stated.
Anxiety regarding a cessation of intelligence sharing arose after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv overnight into Tuesday and Wednesday without prior warning for Ukrainian air defence systems.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy commented regarding the strikes.
The president reported that on the night of 13-14 October, the Russians launched 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 strike drones. Russian missiles hit energy facilities in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv.
Background:
- On 11 October, Trump published a post on his social media Truth Social announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which allegedly took effect immediately. He said that both sides had consented to cease strikes on energy infrastructure, although neither party had been informed of this.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that Ukraine supports it.
- On the nights of 12-13 and 13-14 October, Russian forces launched massive attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities.
- Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, commenting on overnight Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, said Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin has rejected the US-proposed "energy ceasefire". Zelenskyy later called the Russian strikes entirely deliberate.

articles.title: US arms supplied to Ukraine found in war-torn Sudan – Moscow
articles.body:
US arms supplied to Ukraine found in war-torn Sudan – Moscow
Weapons supplied to Ukraine from US military stocks have been found in the possession of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a senior Russian diplomat has said, citing markings linking them to deliveries to Kiev.
Yulia Zhdanova, head of Russia’s delegation to the Vienna Negotiations on Military Security and Arms Control, made the statement on Wednesday at a meeting of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s Forum for Security Co-operation.
Sudanese troops recovered MK19 automatic grenade launchers, M72 anti-tank weapons, and Swedish-made AT4 launchers during an operation near Bara, she said, according to TASS. “A preliminary examination of the markings revealed that these weapons were donated to the Ukrainian Armed Forces in December 2024 from US military stock,” Zhdanova said.
Sudan’s army and the RSF have been at war since April 2023, forcing millions from their homes and exposing civilians to bombardment, hunger, and widespread abuses. In June last year, Sudanese Foreign Ministry official Muhammad Al-Sirr told RT that Ukraine was supplying drones to the paramilitary forces at very low prices and helping its fighters use the technology to strike Sudanese infrastructure.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
Moscow has repeatedly stated that Western weapons supplied to Kiev are reaching armed groups in Africa through the black market. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova raised the alarm as early as 2022, warning that Stinger missiles, Javelin anti-tank systems, and grenade launchers could enter illicit trading networks worldwide.
In February, Russia’s UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia addressed the issue at a Security Council meeting, where he also accused Kiev of directly supplying weapons, including drones, and training militants in the Sahel. Zhdanova previously blamed corruption in Ukraine and failures to track Western-supplied military equipment for weapons reaching terrorists and criminal groups in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.
Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso jointly appealed to the UN Security Council in August 2024, accusing Ukraine of supporting international terrorism following a deadly ambush on Malian forces near Tinzaouaten. Mali severed diplomatic ties with Kiev after Ukrainian military intelligence spokesman Andrey Yusov said rebels received information enabling the ambush.
Addressing the UN General Assembly last month, Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop renewed the accusations, saying Ukraine was backing armed groups undermining his country’s territorial integrity. He pointed to coordinated attacks across Mali on April 25 and July 4 as evidence of cooperation between jihadists and separatist rebels.
Last week, AFP reported that sources within the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), a Tuareg-led separatist rebel coalition fighting Mali’s government, acknowledged receiving Ukrainian training, including instruction in operating drones.

articles.title: 'Mother of all bombs': US potential Iran strike plans include largest non-nuclear weapon - report
articles.body:
The United States military has developed strike plans against Iran that include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), colloquially known as the "mother of all bombs," the largest non-nuclear weapon in the US arsenal, CNN reported on Thursday.
According to CNN, multiple US officials said that the plans called for the MOAB to be used against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain.
Another source said that the phrasing used in the plan was that the attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” meaning that the US might strike Iran and then immediately pull its forces out of the region.
Several of US President Donald Trump's advisors have also told CNN that, despite Trump's claims that he would not take further action against Iran before the US midterms, it remains unclear whether he will change his mind before Election Day.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN that questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
MOAB unlikely to penetrate Iranian nuclear sites
According to several sources, the MOAB likely would be unable to penetrate deep below the ground, where Iranian nuclear facilities, such as Pickaxe Mountain, are believed to be.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” one source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”
The source said the MOAB's main tactical advantage in this scenario would be its psychological effect on Iran.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level… you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the source said.
When asked about the plan, a White House official told CNN that “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” adding that they do not comment on sensitive military plans.
A Pentagon official told CNN that it "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump Says Leakers ‘Should Be Shot’ and Rails Against Media at Rally
articles.body:
President Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that people who leak sensitive information about the government to the media “should be shot,” calling them the “scum of the earth.”
“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said Wednesday during a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
Trump’s remark came as he described a planned raid on Iran that he said had to be delayed after somebody “leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.” He appeared to be referring to Operation Midnight Hammer in June last year, when the U.S., in a surprise attack, struck three of Iran’s most critical nuclear sites as Tehran was in a 12-day war with Israel.
In the wake of the June attack, a leaked Defense Intelligence Agency preliminary report found that Iran’s nuclear sites had not been as damaged as the Trump Administration first claimed them to be and that Iran could still enrich uranium. Reports also said Iran may have also moved enriched material from the facilities before the attack.
“Somebody leaked—some sleazebag,” the President said. “They ought to go to jail and be shot. For the rest of their life, They should be in jail. But they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in the New York Times, CNN.”
Moments later, Trump pointed to the journalists covering his rally and said they were “almost as bad” as leakers. “They leak false information,” the President said. “That makes them a leaker, right?”
Trump’s long-held view that leakers are bad—most of the time
Leakers have incensed Trump even before he was President. In a 2010 clip previewing the radio show of Fox News’ Brian Kilmeade, Trump assailed WikiLeaks, which, at the time, had just released hundreds of thousands of classified U.S. military and diplomatic documents provided by Army private Chelsea Manning. “I think it’s disgraceful,” he told Kilmeade. “I think there should be like death penalty or something.”
As a civilian flirting with the U.S.’s top job, he frequently lashed out at former National Security Agency intelligence contractor Edward Snowden on social media and in public remarks. Snowden’s leaks in 2013 revealed NSA programs that sparked a global debate about government surveillance. Trump, in reaction to the leaks, said that he was a “spy” who “should be executed.”
As President, when the New York Times reported in 2017 that his campaign had repeated contacts with senior Russian intelligence officials in the year before the 2016 presidential election, Trump took to then-Twitter to lament how “leaking, and even illegal classified leaking, has been a big problem in Washington for years” and raged that such leakers “will be caught.”
When a whistleblower came forward in 2019 with a complaint alleging that Trump was "using the power of his office to solicit interference from a foreign country" in the 2020 U.S. election, Trump told the staff of the U.S. mission to the U.N. that he wanted to know who gave the whistleblower information. “That’s close to a spy,” he said. “You know what we used to do in the old days when we were smart, right, with spies and treason, right? We used to handle them a little differently than we do now.”
But Trump has welcomed leaks that benefit him politically. Days before the 2016 presidential election, at a rally in Wilmington, Ohio, he celebrated how WikiLeaks released private emails from John Podesta, the campaign chair of his Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton, as well as emails from the Democratic National Committee. “Boy, I love reading those WikiLeaks!” Trump said. He also mused about Russia having hacked into Clinton’s email, and urged them to publish what they may have found. Trump even said that he could be a fan of Snowden if he released former President Barack Obama’s birth records at a time when conspiracy theories largely fanned by Trump hounded the Democratic former President.
Trump Administration tries to crack down on leaks
The second Trump Administration has since stepped up to limit leaks to the press. When reports of the U.S.’s dwindling ammunition stockpiles amid the war with Iran emerged, the Pentagon subjected dozens of civilian employees and military officers to polygraph tests to identify the source of the leak. Trump had called for the leakers to face long-term jail sentences.
Journalists from the Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post received subpoenas after reporting on national security issues. But the news organizations pushed back against those summons, and the Justice Department withdrew them. In January, the FBI raided a Post reporter’s home, as part of an investigation into a government contractor accused of mishandling sensitive national security information.
The Justice Department has also charged alleged leakers: in April, the department announced it arrested a former Army employee, alleging that she transmitted classified national defense information to unauthorized recipients, including a journalist.
The Defense Department also threatened to withhold Pentagon access to journalists unless they signed an agreement not to publish unauthorized material. Much of the Pentagon press corps declined, and a federal judge sided with the press in March, striking several parts of the department’s press access policy.
Trump has wanted others “shot” too
It’s also not the first time that Trump has floated having certain people shot .
Three years ago, at a California lunch with Republicans, Trump said he was in favor of shooting store robbers and looters, painting himself as tough on crime before the 2024 elections. “They actually go and take everything out of the store, and then you see these guys selling stuff five miles away or selling it from behind cars. It's a horrible thing. When the police are allowed to do their job—and that means, in some cases, shoot them—this will stop immediately.”
The President has also previously pitched shooting migrants to keep them from entering the country. According to the book Border Wars: Inside Trump's Assault on Immigration, by New York Times reporters Michael D. Shear and Julie Hirschfeld Davis, Trump in March 2019 detailed extreme methods to keep them out, privately suggesting to aides that soldiers shoot migrants who cross the border in the legs. But he was told it would not be allowed. Trump addressed the allegations on social media, saying: “I may be tough on Border Security, but not that tough.”
He’s also suggested doing the same to protesters: during the George Floyd protests in the spring of 2020, Trump was reportedly enraged, and, according to his first-term Defense Secretary Mark Esper, the President also considered ordering the military to shoot the racial justice protesters in the legs.
Last week, the President approved what would be the U.S. Army’s first execution of a soldier via firing squad since World War II, and has even shown enthusiasm for livestreaming it. Trump, however, has since changed his tune, amid a chorus of negative feedback.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday. “‘Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

articles.title: King Charles Welcomes Zelensky as Britain Steps Up Military Support for Ukraine
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday, Oct. 14, before holding talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as London pledged faster air defense missile deliveries and tougher sanctions against Russia amid strained US-Ukraine relations.
King Charles received Zelensky for a private audience at Buckingham Palace, underscoring Britain’s continued support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience,” Zelensky said afterward, expressing appreciation for the monarch’s unwavering support and Britain’s assistance to Ukraine.
Britain pledges more missiles and sanctions
Following the royal audience, Burnham welcomed Zelensky to Downing Street with a ceremonial guard of honor involving the Irish Guards.
“We are behind you and that will not change,” Burnham told the Ukrainian president.
Britain announced plans to accelerate a £45 million (approximately $60 million) package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses against Russian drones, including increasingly fast jet-powered models.
The government will bring forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet urgent winter requirements.
London also pledged additional sanctions against Moscow, including restrictions targeting maritime services supporting Russian liquefied natural gas exports.
Burnham said his government would continue providing military and financial support while pressing international partners to increase pressure on Russia.
General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
Burnham seeks to repair US-Ukraine ties
Before meeting Zelensky, Burnham told Parliament he would seek to “repair bridges” between Trump and the Ukrainian president to restore American support.
Despite criticizing Washington’s recent decisions, Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv remained committed to its US partnership.
“We count on our partnership with the United States,” he told Burnham.
“We just want to be very honest, very clear, be strong partners.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan, Zelensky said he believed the overnight Starlink restrictions were not caused by technical problems.
“We are professionals. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he said.
He warned that Starlink restrictions weakened Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones, while separate disruptions in US intelligence-sharing left Ukraine without advance warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, putting civilian lives at greater risk.
