articles.title: Zelenskyy: 850 Shaheds came as Starlink limits hit defense
articles.body:
- Zelenskyy said Russia launched over 850 Shaheds between Oct. 14 and 9 a.m. Oct. 15, during a SpaceX speed cap on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals.
- The 160 km/h Starshield limit, imposed overnight Oct. 13–14, cripples interceptor drones needed against Russian jet-powered Shaheds flying up to 600 km/h.
Russia launched more than 850 Shahed attack drones at Ukraine in roughly a day and a half, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 15, an onslaught that came as a new speed cap on SpaceX’s Starlink network curtailed the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to shoot them down.
Zelenskyy said the count covered the period from the start of Oct. 14 until 9 a.m. on Oct. 15. He said attacks came in constant waves and that Ukrainian airspace was not free of drones for a single hour. Russian strikes killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three more in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian media reported.
“From the start of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there have already been more than 850 Shaheds, and this is precisely at a time of an artificial speed restriction on our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelenskyy said, in remarks translated from Ukrainian.
The restriction he referred to took effect overnight on Oct. 13–14, when SpaceX capped Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s armed forces, at 160 km/h (about 100 mph) for terminals in motion. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said SpaceX imposed the limit unilaterally and without warning, and that any terminal moving faster than that loses its connection, disrupting interceptor and mid-range drone missions as well as frontline reconnaissance, logistics and signal relays.
Under the cap, the restriction falls most heavily on Ukraine’s air defense. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), so interceptors that must chase them down need far more speed than 160 km/h. Starlink has been blocked over Russian territory since February 2026 under a whitelist of approved terminals, and Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian targets rely on other communications. The capped terminals instead serve tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles operating over Ukraine and the occupied territories, which means the limit cuts into Ukraine’s defense.
Service was later restored below the 160 km/h threshold, and Mykhailo Fedorov said attack and interceptor drones should be able to fly again, while adding that Ukraine now needs the Starshield speed limit removed altogether.
Elon Musk said on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the U.S. president, the Associated Press reported, while the White House told Kyiv it does not control SpaceX, according to Axios. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times on Oct. 15 that the restriction was a deliberate decision on the American side rather than a technical fault, though he said he did not know whether SpaceX or the U.S. government made the call.
Zelenskyy also accused Moscow of escalating its strikes after seeing sanctions eased and attempts to pressure Kyiv, and urged Americans to side with Ukraine’s defense instead of the aggressor.
The Defense Ministry said it is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners and is setting up backup communication channels, but neither SpaceX nor the U.S. Department of War has said whether or when the 160 km/h cap will be lifted.

articles.title: Leakers should be shot – Trump
articles.body:
Leakers should be shot – Trump
Government employees sharing confidential information with journalists should face the death penalty, US President Donald Trump has said.
Addressing supporters during a midterm rally in Bullhead City, Arizona on Wednesday, Trump cited an occasion when the Pentagon allegedly had to put off an air raid against Iran after the bombers’ departure and arrival times were leaked to the press, including the New York Times and CNN.
It was not immediately clear which military operation Trump was referring to, although several media outlets conjectured that he was speaking about last year’s bombing campaign targeting Iran’s underground nuclear facilities.
“Somebody leaked – some sleazebag,” Trump said, adding that “they ought to go to jail and be shot.”
He argued that “in the old days we used to shoot leakers… [especially] when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
“The leakers are the scum of the earth,” Trump concluded.
Since the start of the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran in late February, the Republican leader has repeatedly lashed out at government officials leaking information to the press as well as media outlets publishing such materials.
“Keep on leaking you dirty dogs! When we find you, you will pay a big price,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post last month in response to media reports claiming that some of his aides had advised him against attacking Tehran.
In August, the US president similarly accused leakers of making “treasonous statements,” saying that they were “being hunted down” and that “long term jail sentences will be sought!”
The tirade was prompted by a Washington Post report alleging that Trump was frustrated with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth for providing misleading information about supposed ammunition shortages, especially with respect to long-range missiles and air defense interceptors.
Trump dismissed the allegations as “completely FALSE,” insisting that the “US has massive amounts of ‘munitions’,” with yet more being produced and supplied, as needed.
The New York Times subsequently reported that the Pentagon had subjected dozens of civilian employees and military officers to polygraph tests in a bid to identify the source of the leak regarding the supposed ammunition shortages.
In April, Trump demanded that the journalist who had reported the details of a rescue mission for the two crew members of the US F-15E Strike Eagle, which was shot down over Iran, divulge their sources or face jail. The US president suggested that the leak had put one of the service members’ lives in danger.

articles.title: What is the 'mother of all bombs' the US could use against Iran?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What is the 'mother of all bombs' the US is considering to use against Iran?
The United States is considering using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iran as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military strikes, raising questions about its devastating impact and whether it could penetrate Tehran's heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
According to a CNN report on Thursday, US military planners have drawn up options involving the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the "mother of all bombs" or MOAB, to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
The plans reportedly include possible strikes on Pickaxe Mountain, an underground facility near Natanz where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear programme.
The reported plans come as Trump faces mounting pressure to end the war with Iran, with negotiations stalled and the US president seeking a way to bring the conflict to a close without appearing to concede defeat.
No decision to deploy the bomb has been announced, and the White House has said Trump is keeping all options available.
Here is what to know about the weapon, its destructive capabilities and why the US is considering using it against Iran.
What is the 'mother of all bombs'?
The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) is the most powerful conventional bomb in the US military's arsenal.
Weighing approximately 9,800 kilograms (21,600 pounds) and measuring more than nine metres in length, the GPS-guided weapon was developed by the US Air Force in 2003 ahead of the American invasion of Iraq.
Unlike conventional bombs designed to penetrate fortified underground structures, the MOAB is an air-blast weapon that detonates above the ground, generating an enormous explosion across a wide area.
During testing in March 2003, the explosion produced a mushroom cloud visible from approximately 20 miles away.
The weapon was originally designed to destroy large concentrations of troops, military equipment and above-ground fortifications, although its potential targets later expanded to include caves and tunnels.
How destructive is the bomb?
The MOAB is capable of devastating large areas through an immense blast wave that can destroy buildings, military installations and other structures.
The weapon can devastate an area equivalent to approximately nine city blocks, according to the CNN report, although the actual extent of destruction depends on the terrain, surrounding structures and other conditions.
Despite its enormous size, the MOAB is not a nuclear weapon and does not produce the radioactive fallout associated with a nuclear explosion.
The bomb is GPS-guided and is delivered from a military transport aircraft rather than a conventional fighter jet. During its first combat deployment, it was dropped from an American MC-130 aircraft.
Its enormous size and destructive capabilities have also made it a tool of psychological warfare, with US military officials originally hoping that the threat of its use would intimidate enemy forces into surrendering.
Has the 'mother of all bombs' been used before?
Yes. The United States first deployed the MOAB in combat in April 2017, during Trump's first presidential term.
The bomb was dropped on a network of tunnels used by Islamic State (IS) militants in Afghanistan's eastern Nangarhar province, near the border with Pakistan.
The US military said the strike targeted underground tunnels and caves used by IS fighters to move between positions and launch attacks against Afghan and US forces.
Afghan officials reported that 36 IS fighters were killed and three underground tunnels destroyed, along with weapons and ammunition.
US and Afghan officials said at the time that no civilians were killed, although the strike attracted criticism over the use of such an enormous weapon.
Former Afghan President Hamid Karzai condemned the bombing, accusing Washington of using Afghanistan as a testing ground for destructive weapons.
Trump praised the operation at the time, describing it as "another successful job".
The 2017 strike remains the only publicly acknowledged combat use of the MOAB.
Why is Trump considering using it against Iran?
The reported plans come amid uncertainty over how Washington intends to end the conflict after more than six months of US military operations against Iran.
According to CNN, some Trump administration officials have discussed launching a final round of strikes before withdrawing American forces from the region, potentially allowing the president to present the operation as a military victory.
One source familiar with the plans said the proposed attacks could take place before a US military withdrawal from the region covered by Central Command.
The MOAB's psychological impact could also be a factor, with officials suggesting that its deployment could demonstrate overwhelming American military power and increase pressure on Tehran.
However, sources familiar with the discussions have questioned whether such an operation would achieve Washington's strategic objectives or bring the conflict any closer to an end.
Trump has publicly suggested he would refrain from additional military action before November's US midterm elections, although advisers reportedly remain uncertain whether he will maintain that position.
Could the bomb destroy Iran's underground nuclear facilities?
Military officials have expressed serious doubts about whether the MOAB could destroy Iran's most heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
Unlike specialised bunker-busting weapons, the MOAB is designed to unleash a massive explosion across the surface rather than penetrate deeply underground.
Pickaxe Mountain, for example, is believed to be protected by substantial layers of granite, potentially shielding its underground facilities from the bomb's effects.
The US possesses another weapon specifically designed for such targets: the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP), which can penetrate hardened underground structures before detonating.
American B-2 bombers deployed 14 of these penetrator bombs during US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025, according to a US Department of Defense report.
The difference highlights a central question surrounding the reported plans: whether deploying the MOAB would inflict meaningful damage on Iran's nuclear programme or primarily serve as a show of force.
What would be the consequences of using it against Iran?
Deploying the MOAB against Iran would represent a significant escalation in the conflict, particularly if the weapon were used against energy infrastructure or facilities near populated areas.
Its enormous blast could cause widespread destruction, while damage to electricity supplies, industrial installations and other essential infrastructure could have consequences far beyond the immediate target.
The International Committee of the Red Cross has warned that explosive weapons with wide-area effects are particularly dangerous in populated areas because their impact can extend beyond intended military targets.
Such attacks can kill and injure civilians, destroy homes and disrupt services essential for survival, including water, electricity and healthcare.
The US military's use of the MOAB would also raise serious questions under international humanitarian law, which requires attacks to distinguish between military objectives and civilians, prohibits disproportionate civilian harm and obliges forces to take feasible precautions to protect civilians.

articles.title: Meink: Operational Prototypes for MMA Drones Coming in 2028
articles.body:
The Air Force will field operational prototypes for an autonomous drone to replace its MQ-9 Reaper in 2028, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said Oct. 14.
“We’re going to be fielding operational prototypes by ’28, and we’re just awarding the contract now,” Meink said during a panel discussion with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, other service secretaries, and senior Pentagon officials at the annual AUSA conference in Washington. “That’s the speed of what we’re fielding capability, and into production—large-scale production—starting in ’29. That is the goal.”
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that Meink was referring to the Massed Modular Aircraft, the planned successor to the Reaper.
“The autonomous fighters are already in production,” Meink said, in reference to the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury have been selected for production and are undergoing testing with the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev.
“Now we’re looking at essentially the autonomous strike platform, the autonomous bomber,” Meink said, referring to MMA. The aircraft is envisioned as a multimission aircraft, like the MQ-9, that can conduct strike missions as well as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. In contrast, CCAs are currently focused on an air-to-air role paired with crewed fighters.
Meink previously announced at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the Air Force would field 100 MMAs by 2029 and 500 by 2032.
Air & Space Forces Magazine reported Sept. 30 that the Air Force and Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit had narrowed the field for MMA down to seven companies. An Air Force spokesperson declined to confirm any selections, but Meink said Oct. 14 that “we just awarded those contracts … in collaboration with DIU.” He did not name the specific companies or say how many finalists there are.
Sources have told Air & Space Force Magazine the seven companies still in contention are Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero. They will develop their MMA candidates and submit a proposal to build a prototype.
The Air Force and DIU want each MMA drone to cost $10 million for the base aircraft, not counting the sensors, weapons, or other equipment it may carry. That’s half the $20 million target price the Air Force envisions for CCAs. MMAs will also use open architecture so they could be more easily upgraded with new sensor packages or weapons capabilities.
But while MMAs will have some autonomous capabilities, they won’t be built with all the latest cutting-edge technology in a bid to keep their price down below that of CCAs. They will likely be powered by turboprop engines, for example.
MMA drones are intended to be able to fly about 4,000 miles, twice the range of CCAs, and carry a heavier payload than CCAs. But they will be slower than CCAs.
The MMA effort is part of the broader push by the Pentagon and the Air Force to field more autonomous systems at a lower cost than crewed platforms, or even the drones that are in service today. The goal is to build “combat mass” to counter China’s growing military, which Meink said is going through “the largest weapons buildup probably in the history of the world,” and to respond to the proliferation of autonomous systems in conflicts of today, and the Pentagon’s view, tomorrow.
“There’s no question that there’s a shift coming,” Meink said. “It’s adaptability, scalability, and affordability. The only way we’re going to meet the threat is with autonomous systems.”
Meink said the Pentagon will work with Congress to secure the funding needed for MMA. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request for the Department of Defense is currently stalled on Capitol Hill. With midterm elections approaching next month, Democrats could take control of one or both chambers, which could lead to congressional gridlock, particularly surrounding the Pentagon’s request for a massive budget increase—and plans to continue that—amid the war with Iran. The DOD plans to devote tens of billions to autonomous warfare just this fiscal year.
Meink acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the Pentagon’s budget, but expressed confidence the Air Force would be able to hit its targets for MMA.
“It is heavily dependent upon the resources we get from the Hill, but I think we are not only going to deliver significant combat capability, but we’re going to deliver quickly and efficiently,” Meink said.
“We’ve got to make sure this stuff is affordable,” Meink added, referring to efforts across the Air Force and Space Force. “We’ve got to make sure we’re buying it efficiently. And depending on how you do the comparisons, we’re talking five to 10 times cheaper to field some combat power with these autonomous systems compared to not. So it’s critically important. The good news is, in my mind, there’s no question that the leadership we have in the Air Force, in the Space Force, both military and civilian, is ready to do that. And you see that with the results already. We are integrating autonomous fighters into experimental ops units out at Creech right now, from a year from when they first flew to when we were integrating them into experimental ops units. That’s unheard of. And it only took two years to build the first one.”
The goal for MMA is similarly ambitious.
“It’s in the scalability and the producibility,” Meink said. “In many ways, cost goes with schedule. If something is super expensive, there’s a reason for it, which means it’s probably going to take a long time to build, so we’re really focusing on rapid production and scalability, which means we have to get the cost down on these systems as well.”
Meink’s comments came during a panel focused on the Pentagon’s Project Agincourt, a drive to accelerate the fielding of autonomous systems and create a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, which Hegseth announced during a speech late last month.
“The folks who acquire it need to be right there up with the warfighter at the same time who understand how to iterate it and change on and innovate on it,” Hegseth said.
Adversaries such as Russia and Iran have fielded one-way drone attacks to wreak havoc in Ukraine and across the Middle East. Ukraine has used autonomous systems to great effect to defend against Russia’s invasion. Kyiv’s ongoing and thus far successful Operation Vivaldi offensive has relied heavily on the innovative use of drones, including dropping uncrewed ground vehicles behind enemy lines.
“That’s a different battlefield,” Hegseth said. “We’ve learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can’t use everything that’s in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it. So you’ve got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned … and then push it through [with] an AUTOWARCOM commander with four stars who has the ability to drive that change. So we’ve done a lot with acquisitions and a lot with industry from day one to modernize, realizing this is the future of warfare.”

articles.title: Zelensky discusses new air defense packages with Rutte
articles.body:
Zelensky discusses new air defense packages with Rutte
The Ukrainian president announced the meeting on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
"I began my visit to Brussels with a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. As always, we are coordinating closely to provide greater protection and security for Ukraine," Zelensky wrote.
He noted that Russia had responded to another attempt by the U.S. president to reduce the intensity of attacks by launching new waves of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure, residential buildings, and other facilities.
"Over the past few days, there have been several waves of ballistic missile strikes, and attack 'shahed' drones are in our skies almost constantly. Since midnight yesterday and up to now, the Russians have already launched around 1,000 drones," he emphasized.
The president said these attacks posed significant challenges, particularly amid restrictions affecting Starlink operations in Ukraine. In this context, Zelensky stressed, "it is so important that defense supplies from NATO partners continue."
"This is especially true for ballistic missile interceptors and munitions for F-16s. We are working on new air defense packages. Literally every day and every hour, such new packages can save the lives of Ukrainians. We discussed this and other important issues during our meeting. I thank Mark for his support and readiness to help" the president said.
As Ukrinform previously reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Brussels to participate in the European Union summit. Several important bilateral meetings were also scheduled during his visit.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: The fall of the “Godfather”: How Putin’s former bodyguard helped bring down an FSB general
articles.body:
Whether by coincidence or not, soon after 67-year-old Sergei Alpatov stepped down from his post as head of the FSB’s Economic Security Service “for health reasons,” his subordinate, General Alexander Kumanyaev, was taken into custody — as was Maxim Denisov, head of the FSB directorate in the Yaroslavl Region. Arrests of FSB generals at this level are extremely rare. Formally, both are accused of protecting major construction contractors, extortion, and using classified information for personal gain. But sources who spoke to The Insider believe corruption was only a pretext for the arrests of both men. The real reason, they say, was that Kumanyaev and Denisov “went after” a major construction company whose founders are tied to Alexei Dyumin, Vladimir Putin’s former bodyguard and one of his closest allies.
“He thought he had God by the beard”
The Insider found that for several years, FSB General Alexander Kumanyaev provided protection to the EKS group of companies, a contractor handling hundreds of billions of rubles in public funds. The security official shielded the company’s financial activities from inspections by various oversight bodies and put pressure on competitors.
For example, in 2019, the Moscow office of Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service found that EKS had entered into a cartel agreement with JSC Everest Financial Group, LLC EKS, and LLC Esterplast to coordinate participation in 428 auctions involving Mosvodokanal, Moscow’s water utility, and received 10 billion rubles ($117.5 million) through artificially inflated or reduced bids. LLC EKS and LLC Esterplast, which took part in the cartel scheme, created the appearance of competition. The case was registered as administrative proceeding No. 077/01/11-19037/2019.
Everest’s founder is listed as Denis Kulakov, a native of Kumanyaev’s home region of Saratov. In reality, he served as deputy CEO of the EKS group. The general’s wife, Oksana Kumanyaeva, worked as Everest’s accountant. Investigators allege that billions of rubles ended up in her secret bank accounts.
The case appeared headed toward criminal charges, but according to a source, Kumanyaev blocked the investigation. As a result, the companies escaped with relatively small fines and later increased their turnover many times over.
Everest, whose management cadres included Kumanyaev’s fellow Saratov native Kulakov and his wife Oksana, built 400 facilities for government departments including the Defense Ministry, Interior Ministry, Emergency Situations Ministry, and Moscow government, and supplied diesel fuel to the FSB. Another 250 contracts are currently being carried out. The company reported revenue of 10 billion rubles ($117.5 million) in 2025.
The owner of another company involved in the cartel, JSC GC EKS, is Alexei Vlasov, a reserve officer in Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Vlasov graduated from the Defense Ministry’s Military University and previously conducted espionage work in Portugal and Brazil. During the antitrust proceedings, company founders Vlasov and Kulakov insisted they did not know one another. However, telephone billing records obtained by The Insider indicate otherwise: the two spoke both before and after the auctions.
GC EKS, which Kumanyaev was protecting, had previously repaired boiler houses in Moscow and later worked on construction projects in Smolensk. It registered in Yaroslavl in 2017 at a time when the region was headed by Dmitry Mironov, a former Putin bodyguard. Its sole founder was Maxim Krylov, another graduate of the Defense Ministry’s Military University. Krylov later receded from public view after a series of scandals, but he nevertheless still controls the company. In 2014, Putin awarded Krylov the Medal of the Order “For Merit to the Fatherland,” Second Class, and in 2015 presented him with the Order of Alexander Nevsky.
In 2018, the owners of GC EKS were also caught on camera during a Moscow traffic police operation targeting drivers who were illegally using government emergency vehicles as VIP taxis — Krylov and Vlasov were found inside an Emergency Situations Ministry vehicle with its flashing light activated. A correspondent from the Kremlin-controlled news channel Rossiya-24 arrived on the scene in time to pose a question, to which the businessmen gave an incoherent answer.
After GC EKS “registered” in Yaroslavl, it received a flood of state contracts. Over the past seven years, the company has completed 2,500 projects for clients including Moscow’s City Hall, the FSB, the Emergency Situations Ministry, the Defense Ministry, the Health and Social Development Ministry, the Culture Ministry, Gazprom, Rosavtodor, the Education and Science Ministry, the Russian Orthodox Church, and the governments of the Leningrad, Murmansk, Kaliningrad, Smolensk, and Nizhny Novgorod regions.
In Tula, where former Putin bodyguard Alexei Dyumin was serving as governor, GC EKS built a perinatal center for 2.4 billion rubles ($28.2 million) — and the governor personally visited the construction site. In Yaroslavl, the company built a volleyball center, a children’s clinic, a new wing of an oncology center, and an ice complex in the Nekrasov District. Regional head Dmitry Mironov attended ceremonial events where time capsules were laid for future generations.
GC EKS also has 12 branches across Russia and opened new offices in occupied Donetsk and Mariupol. In 2025, the company earned 260 billion rubles ($3.0 billion). In most of its projects, it served as the sole-source supplier.
In August 2026, Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed head of annexed Crimea, designated GC EKS as the sole contractor for construction of a gas pipeline to the large “Golden Sands of Russia” resort between Saky and Yevpatoria. The project is valued at nearly 739 million rubles ($8.7 million).
“What is there to be surprised about? They are kings of state contracts, and they have everything sewn up at every level. Everyone knows the company’s founders are on close terms with former Putin bodyguards Mironov and Dyumin. They also know Nikolai Patrushev, Shoigu, Sobyanin, Mikhalkov, and the Rotenbergs. Our lawmaker from the Yaroslavl region, Valentina Tereshkova, is always ready to help. And General Kumanyaev personally had ‘explanatory conversations’ with particularly stubborn competitors. He really thought he had God by the beard. If an ordinary general was moving billions around, imagine the sums they deal with at Lubyanka,” a Yaroslavl businessman who said he had been barred several times from auctions involving GC EKS told The Insider.
Ingushetia and Yaroslavl
Alexander Kumanyaev began his career in the security services in 1994 with the FSB directorate in the Saratov region, where he acquired the nickname “Kum” (which roughly translates as “godfather”). After studying at the FSB Academy, Kumanyaev returned to Saratov and was appointed deputy head of the regional directorate. In 2014, then-Colonel Kumanyaev was transferred to Ingushetia, where he became head of the FSB directorate, military unit 29535.
There was a long line inside the FSB to get assigned to Ingushetia, as the republic was considered a “hot spot.” Even a short deployment there could bring another star on an officer’s shoulder boards and awards for supposed participation in combat (even if FSB officers rarely left the military compound in the region’s capital, Magas).
Local residents remembered Kumanyaev as an official who repeatedly announced counterterrorism operations in different parts of the republic.
In Ingushetia, Kumanyaev was remembered as an official who repeatedly announced counterterrorism operations
In June 2018, trouble began to gather around Kumanyaev, who by then had been promoted to general. During a special operation in Nazran, his subordinates shot dead Madina Ayupova and her two sons, Umar and Magomed, declaring them terrorists.
A day later, they beat to death Ibragim Aliyev, who had been detained during an FSB raid. When relatives asked what had happened to him, Kumanyaev said Ibragim had been killed during interrogation after allegedly shouting “Allahu Akbar” and attacking an investigator with office scissors. His body was not returned to relatives for an independent examination (officials cited an internal investigation as the reason for keeping the body).
The deaths of the four Nazran residents really did begin to look as though they could lead to a criminal case against the Russian officers themselves — and then, Kum’s patrons in the FSB personnel department hurriedly transferred him to the Yaroslavl region to head the local FSB directorate there. At his farewell, Ingushetia’s then-leader Yunus-Bek Yevkurov thanked the security official for his work fighting terrorism in the republic.
In Yaroslavl, Kumanyaev and his wife became especially close with the family of Boris Dyachenko, the former head of the FSB office in the city of Rybinsk. Dyachenko was forced into retirement in 2019 after building himself an excessively large mansion (by local standards). The families celebrated holidays together, and Dyachenko’s son Dmitry, who is well known in local criminal circles, kept Kum informed about developments in the business community.
Yaroslavl Governor Mikhail Yevraev personally congratulated Kumanyaev on his birthday, presenting him with a Badge of Honor on Security Service Workers’ Day:
“Thanks to your competent and prompt actions, 28 people were convicted and more than 50 criminal cases were opened. You secured compensation for damage from criminal activity totaling 2.3 billion rubles and prevented nearly another 1 billion rubles in losses. You created conditions for more than 250 million rubles to enter the federal budget. And, especially important now, as Russia conducts its special military operation while defending the interests of peaceful citizens, you managed to stop the illegal export of military products disguised as civilian goods and to uncover attempts by individuals to profit from fulfillment of the state defense order.”
After Kumanyaev’s arrest, however, the laudatory material was quickly removed from the regional government website, as well as from state broadcaster GTRK Yaroslaviya.
“Or it’ll be like with Navalny”
In 2021, GC EKS became embroiled in another scandal. While renovating Switzerland Park in Nizhny Novgorod, company employees Roman Asabin and Pyotr Sedelnikov failed to install the required amount of rubber crumb in the surfaces of sports and children’s playgrounds, causing an estimated 39 million rubles ($458,000) in damage.
Both construction workers were charged with large-scale fraud and placed in custody during an investigation that lasted more than three years. In February 2024, the Nizhny Novgorod District Court accepted the defendants’ expressions of remorse and gave them four-year suspended sentences with five years of probation.
In October 2020, investigative outlet Proekt began examining GC EKS after the company received $1 billion in construction contracts from Moscow City Hall. A reporter traveled to Yaroslavl but did not take into account the fact that Gen. Kumanyaev was overseeing the company. On the general’s orders, the journalist from Moscow was placed under telephone surveillance.
Soon afterward, a GC EKS employee who had met secretly with the reporter the previous day called the Proekt newsroom and said management had learned of his contact with the journalist: “Forget everything we talked about and destroy all the records if you don’t want what happened to Navalny to happen to you.” The reference was to the 2020 poisoning of Alexei Navalny.
While in Yaroslavl, the article’s author also noticed he was being followed, and his email account was subjected to phishing attacks for two days.
Reasons for the arrest
In April of this year, as part of an FSB personnel rotation, Kumanyaev was transferred to Lubyanka in order to head one of the key departments in the FSB’s Economic Security Service, a post that would have given him sweeping powers and opportunities. In Yaroslavl, he was replaced by close acquaintance Colonel Maxim Denisov, who had previously served in the FSB directorate in the Samara region.
Before moving to Moscow, Kumanyaev introduced Denisov to the same people he had worked with. Three months later, however, Denisov was removed from his post. Internal security officers from the FSB were waiting for him with handcuffs at Yaroslavsky railway station in Moscow. General Kumanyaev was arrested next and placed in Moscow’s Matrosskaya Tishina detention center. Pro-government bloggers quickly published reports claiming that the FSB had finally begun a serious fight against systemic corruption.
There are several competing explanations for the arrests of Kumanyaev and Denisov. Under the first, the case is part of the standard struggle between rival clans within the FSB leadership.
One version holds that the arrests are part of the continuing struggle among rival factions within the FSB leadership
Another version, however, concerns a senior GC EKS manager who had donated to the late Alexei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation (The Insider knows the person’s surname). During questioning by the FSB, he was threatened with prison, and the frightened businessman began identifying associates involved in corruption schemes — naming “Kum” as their patron.
The third version appears considerably more convincing: The owners of GC EKS broke their previous agreements with the FSB and refused to continue paying monthly bonuses to Colonel Denisov; Denisov then complained to his patron, and Kumanyaev began threatening the businessmen with serious trouble. The businessmen then approached Alexei Dyumin — the former Putin bodyguard who served as governor of Tula (and has since gotten a promotion that brought him to Moscow) — who gave the order to arrest the FSB officers. Several officials from different regions and a group of businessmen involved in cartel schemes are also defendants in the criminal case.
Meanwhile, Colonel Ivan Meshchan, who previously served in the Rostov Region, took over as head of the FSB directorate in Yaroslavl. Meshchan is an avid hunter and flies to Salekhard almost every summer to shoot brown bears and elk. Local residents say he is accompanied by Vasily Kryuk, a former United Russia lawmaker in the Yamalo-Nenets regional legislature who owns 194 plots of land covering a combined 359 square kilometers, roughly comparable to the land area of the Maldives.

articles.title: Why Ukrainian strikes on data centers are a real problem for Russia — and beyond
articles.body:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with members of the government via videoconference in Moscow on June 23, 2026. | Pool photo by Gavriil Grigorov via AFP/Getty Images
Ukraine’s strikes on data centers inside Russia aimed to disrupt military planning and communication services. There were also reports of another kind of disruption: to customers waiting for their dinner from food-delivery apps.
Kyiv’s drone strikes on three Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir saw delays and interruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex's cloud infrastructure, including e-commerce, digital payment platforms and apps of food delivery and car services. Ukrainian drones on Wednesday targeted a major Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region, though a senior company executive said it hadn’t affected operations.
After the strikes on Russian data centers, Kyiv noted that Moscow has already repeatedly targeted its digital infrastructure. “Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that two can play this game,” a senior official familiar with the operation told POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Advertisement
The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy.
The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill.
Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia.
“To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov.
Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences.
“These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO.
Advertisement
When servers become targets
Data centers have entered the crosshairs of other recent armed conflicts. During the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran earlier this year, drone strikes hit three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
Since data centers can serve civilian and military purposes simultaneously, the legal status of targeting them is far from straightforward.
Kubo Mačák, an expert on international humanitarian law, said a data center must meet two conditions to qualify as a military objective under the Geneva Conventions: it must make an effective contribution to military operations and destroying it must offer a “definite military advantage.”
A Yandex delivery robot moves through Moscow on Aug. 11, 2022. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images
“If you know that they are storing military intelligence or that they're using the data center to power military artificial intelligence tools,” Mačák said, there could be grounds to consider it a military objective.
Following the most recent strikes of the Yandex data centers, users on social media platform X reported a sudden drop in automated bot activity, including from accounts associated with pro-Russian, pro-Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narratives.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on the reports to boast that the strikes had made social media less toxic, even as independent researchers and national research institutes found no evidence they specifically disrupted any Russian disinformation campaigns.
Advertisement
Mačák said that even if a data center is being used to “let's say, run some trolls or these bot farms to interfere with elections abroad … that would not be sufficient.” In other words, hosting propaganda bots does not, by itself, make a data center a lawful military target.
The dual-use quandary has often focused on the targeting of energy infrastructure, which has been frequent in the Russia-Ukraine war. On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for rising fuel prices. He has since called for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, although the existence of any ceasefire agreement remains disputed.
As data centers become increasingly central to national economies, they will become more consequential targets. A senior NATO official granted anonymity to discuss the matter told POLITICO that data centers are already considered potential targets and that the alliance is factoring their vulnerability into its planning.
NATO allies recognize that their data centers could come under attack in a conflict, the official said: “We would get it in a fight.”
Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed to this report.

articles.title: Israel received Iranian, Russian weapons in secret transfer from Ukraine, fmr. ambassador says
articles.body:
Security collaboration between Israel and Ukraine is expanding, particularly in the study of Iranian weapons and Russian drones, according to former Israeli ambassador to Ukraine, Michael Brodsky.
Brodsky discussed the growing security ties earlier this week during a meeting with a delegation of Ukrainian journalists. He confirmed that the two countries are working together to study weapons used in Russia's war against Ukraine and that Israel has received several weapons from Kyiv for examination. He did not specify which weapons or systems were involved.
According to Ukrainian media reports, Israel is examining samples of Russian attack drones provided by Ukraine, including newer models from the Geran family, which are based on Iranian-made Shahed drones.
Ukrainian officials also confirmed to Maariv that the cooperation is underway, saying one of its earliest stages involved Ukraine transferring an Iranian Shahed drone to Israel. Russia has used these drones extensively in its war against Ukraine.
Israel is actively developing defenses against drones, laser-based systems, other tech
Brodsky said Israel is actively developing defenses against drones, including laser-based systems and other technologies. However, he assessed that no effective solution capable of countering all types of drones has yet been developed.
"Unmanned aerial vehicles are the number one problem for the entire world today," he told Ukrainian media outlets. "Whoever is first to find an effective solution will gain a significant advantage, and that solution will subsequently be adopted by others as well."
Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly modified its weapons, changed its tactics for penetrating air defenses, and adjusted the scale of its attacks. Ukraine has responded by developing and improving its drone detection and interception capabilities.
For Israel, Ukraine's battlefield experience is particularly relevant because Iran and its allies use weapons based on similar technology. According to Ukrainian reports, the samples provided to Israel could help researchers better understand the modifications Russia has made to its drones and develop ways to counter them.
Ukraine, meanwhile, could also benefit from Israeli expertise. Israel has extensive operational, intelligence, and technological experience in confronting Iran, including its missile and drone capabilities and other military threats in the region.
Sharing intelligence, threat assessments, and lessons learned from military operations could benefit both countries and further strengthen their security cooperation.

articles.title: Houthis target Yemen gov't headquarters in Aden
articles.body:
• Yemen's Houthis have launched a missile attack on the presidential palace in the southern city of Aden. The government - which is headquarted at the palace - said that the prime minister and other ministers were unharmed by the attack.
• Media affiliated with the group said it targeted the "headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers" at the palace.
• Major fighting continues across multiple fronts in Yemen's Taiz, with significant casualties reported on all sides.
• The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down a missile near Medina. The Houthis denied launching the attack.
• Two ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz, one hit by a projectile and the other by a sea mine, as ongoing attacks impact maritime traffic.
• Iran says it is preparing for war amid US reports that the Trump administration is mulling using its largest munitions if it resumes attacks.
Israeli army says it killed two Palestinians in Gaza
The Israeli military said Thursday it had killed two Palestinians in Khan Younis the day before, claiming they were smuggling weapons into Gaza, without providing evidence.
Palestinian news agency WAFA reported that two men, identified as Basel Nabil Abd al-Rahman Kashta and Ahmad Raja al-Shaer, were killed in an airstrike targeting a vehicle in the southern city. The attack also injured a Palestinian woman.
UN warns of food shortages if Hormuz crisis continues
A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
The Trump administration has issued fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities, according to a notice posted on the US Department of Treasury website on Thursday.
Hezbollah admits seized explosives belong to group
A Hezbollah MP acknowledged on Thursday that a 500-kilogram shipment of explosives seized last week by Lebanese authorities belonged to the group, a rare admission by the Iran-backed group.
"The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" against Israel, lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said.
He said Hezbollah also called for the immediate release of those arrested over the seizure.
Fadlallah demanded the return of the shipment, seized on a road linking eastern Lebanon to Beirut, saying it constituted "capabilities" used by Hezbollah against Israel.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has said the state will no longer tolerate any possession of "illegal weapons".
Houthi attack on presidential palace in Yemen's Aden kills 4
At least four people were killed and 10 more wounded in the Houthi missile attack on Yemen's presidential palace in Aden, three government military sources told AFP.
Yemen govt says Houthis targeted Marib city with missiles
The forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government said Thursday that the Houthis had fired ballistic missiles at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
"Houthi terrorist militias fired several ballistic missiles at the densely populated city of Marib," the government forces said on X.
Yemen's prime minister and other cabinet ministers were unharmed in the Houthi attack on the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden.
Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said that the group had fired five missiles at the palace, which is the headquarters of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government.
Houthi media have said that the group targeted a military headquarters at the palace.
Houthi media says group targeted military HQ at Aden palace
Yemen's Houthis attacked a military headquarters at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the seat of the internationally recognised government, media affiliated with the group reported Thursday.
The pro-Iranian fighters targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them", according to the group's news agency.

articles.title: The Gulf needs a security order that Washington cannot switch off
articles.body:
The Gulf has spent decades buying security from the world’s most powerful military. American bases dot the region, advanced weapons fill its arsenals, and defence agreements bind its rulers to Washington. Yet the war involving Iran has exposed a troubling paradox. The Gulf’s security arrangements may help deter adversaries, but they cannot guarantee that the region will escape a conflict shaped by decisions made elsewhere.
The consequences are no longer confined to military installations or oil terminals. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz threatens energy exports and maritime commerce, while attacks on critical infrastructure jeopardise the economic transformation programmes on which Gulf governments have staked their futures. Wealth can finance reconstruction, but it cannot restore lost confidence overnight.
The problem is not that the United States has become irrelevant. Its intelligence, airpower, naval capabilities and logistical reach remain difficult to replace. Nor does greater independence mean that Iran’s regional ambitions should be ignored. Rather, the Gulf faces a structural dilemma: the states most exposed to escalation do not necessarily possess the greatest influence over the decisions that produce it.
That dilemma demands a different ambition.
The Gulf does not need a security order without Washington. It needs one that can survive Washington’s changing priorities. The objective should be to turn external protection into one pillar of regional security, rather than the foundation on which everything else depends.
The limits of an American security umbrella
For decades, American military power has underwritten the security of the Gulf monarchies. The US Fifth Fleet operates from Bahrain, while Qatar hosts Al Udeid Air Base, a major centre for American air operations. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have invested heavily in American aircraft, missile defence and other advanced systems. These arrangements provide capabilities that would be costly and difficult to reproduce independently.
But military protection is not the same as strategic control. Washington ultimately decides how to deploy its forces, which threats deserve priority and when military action serves American interests. Gulf governments can influence these calculations through diplomacy and cooperation, but they cannot assume that their preferences will prevail.
The distinction becomes critical when Washington’s objectives collide with the region’s exposure to retaliation. An American operation may be designed to weaken an adversary or restore deterrence, yet its consequences can fall disproportionately on neighbouring states whose ports, airports, energy facilities and shipping routes become vulnerable. The presence of American forces can strengthen deterrence without eliminating the risks associated with escalation.
Recent events have also exposed the limits of military expenditure as a measure of security.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Saudi Arabia spent an estimated $83.2 billion on its military in 2025, making it the Middle East’s largest military spender. Nevertheless, sophisticated arsenals cannot automatically prevent attacks by adversaries using drones, missiles and other asymmetric capabilities.
The lesson is not that American protection has failed or that Gulf governments should abandon their alliances. It is that a security model built around external military superiority leaves too much dependent on decisions that regional governments cannot control. A durable system must preserve the benefits of American power while reducing the consequences of its possible absence, inconsistency or strategic redirection.
READ: Gaza’s future is not Washington’s to decide, says rights chief
Why the Gulf cannot secure itself alone
Reducing dependence on Washington, however, is easier said than done. The Gulf Cooperation Council has existed since 1981, yet its members have struggled to translate shared vulnerabilities into a fully integrated security system. They differ in their perceptions of Iran, their relationships with outside powers and their preferred responses to regional crises. Their rulers also remain reluctant to surrender sovereign authority over national defence.
These divisions matter more than the number of weapons purchased. A regional security order requires compatible warning systems, reliable intelligence-sharing, coordinated responses and clear procedures for consultation when a crisis erupts. Without these mechanisms, neighbouring states may possess formidable individual capabilities while remaining collectively vulnerable.
Nor would replacing American dependence with a collection of new foreign partnerships solve the problem. Saudi Arabia’s expanding defence relationship with Pakistan and Turkey illustrates the search for additional strategic options.
Their Mecca Joint Defence Agreement promises closer military cooperation, including coordination among their armed forces. Such arrangements can broaden the Gulf’s choices, but their value will ultimately depend on operational coordination, credible commitments and the ability to respond effectively under pressure.
The danger is that diversification becomes an exercise in accumulating partners rather than building regional capacity. Multiple alliances can offer useful insurance, but they can also create competing expectations and overlapping commitments. A state that depends on several external powers without developing its own mechanisms for crisis management may remain exposed to the same underlying problem.
Iran must also be part of the equation. No credible Gulf security order can simply assume away Tehran’s military capabilities, its regional relationships or its ability to threaten maritime commerce. Yet treating Iran exclusively as a target to be deterred leaves little room for managing incidents before they become wars. Deterrence and diplomacy are not alternatives; each is more effective when the other exists.
The challenge, therefore, is political as much as military. Gulf governments must recognise that national security cannot be secured through bilateral relationships alone when threats cross borders and the consequences of conflict spread across the entire region.
Building an order Washington cannot switch off
A more resilient security order should begin with practical cooperation rather than grand declarations. The GCC needs stronger mechanisms for sharing intelligence, coordinating early warning and integrating air and missile defence. Common operating procedures would help governments identify threats, distinguish deliberate attacks from accidents and coordinate responses before confusion escalates into confrontation.
Second, the region needs institutionalised crisis diplomacy. Direct communication channels, maritime incident protocols and regular consultations involving Gulf states and Iran could reduce the danger of miscalculation. Such arrangements would not resolve every dispute or eliminate the need for deterrence. Their purpose would be narrower but essential: to prevent individual incidents from triggering a regional conflict that no government can easily contain.
Third, economic resilience must become part of security planning. The International Monetary Fund has highlighted the potential benefits of completing the GCC Railway and Saudi Landbridge projects, which could reduce economic losses during a closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative energy routes, diversified shipping arrangements and stronger regional logistics would likewise give governments more options when maritime traffic is disrupted. Infrastructure should be assessed not only by its commercial return, but also by the strategic flexibility it provides.
Finally, Gulf governments must define more clearly what collective security means in practice. Which threats require immediate consultation? How should members coordinate assistance after an attack? What commitments can each state credibly make, and how can those commitments be implemented without undermining national sovereignty? Answering these questions will be more valuable than announcing another ambitious pact whose operational foundations remain uncertain.
None of this requires the United States to withdraw. Washington can remain an indispensable partner, providing capabilities that regional states cannot quickly replicate. But a stronger regional framework would also make that partnership more sustainable by giving Gulf governments greater agency, reducing the risk of unilateral escalation and ensuring that essential security functions do not depend entirely on decisions made abroad.
The ultimate test of Gulf power is not how much its governments spend on weapons or how many foreign partners they can attract. It is whether they can shape the conditions under which their people, economies and infrastructure remain secure.
The Gulf cannot dictate Washington’s choices, any more than it can eliminate rivalry with Iran. It can, however, build institutions, capabilities and diplomatic channels that make those choices less decisive for its future. That is the difference between being protected by a powerful ally and possessing a security order of its own.

articles.title: Who Are the Houthis and Why Are They Attacking Saudi Arabia’s Airports?
articles.body:
The European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council on Thursday announced the postponement of a joint summit set to take place in Saudi Arabia next week, amid safety concerns prompted by Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom.
Citing the “continued attempts by the terrorist Houthi militia to target the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its civilian infrastructure, which threatens the security and safety of innocent civilians,” the council said the Gulf-European Summit will be rescheduled.
The postponement comes after Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Wednesday vowed to forge ahead with the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities, just hours after striking oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters.
“Operations toward Saudi depths will continue in the coming days,” said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, describing the locations as “legitimate targets” and framing their attacks as a direct response to Saudi strikes on Yemen. Saudi-led forces said they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday and local journalists reported hearing “loud blasts” in the Saudi capital.
The escalation follows weeks of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The conflict reignited amid the widespread fallout of the U.S.-Iran war, bringing further instability to the Gulf region. In September, the Houthis said they had captured the strategic Perim Island that sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime chokepoint. They also seized other islands in a bid to tighten their grip on the Red Sea coastline. Amid fears that a stronger Houthi position along the coast could further constrain global energy supplies, Saudi-backed forces recaptured key areas around the strait in early October. The Houthis have since ramped up their focus on Saudi Arabia’s airports and energy infrastructure.
Tuesday night’s attack on Aramco’s executive offices in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a limited fire, Saudi’s Ministry of Energy confirmed. No injuries were reported. TIME has reached out to Aramco and the Saudi government’s media office for further information. Saudi authorities said several missiles and drones had been intercepted elsewhere, and that falling debris injured four people in the capital of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia launched strikes on an oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital Sanaa on Tuesday, as the tit-for-tat attacks escalated.
The Saudi strike on the oil depot appeared to be in response to the Houthis’ attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left over 300 injured. A projectile hit that same airport on Sunday, killing one person, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed. The week before, an attack on Abha International Airport killed two people and wounded 28, said GACA.
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. However, it is struggling to defend itself against the Houthis, who are positioned to strike deep into the kingdom. The Saudis are currently investigating how their defense systems failed to stop the deadly attacks. Experts cite the vast mass of Saudi land as one reason why defensive measures may have failed. The Saudi border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles. “Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” said Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, in an online post.
Operations at King Khalid remain suspended in the wake of the attacks. Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Philippine Airlines are among the carriers to announce a suspension of flights to Riyadh.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans in the country of “potential flight cancelations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” stipulating that U.S. government employees now require “special authorization” to use any airport in the country.
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the Houthis “are behaving very badly.” In a Truth Social post, he continued, “I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the hell out of them and, at their request, stopped,” seemingly referencing the U.S. strikes between March and May last year, which came in response to the Houthis attacking vessels in the Red Sea and disrupting global trade. Weeks after the strikes began, a cease-fire between the U.S. and the Houthis was reached via Omani mediations.
On Saturday, Trump suggested that the U.S. may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. Asked about the possibility of U.S. strikes, a senior U.S. official told TIME that Washington is “in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability and we will always fulfill our commitments to our partners.”
As tensions in the region continue to escalate, here’s what to know about the Houthis, their history with Saudi Arabia, and why they are attacking airports.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis are a political and armed group in Yemen that first emerged in the 1990s and have been fighting the country’s internationally recognized government for around two decades. The group is a revivalist movement for Zaidism, a branch of Shi‘ite Islam. The Zaidi muslim population in the country represents around 35% of the Yemeni population.
The Houthi movement was largely born from a transformation of the Believing Youth Forum (BYF), according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The group became known as the Houthis in honor of their founder and leader, Hussein al-Houthi. Before he was killed by Yemeni forces in 2004, al-Houthi had developed the group into a more militarized movement. The group is now led by his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi.
Civil war broke out in 2014 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, forcing the government to flee to the southern city of Aden. Since then, the group has been engaged in fighting against a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government. The Houthis currently have control of most of the country’s west, including Sanaa.
Experts compare the Houthis to authoritarian regimes on account of the social restrictions imposed in areas under the group’s control and alleged human rights abuses.
“The Houthis are dominated with very ideological and radical ideas, like a Zaidi ISIS. They have similarities also with the Taliban in terms of social control," says Mahmoud Shehrah, a Yemeni political analyst at London-based think tank Chatham House.
How are the Houthi rebels linked to Iran?
The Houthis hold strong ties to Iran, often taking action in line with Tehran’s objectives.
“Since 2009, Iran [has] started to speed up weapons supplies, training, but also a lot of funding to the Houthis,” says Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemeni research fellow at Chatham House, noting that links between the two began as early as the 1990s.
The Houthis are often considered part of Iran’s proxy network, known as the “Axis of Resistance,” which also includes Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Islamic Resistance network in Iraq, and previously the Assad regime in Syria, until its collapse in December 2024.
In response to the Israel-Hamas war, the Yemeni militia launched several strikes on shipping vessels in the Red Sea, disrupting global trade in late 2023 and the early months of 2024. The U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024 for a series of strikes on Houthi targets across Yemen in retaliation for the attacks on unarmed vessels. The U.S. carried out an additional campaign against Houthi targets later that year.
The Houthis entered the Iran war in March by firing a barrage of ballistic missiles at southern Israel. In the months since, the group’s advances along the Red Sea are widely considered to serve the interests of Iran. A Houthi blockade in the region against Saudi Arabia was declared in July, and several vessels have been attacked. The threat that the Houthis could bring another critical maritime chokepoint to a standstill, much like Iran has done with the Strait of Hormuz, could give Tehran significant leverage in its negotiations with Washington.
However, experts say it’s not entirely accurate to call the Houthis a direct proxy.
"The Houthis are one of the more independent regional allies of Iran in the Middle East. They have their own independent interests, even though their interests converge regionally and globally,” says Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.
Even so, the Houthis have become increasingly vital for Iran. “With the fall of Assad, with the weakening of Hezbollah, the Houthis became the most important regional ally Iran has,” says Al Muslimi, pointing specifically toward the Houthis' ability to disrupt trade in the Red Sea.
What do the Houthis want?
The group’s goals have changed over time, as regional developments have unfolded, experts note.
“The Houthi's ultimate goal is to be a regional power,” says Al-Muslimi. With regard to the reignited civil war, the Houthis ultimately want an end to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory.
“The Houthis want to have the skies and the ports of the country open for trade, for goods and services,” says Gerges. “They want money to flow into the coffers of the Houthis.”
The civil war has had a disastrous effect on Yemen, with nearly half of the population in government-controlled areas facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the United Nations. “The current situation is very dire for the Yemeni population, but also for the ability of the Houthis to rule Yemen effectively,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis want to consolidate rule and regime. They want to be recognized as the legitimate government in Sanaa, as opposed to being considered a non-state actor,” he adds.
When did the Houthis and Saudi Arabia begin fighting again?
A cease-fire brokered by the United Nations in April 2022 largely held for over four years, before collapsing in July. The Houthis claimed Saudi Arabia had launched strikes on Sanaa Airport, targeting a Houthi delegation returning from Iran. In a move they framed as retaliatory, the Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia.
“The Houthis saw this as a golden opportunity to change the balance of power against Saudi Arabia and Yemen itself and launch a lightning offensive,” says Gerges.
Following further strikes on Houthi targets later that month, the militia group began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, belonging to the state-owned petroleum company Aramco.
In September, strikes on oil refineries and other related facilities ramped up, and Saudi Arabia’s airports became a target.
Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports?
Prior to the 2022 cease-fire, attacks on airports were largely considered a signature move of the Houthis.
In a highly-publicized attack, the group struck Abha International Airport in June 2019, injuring at least 26 people, Saudi authorities said. The strike earned international condemnation and was deemed a possible war crime by Human Rights Watch.
Now, after fatal strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the Houthis have threatened to keep targeting airports. The main motivation behind these attacks is the economic and geopolitical pressure they apply to Saudi Arabia, experts say.
“The Houthis want to put severe pressure on the Saudi Arabia economy, airport infrastructure, and security,” says Shehrah. “They want to squeeze Saudi Arabia's arms to push them to a political settlement.”
The unrest threatens to have a strong economic and political impact on Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman's governance. The disruption is “costly” to him, says Al-Muslimi, who notes that Bin Salman is eager for Saudi Arabia to be seen as a “safe harbor.”
The financial and reputational damage of these strikes has also put the Saudi public on the frontline of the conflict. It’s a “shock, because it's the first time in years that such major attacks have targeted deep inside Saudi Arabia,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis are trying to exert tremendous pressure on the leaders of Saudi Arabia to force them to accept conditions for lifting the blockade on Yemen and recognizing their legitimacy,” he continues. “Although, I doubt that the Saudi leadership will concede to Houthi demands… this would be seen as a surrender and humiliation."

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Kyiv observed the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump, only to face intensified Russian attacks and slower Starlink satellite communications.
Source: Financial Times
Details: "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy said in a forthright interview with the FT in London. He also sharply criticised Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent affinity for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Asked to explain the relationship between the two leaders, Zelenskyy said Trump has an instinctive affinity for autocrats and extremely wealthy people.
"He [Trump] speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong," Zelenskyy said.
The FT noted that Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that a moratorium on the attacks, together with an agreement to purchase hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel, is necessary to bring down fuel prices in the US.
Zelenskyy said he had suspended strikes on energy facilities for three days to accommodate the US request. However, Moscow continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure and kill civilians, with more than 100 people killed in the past week.
The president also said that, despite Ukraine suspending its strikes, its forces had been left without US early-warning systems for incoming ballistic missiles. Starlink satellite communications, operated by Elon Musk's company, had also been slowed across the country, making battlefield operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military facilities more difficult.
The FT wrote that the deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington marks the most serious crisis between Ukraine and its most important security partner since the Oval Office spat in February 2025.
"Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine's relationship with the US as an 'honest' and 'strategic' partner was essential in the fight against Russia, comparing it to Kyiv's relationship with the UK," the FT noted.
Asked whether Ukraine would stop striking oil refineries even if Russia continued its attacks, in an effort to repair relations with the White House, Zelenskyy said he would agree to do so only if the US supplied him with more American-made Patriot interceptors.
He believes that halting strikes on oil refineries could simply encourage the US and Russia to strike further deals, potentially providing additional funding for Putin's war machine.
"The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas," Zelenskyy said.
He added that the US suspension of intelligence sharing and disruption of Starlink services has become "dangerous" for Ukraine.
"We will find a way out . . . but it's better not to give him [Putin] the new life or the new will to fight," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- On 11 October, Trump published a post on his social media Truth Social announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which allegedly took effect immediately. He said that both sides had consented to cease strikes on energy infrastructure, although neither party had been informed of this.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that Ukraine supports it.
- Later, Zelenskyy reported a Russian strike on CHP-5 [a combined heat and power plant] in Kharkiv and a power station in Kyiv following Trump's statement.
- On 13 October Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and energy facilities for two days in response to a proposal by Trump. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure.
