articles.title: Ukraine has exhausted its stockpile of missiles for Patriot systems - media
articles.body:
Ukraine has exhausted its stockpile of missiles for Patriot systems - media
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has exhausted its stockpile of Patriot missiles, CNN reports. Due to the shortage, nearly all ballistic missiles were not intercepted during the latest strike.
Ukraine is running out of Patriot air defense missiles, making it more vulnerable to Russian attacks. CNN reports this, according to UNN.
Ukraine has exhausted its stockpiles of missiles for the American Patriot air defense system, making it more vulnerable to attacks by Russian ballistic missiles
As noted, for several months, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly warned that Ukraine is running out of American Patriot interceptor missiles, which are one of the few types of defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
However, these interceptor missiles are expensive, and there are not enough of them in the world, as other countries have depleted their stockpiles or are trying to strengthen their own defense systems amid the war in Iran.
A source told CNN that "almost all ballistic missiles during the latest strike were not intercepted due to a shortage of missiles."
It should be recalled
Greece and Spain have stockpiles of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems whose service life is nearing its end. These missiles could be transferred to Ukraine, but the countries are so far refusing.

articles.title: Musk Tells Zelensky to ‘Go’ as Ukraine Questions US Support
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “to go” on Thursday, as Kyiv raised concerns that US restrictions on satellite communications and intelligence sharing were weakening Ukraine’s defenses against Russian attacks.
“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The dispute escalated after Ukraine reported restrictions on military Starlink services, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations.
And so the slaughter continues …
Time for Zelensky to go https://t.co/tMBThajxhH
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 15, 2026
Zelensky warned that the restrictions could lead to significant casualties as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“It’s a big mistake,” he said. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses… People will die.”
He urged Musk, whose SpaceX operates Starlink, to restore the service, saying he hoped the disruption was the result of a technical problem.
Musk said on Wednesday that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, which determines restrictions on its use.
He distinguished it from Starlink, a commercial satellite network used by Ukraine for communications, and said it should not be used for offensive military operations.
The satellite dispute comes amid concerns that reduced US intelligence sharing could leave Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian missile attacks.
Trump Weighs Easing Shadow Fleet Sanctions to Lower Oil Shipping Costs
Ukrainian officials told CNN that the loss of intelligence could give Russian forces an advantage on the battlefield. A European official also questioned Washington’s explanation that weather had caused gaps in missile-warning information.
For two consecutive nights, air raid alerts in Kyiv came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the capital.
On Oct. 12-13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, hitting civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Zelensky said Ukraine had received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners.
The Trump administration has previously warned it could suspend intelligence sharing and halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to stop deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The growing dispute has also spilled into relations between Kyiv and Washington over energy policy.
Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel supply deal with heavily sanctioned Russia.
Trump, facing key midterm elections next month, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for contributing to fuel shortages and rising prices at US gas stations.

articles.title: Kyiv has run out of missiles for its Patriot air defense systems, CNN reports
articles.body:
Ukraine has run out of missiles for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, CNN reported, citing a source familiar with the situation.
The source said Ukrainian forces intercepted almost none of the missiles in the latest ballistic missile attack overnight into October 14 “due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”
Russian ballistic missiles hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy infrastructure in Kharkiv during the attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has been warning for months that a shortage of Patriot missiles undermines the country’s ability to defend itself, especially ahead of an expected increase in attacks on energy infrastructure this winter. In August, Zelensky said he was making “millions” of phone calls to secure supplies and that Ukraine had only a tenth of the interceptor stockpile it needed.
On October 15, Zelensky said Ukraine would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries because Moscow had continued its attacks during the three days Kyiv refrained from attacks at the request of the United States. He suggested he could soften his position in exchange for additional Patriot missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries after Zelensky condemns withdrawal of US intelligence
articles.body:
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian refineries with a strike at an installation in the Ryazan region, the regional governor said on Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced his anger at a "dangerous" withdrawal of US intelligence.
Since US President Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, Kyiv had refrained from attacking Russian refineries, which the US leader had blamed for raising diesel prices on global markets.
But Zelensky had voiced increasing frustration with Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, which he said on Wednesday had left 600,000 people without power. He warned that Ukraine would not suspend its own attacks indefinitely if Russia did not reciprocate and also criticized what he said was Trump's favoritism toward Russia.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, he said Ukraine's patience had run out.
"The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” he told the newspaper.
Pavel Malkov, the governor of Ryazan, said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the region had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
"The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene," he said.
In his interview, Zelensky criticized Washington’s eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump’s apparent admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump calls for Ukraine to replace Zelensky after announcing Russia diesel deal
Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky and railed against Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, one day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia, aiming to lower fuel prices that have soared since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
Despite Ukraine's suspension of refinery attacks, Ukrainian officials complained that they had not received any US early-warning alerts in recent days for incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
They also said the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications service had been slowed across the country, hampering frontline operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military sites.
Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X/Twitter that Starshield - the military version of Starlink - was owned and controlled by the US government, which decided on any limits on speed.
Zelensky has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In the FT interview, Zelensky said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he dismissed the idea that failures of the Starlink satellite system might have been caused by a fault.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT.
Zelensky demands US interceptors in exchange for halting strikes on refineries
Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, he told the newspaper he could only agree if, in return, he was given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable.
"We didn't destroy any relationship," he said, claiming it wasn't up to him to repair US-Ukraine relations.
Ukraine claims to have damaged six Russian military aircraft
Ukraine's military said on Thursday it had damaged six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region.
In a Telegram statement, Ukraine's military general staff said it had confirmed damage of varying degrees to all six aircraft.
The Su-34M is a large fighter-bomber, costing tens of millions of US dollars apiece and frequently used by Russia to drop devastating glide bombs onto Ukrainian cities near the frontline.
Ukraine said on Telegram that it used its Neptune coastal missile system in the attack.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Kremlin condemns Ukraine refinery strikes as ceasefire violation
The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts, after a Ukrainian drone struck a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia did not perceive that Ukraine had ever complied with an energy ceasefire announced last week by Trump. Ukraine says it paused such strikes for three days but resumed them after Russia continued to attack its own energy sector.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘We’re done,’ Zelensky says, as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries. The Kremlin claims the attacks never stopped.
articles.body:
‘We’re done,’ Zelensky says, as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries. The Kremlin claims the attacks never stopped.
Ukraine is resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
Zelensky said Ukraine had held off on striking Russian oil refineries for three days at the request of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russia, meanwhile, had not honored the so-called energy ceasefire, Zelensky said, continuing to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and killing about 100 civilians over the past week.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday morning, October 15.
The first strike by Ukraine’s military after the pause appears to have hit the Ryazan oil refinery. The plant, owned by Rosneft, is one of the key fuel suppliers for Moscow and the Moscow region.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov announced the morning of October 15 that classes had been canceled in 14 schools and 25 kindergartens in Ryazan because of “a mass drone attack on the region.” The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published a photo early that morning showing a flare over the Ryazan oil refinery, suggesting it was linked to the drone attack.
Authorities in the Ryazan region confirmed the strikes, saying a fire had broken out at the refinery. Malkov also said that “a warehouse and vehicles on the grounds of another enterprise in Ryazan” had been damaged. He declined to give further details, adding that the damage was being assessed.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Ukraine’s military attacked the Ryazan oil refinery with 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. The Russian military said it had shot down the drones and missiles, but added that “a fire broke out at the refinery as a result of falling drone debris.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Wednesday afternoon, October 14, that Ukrainian forces had struck two oil refineries, one in the Saratov region and one in the Ryazan region. “We see that the Ukrainian side is not showing any movement toward an energy ceasefire,” he said. At the time, authorities in the Ryazan region and eyewitnesses had not reported any strike on the refinery there, and Novak’s claim about a strike on an oil refinery in the Saratov region remains unconfirmed.
Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov, commenting on Zelensky’s remarks about resuming strikes, referred to Novak’s statement. According to Peskov, there had been no moratorium on Ukraine’s part, and strikes on Russian oil refineries and energy facilities had continued throughout this period. “There is nothing new here,” Peskov said, once again accusing Ukrainian authorities and Zelensky personally of “not wanting to make peace.”
War in photos. Aftermath of a Russian strike on Kyiv.
Russian forces struck Kyiv with drones and missiles overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring about 20. A nine-story apartment building caught fire in the Desnianskyi District as a result of the strike.

‘We’re done’: Zelensky says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Ukraine’s president said in an interview with the Financial Times.
He said Ukraine had not struck energy facilities in Russia for three days, in keeping with a request from the United States. Moscow, meanwhile, continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, killing more than 100 civilians over the past week.
Zelensky said that although Ukraine stopped striking oil refineries, it received no American warnings about Russian ballistic missile attacks. He also said Starlink terminal operations had been restricted.
He confirmed that American officials had warned Ukraine that if Kyiv did not stop striking oil refineries, the United States would stop sharing intelligence. Zelensky also rejected the idea that a malfunction had caused the Starlink problems. “It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he said.
Asked whether Ukraine could stop striking oil refineries to improve relations with Washington, even if Russia continued its own attacks, Zelensky said he could agree to that in exchange for additional shipments of missiles for Patriot systems. That, he said, was the “minimum” he had asked for.
Donald Trump said October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a truce in the energy sector. Zelensky soon said the Ukrainian Armed Forces had “received all relevant orders” in connection with the truce. Ukraine then stopped striking Russian oil refineries, while Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that Russian forces had struck communications and energy infrastructure in Kyiv.
According to Axios, Trump is counting on Zelensky to observe the energy truce and stop striking Russian oil refineries. “Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted,” a White House source told the outlet.

articles.title: Musk blames Trump for throttling ‘military Starlink’ in Ukraine
articles.body:
Musk blames Trump for throttling ‘military Starlink’ in Ukraine
Elon Musk has denied instructing his company SpaceX to abruptly restrict Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services used by Ukrainian forces to operate drones.
Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders said terminals suddenly stopped working overnight Tuesday into Wednesday when drones flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. The problems with Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink service, occurred as US President Donald Trump was pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for surging energy prices.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X on Wednesday in response to criticism from Ukraine. He had earlier suggested that the disruption might have been “a mistake” and said he was working to restore connectivity.
Musk also said that Starlink should be used only for civilian and defensive purposes, arguing that using it for offensive operations would be “inappropriate for a commercial company.”
Although Trump has not commented directly on the restrictions, a senior US official told Axios that his administration had nothing to do with the disruption of Starlink services.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev unless Ukraine halted attacks on Russian energy facilities.
Ukrainian officials also said they had received no advance warning from their Western partners before Russian missile strikes on Kiev on two consecutive nights, Monday and Tuesday. According to media reports, US officials attributed the failure to detect the missile launches to bad weather, an explanation their Ukrainian counterparts reportedly found hard to believe.
Asked by British talk show host Piers Morgan on Wednesday whether he had been “betrayed” by the Trump administration, Zelensky replied, “Yes.”
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” he added.
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov said Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 100 mph was being restored, but urged the removal of speed restrictions on Starshield altogether.
Ukrainian media reported on Thursday that the operation of Starshield systems had been fully restored. Sources within the country’s Ministry of Defense said military units confirmed that communications were back online while officials continue to investigate the reasons for the restrictions.
Russia has argued that Ukraine would use a ceasefire without preconditions to regroup and replenish its forces. “We want not a ceasefire but a lasting peace, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday.

articles.title: US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel
articles.body:
The Trump administration is weighing looser sanctions on shadow fleet tankers that have hauled oil from Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, a US official said on 14 October, Reuters reported. An industry research group expects the change to do little for freight rates.
With Reuters calling high fuel prices a risk for Trump before the 3 November midterms, Washington has already eased sanctions on Russian oil and diesel this year and is now looking at the ships blacklisted for hauling sanctioned cargoes. In March, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a waiver on Russian oil at sea would bring Moscow no significant financial benefit, yet Russia’s seaborne oil income jumped by $890 million in the week to 15 March, Bloomberg data showed.
“Legal oil” on blacklisted ships
The talks center on letting “legal oil” sail on previously sanctioned vessels, the official said. Only crude or fuel free of US sanctions would qualify, not Russian or Iranian oil. Washington wants more crude and refined products moving out of the Gulf, the official added. Companies would need US Treasury approval to use the ships.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Research group Energy Aspects said US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh, tied the easing to record freight rates. Those rates hit records after the Iran and Ukraine wars drove up inflation and left US crude too costly for Asian refiners, Reuters said. Energy Aspects itself expects the easing to do little for freight rates, since most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have kept trading for the past three months.
The Energy Department said any relief would do nothing to help Russia ship its oil or refined products. Treasury referred questions to the Energy Department. Yet Reuters noted that both departments could face pressure to let these vessels carry Russian diesel, given Trump’s push to get it onto world markets fast.
Britain is pushing the other way. UK finance minister John Healey urged counterparts at International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok on 15 October to keep tough sanctions on Russia, “especially a tighter ban on shipping services” that keep Putin’s shadow fleet operating.
Diesel license criticism and an unconfirmed ceasefire
On 9 October, the US Treasury issued a license clearing Russian-origin diesel trade until 7 April 2027. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters it was a weak decision unworthy of Ukraine’s partners. Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren called it a “total betrayal of Ukraine.” Republican Senator Thom Tillis said there is “a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law.”
“He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
Trump then pressed Kyiv to spare Russian refineries and declared an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. A White House official told Axios it covers only oil refineries. Neither side confirmed a similar announcement Trump made in mid-September, AAP reported.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on 13 October that contacts on the ceasefire were continuing and referred further questions to Trump, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported. He claimed the diesel deal was “a very mutually beneficial item of Russian-American cooperation” that serves the interests of Russia, the US, and world energy markets, Russian newspaper Kommersant reported.

articles.title: US military weighs use of 'mother of all bombs' on Iran: CNN
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US military weighs use of 'mother of all bombs' in potential future strikes on Iran, CNN says
The US military has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US officials familiar with the matter.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant development in the war, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Iran, meanwhile, has placed its military on heightened alert, conducting new missile tests in recent days and threatening to unveil additional weapons.
Tehran has also warned Washington and regional governments that another round of war could trigger retaliation across a wider geographical area, including potential ground incursions.
The US Department of War recently reported that the death toll of US personnel in its war on Iran is 21 killed and 865 wounded in an acknowledgement that losses faced during the conflict were greater than previously admitted.

articles.title: Turkish army buys CAKIR ground-launched cruise missiles
articles.body:
- Türkiye signed a contract with Roketsan for land-based ÇAKIR cruise missile systems for the Turkish Land Forces, defense industry chief Haluk Görgün said.
- ÇAKIR is a jet-powered cruise missile with a range of more than 150 km and a 70 kg warhead.
Türkiye has signed a supply contract with missile maker Roketsan for land-based CAKIR cruise missile systems for the Turkish Land Forces, Haluk Görgün, head of the country’s Presidency of Defense Industries, announced on Oct. 15.
Görgün said in a post on X that the contract is meant to strengthen the army’s long-range strike capability, and that more than 200 subcontractors took part in the project, including nearly 20 large and medium-sized companies.
“We have signed the ÇAKIR Project Supply Contract for land-based systems to enhance the strategic strike capabilities of our Land Forces,” Görgün said, in a statement translated from Turkish.
Roketsan’s ÇAKIR is a compact, jet-powered subsonic cruise missile that can be fired from aircraft, armed drones, ships and uncrewed surface vessels, as well as tactical wheeled vehicles. According to the company’s specifications, the missile weighs up to 275 kg (606 pounds) on its own and up to 330 kg (728 pounds) with the solid-fuel booster used for ground and ship launches. It carries a 70 kg (154-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 150 km (93 miles).
The missile is powered by the KTJ-1750 turbojet engine developed by Turkish firm Kale R&D. Its guidance combines inertial navigation with jam-resistant satellite navigation and a radar altimeter, so it can keep flying on course under heavy electronic jamming. Roketsan says ÇAKIR can fly very low over water or follow terrain to stay below enemy radar, and that its airframe uses radar-absorbing materials. The family includes land-attack, anti-ship and electronic warfare versions with different seekers.
Roketsan carried out the first publicly announced ground launches of ÇAKIR in August, when two missiles fired from a mobile launcher hit separate land and sea targets, Naval News reported. Indonesia’s ambassador to Türkiye said the same month that his country had bought ÇAKIR missiles, and the missile has been linked to Qatari fast attack craft projects.
Görgün placed the deal alongside Türkiye’s other surface-to-surface missiles, saying deliveries of the BORA and TAYFUN ballistic missiles to the army are continuing while ÇAKIR and the land-based KARA ATMACA cruise missile add to the country’s deterrent. Roketsan made its first delivery of KARA ATMACA, a ground-launched version of the Atmaca anti-ship missile, to the Turkish Land Forces in April 2026.
He said Türkiye is expanding serial production of missile and air defense systems to meet demand from its own army and from friendly and allied countries, as part of a wider push to make the Turkish defense industry fully independent.
The contract brings a ground-launched cruise missile with a 150-km reach into Turkish army service alongside the longer-range KARA ATMACA and Roketsan’s ballistic missiles, with more than 200 Turkish subcontractors involved in its production.

articles.title: After Trump, Musk tells Ukraine’s president to go. Zelenskyy says he won’t resign and will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk wrote on X on 15 October: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.” Four days earlier, he had posted that Zelenskyy had gone too far, after US President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Asked by Morgan on 14 October whether he would resign, Zelenskyy said he would not: “It’s my responsibility.”
Musk’s post comes as Washington squeezes Kyiv instead of Moscow: Ukraine’s military satellite links slowed, US missile warnings went missing, and the US threatened to cut intelligence unless Kyiv stops hitting Russian refineries.
Land and elections
Zelenskyy said elections could not be held under constant Russian attack: “From the point of security, you can’t do elections.”
Of any future president, he said: “I’m sure the new man or woman will defend our country.” He also reminded Trump that Crimea and parts of Donbas were already occupied when he took office, under another president, long before the full-scale invasion.
“I’m a realist, and I understand that people are more important than one kilometer or two kilometers. It’s not about kilometers. It’s about land and homes,” he told Morgan.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is ready for elections if a full 60-day ceasefire is in place. Numerous sources told The Atlantic that Trump sees Zelenskyy as the main obstacle to a peace deal and related business deals with Russia. One Trump adviser said he is also an obstacle to Trump’s hopes for the Nobel Peace Prize.
Starlink
Ukrainian forces reported restrictions on Starshield, the SpaceX satellite system they use for battlefield communications and drone operations, and Zelenskyy warned the decision would cost lives. On 14 October, Musk said Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, which sets its limits, and that commercial Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action. Zelenskyy told the FT he did not know whether the decision was SpaceX’s or the US government’s, adding: “I think it’s about SpaceX.” A senior US official told Axios the Trump administration had nothing to do with the restrictions.
Intelligence and refineries
On two consecutive nights, air raid alerts in Kyiv sounded only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the capital. Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no warning from partners of the launches on 12 and 13 October, which hit civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. A Ukrainian official told CNN the loss of intelligence “will give Russians a real leverage on a frontline.” A European official questioned Washington’s explanation that weather caused the gaps in missile warnings. Trump denied halting intelligence sharing.
Washington had warned it could suspend intelligence sharing if Ukraine kept striking Russian refineries, Axios reported. A US official disputed that any explicit threat was made. Sources told CNN the US had also threatened to halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine. Zelenskyy told the FT the warning came through military channels.
To lower energy costs before next month’s midterm elections, Trump has pressed Kyiv to stop refinery strikes, CNN reported. Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia. On 14 October in London, he told the FT that Ukraine would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Read also
- “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine
- Fears that Ukraine will lose Starlink are back after Musk backed Trump against Zelenskyy. Adviser says profit makes cutoff unlikely
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms

articles.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
Saudi Arabia on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis in the dramatic escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic republic continued to arm and train the group.
In a virtual briefing with reporters including AFP journalists, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude oil exporter, has come under sustained attack by the Houthis in recent days, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
It has launched retaliatory strikes on Houthi strongholds in Yemen - one of the world's poorest countries - but the Iran-backed group remains undeterred.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions," said Dr. Rayed Krimly, the deputy minister.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
The official said the kingdom continued "to have direct communications with Iran", but added: "Overall, it doesn't seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution."
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
"This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago."
Airport strikes
On Saturday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and wounding around 300 others, in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Thursday said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times in October.
During a presentation in Riyadh covering the strikes, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
"The terrorist Houthi militias have worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors," he said, adding that the group now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
Yemen's civil war reignited in July after a years-long UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The situation took a sharp turn for the worse in September, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them capture swathes of new territory in Yemen, including along the Red Sea coast where a waterway crucial to global energy flows is located.
On Thursday, the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the headquarters of the internationally recognised government, security sources told AFP, while a journalist saw smoke rising from the site.
"Houthi missiles targeted the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden," the government's interim capital, three local police sources said on condition of anonymity, after residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions.
Since their offensive began, the Houthis have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government whose forces they are battling on the ground.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
(AFP)

articles.title: Axios: White House denies role in Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
articles.body:
A senior official in the U.S. presidential administration told Axios the White House had nothing to do with restricting Starlink’s operation in Ukraine.
Axios’s sources said the Trump administration plans to contact SpaceX to find out what happened with Starlink in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry earlier announced that it had run into restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink used by Ukrainian forces. Ukrainian servicemen and officials said the restrictions disrupted some missions.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk announced that U.S. authorities own and control the Starshield systems. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he wrote on the social media platform X.
The White House has not officially commented on the reports of restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine.
The restriction on Starlink’s operation was reported amid a crisis in relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Ukraine also said it had stopped receiving warnings from American allies about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles. Western media, citing government sources, reported that the U.S. told Ukraine it would withhold intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: ‘We’re Done’: Zelensky Says Ukraine Will Resume Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Washington pressured Ukraine to halt attacks, warning that the US has endangered Ukrainian lives by restricting access to intelligence and Starlink satellite communications.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview in London.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky said Ukrainian military officials had been warned by their US counterparts that Washington would restrict intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian energy facilities.
The comments mark a further deterioration in relations between Zelensky and US President Donald Trump, who has pushed Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil infrastructure as Washington seeks to lower fuel prices.
Last week, Trump announced an agreement for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, drawing criticism from US lawmakers and European allies.
Zelensky described the deal as a “simple victory” for the Kremlin in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday.
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky said.
He also accused Trump of taking Russia’s side in the war, arguing that Washington should remain neutral rather than favor Moscow.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children,” Zelensky said. “That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 14, 2026
“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side,” he added. “This is not the right side of history.”
Starlink restrictions raise alarm in Kyiv
The dispute escalated after Ukraine reported restrictions on military Starlink services, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations.
Zelensky warned that the restrictions could lead to significant casualties as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“It’s a big mistake,” he said. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses… People will die.”
He urged Elon Musk, whose SpaceX operates Starlink, to restore the service, saying he hoped the disruption was the result of a technical problem.
Musk said on Wednesday that Starshield, the military-grade satellite system, is owned and controlled by the US government, which determines restrictions on its use.
He added that Starlink is a commercial service intended for civilian and defensive purposes and should not be used for offensive military operations.
The reported Starlink restrictions came amid concerns that a reduction in US intelligence sharing could weaken Ukraine’s ability to detect incoming Russian missile attacks and protect its cities.
Ukrainian officials told CNN that the loss of intelligence could give Russian forces an advantage on the battlefield, while a European official questioned Washington’s explanation that weather had caused gaps in missile-warning information.
For two consecutive nights, the air raid warnings that normally give Kyiv residents precious time to seek shelter came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the Ukrainian capital.
On Monday and Tuesday, Oct. 12-13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, striking civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Ukraine received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
The Trump administration has previously warned that it could suspend intelligence sharing and halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to stop deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
The dispute comes as Russian forces continue attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Zelensky said Russian strikes had left more than 600,000 people without electricity.
Moscow has also intensified aerial attacks as battlefield advances remain limited, with both sides targeting energy infrastructure.
Zelensky has sought to strengthen European support amid uncertainty over Washington’s commitment. During his visit to London on Wednesday, he met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III.

articles.title: EU Disburses Another €2.86B to Cover Ukraine’s ‘Most Urgent Needs’ – Drones and Missiles
articles.body:
The European Union (EU) has disbursed another €2.86 billion ($3.1 billion) to Ukraine for air defense, particularly drones and missiles, as the country nears its fifth winter of Russia’s aggression.
The European Commission confirmed the payment on Wednesday, Oct. 14, made under the defense component of the €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) Ukraine Support Loan. The funds will also cover radars, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Amid intensified Russian attacks on our cities and critical infrastructure, this support is vital,” Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
“More drones, air defense systems, missiles, and ammunition mean stronger protection for our people and greater capabilities for our defenders on the front line,” he added, noting that Kyiv is working with European partners to secure the rest of the defense funding without further delays.
Funds arrive as Russia escalates its air campaign
The disbursement follows one of Russia’s heaviest strikes on Ukraine’s energy system this autumn.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukraine’s Defense Forces recorded roughly 39 missiles and 128 launched by Russia, which left at least 600,000 people without power according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks – cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure,” President of the European Commission Ursula von Der Leyen said.
Russian Strikes Destroy Epicentr K’s Last Major Logistics Hub
The defense payments are expected to reach Ukraine in the upcoming weeks.
What remains for 2026
Ukraine still has €29.64 billion (roughly $33 billion) in EU financial support available for the rest of the year, according to the Commission.
That includes €25.24 billion ($28 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan, split between €12.54 billion (approx. $14 billion) for Ukraine’s defense industry and €12.7 billion (about $14 billion) in budget support, plus €4.4 billion (about $5 billion) left under the earlier Ukraine Facility.
Budget payments depend on Kyiv meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and a memorandum of understanding with the EU.
Ukraine had received €1.2 billion (roughly $1.3 billion) just a week earlier, on Oct. 7, bringing total funding received under the program to nearly €13 billion ($14.5 billion) according to Koretskyi.
Mid-September, Koretskyi warned Ukraine risks losing a substantial amount of $29.5 billion in planned international financing if the parliament misses deadlines for required legislation.
The government has moved its deadline for 42 required decisions to Oct. 15 as it prepares for winter pressure on the budget.
According to the European Commission, the Ukraine Support Loan was adopted in February 2026, and it provides up to €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) over 2026-27, with an indicative €60 billion ($67 billion) for defense and €30 billion ($33 billion) for the budget.
The Council approved this year’s allocation on April 23 after Ukraine submitted its financing strategy.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion ($258 billion) in total support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion ($4.2 billion) from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.

articles.title: WATCH aftermath of Ukrainian drone attack on Russian oil refinery
articles.body:
WATCH aftermath of Ukrainian drone attack on Russian oil refinery
Videos online have captured a fire that broke out at an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Region following a major overnight Ukrainian drone raid.
The Russian Defense Ministry said air defenses and military aircraft shot down four Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing drones between 4 AM and 7 AM local time on Thursday. The blaze was caused by the debris of a fallen UAV, it added. Ryazan Region lies less than 200 kilometers (124 miles) southeast of Moscow.
The attack came as Ukraine continued its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure for a second consecutive day, with two oil refineries – in Ryazan and Saratov Regions – being targeted by UAVs on Wednesday, according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak.
The Russian military has warned that it will respond in kind to the strikes by Ukraine. Novak earlier said that Kiev had shown no signs of moving towards an energy truce, which US President Donald Trump is trying to broker.
On Thursday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said Kiev will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after a three-day pause he introduced under pressure from Trump.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said later in the day that “in fact, there was no moratorium on the part of Ukraine. Strikes on our oil refineries and energy facilities continued throughout this whole period. Therefore, there is nothing new here.”
The Trump administration’s “active attempts” to settle the Ukraine conflict “are being crushed by the unwillingness of the Kiev regime and Zelensky, in particular, to agree to peace,” Peskov added.

articles.title: Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better
articles.body:
Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better
Estonia continues to insist that Russian oil refineries and energy facilities should be destroyed because they fund Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Prime Minister of Estonia Kristen Michal ahead of a European Council meeting on 15 October, as reported by European Pravda's Brussels correspondent
Details: Michal repeated an argument he has made before: that Russian oil refineries must be destroyed because sales of energy finance the war.
Quote: "I have said publicly in Estonia that the faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens, the better. Because Russia is funding the war with that."
Details: Michal stressed that Estonia relies on the US as a partner and NATO ally that assists with security matters.
"We rely on them. And also sometimes even good friends need a remind[er of] what is right," the Estonian minister said.
Michal mentioned that Estonia shares a border with Russia and has the support of the three nuclear powers within NATO: the US, UK and France.
Quote: "We have had shadow fleet cutting our cables, different kind of pipelines. We have had Russian fighter jets in our airspace. We have even had to shoot down different drones in our airspace. They all came. Help came from NATO… So, basing on that, I must say that NATO is working well and the US is a partner in NATO. Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following NATO and also Article 5."
Background:
- The European Council is meeting in Brussels on 15-16 October. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to attend on 16 October.
- No additional decisions regarding financial aid for Ukraine are planned to be made at the meeting, and the question of using frozen Russian assets is not on the leaders' formal agenda, although the topic may be raised during the discussions.
- European Pravda previously reported that the European Council plans to call for stricter visa requirements for Russian citizens.
- The European Council will also "express regret over the agreement reached between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin on the supply of Russian diesel".
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles, complicating defence against Russian ballistic attacks – media
articles.body:
Ukraine has run out of U.S. interceptor missiles for its Patriot air defense systems, which is why nearly all ballistic missiles were not shot down during the latest Russian attack, CNN reports, citing a source familiar with the situation.
According to the network's source, the shortage of interceptor missiles meant that most ballistic targets were not intercepted during the attack on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning. Russian missiles struck three power plants in Kyiv and damaged energy infrastructure in Kharkiv.
"Almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles," the publication said citing the source.
As CNN notes, this is likely not the first time Ukraine has completely exhausted its stockpile of interceptor missiles for the Patriot system. In the middle of August, when the network gained access to one of these systems on Ukrainian territory, Ukrainian officials reported that the country had virtually exhausted its stockpile of these missiles.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after a three-day halt due to an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy expressed support for his US counterpart's proposed energy ceasefire, but claimed Russian strikes continued despite Kyiv’s halt.
“That's it. Block is out,” Zelenskyy said, responding to a question about how much longer Ukraine will maintain a halt to energy strikes.
On reports that the US suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Zelenskyy said that over the course of Ukraine’s three-day halt to strikes in Russia, his country was subject to ballistic missile attacks and did not receive any early warning alerts.
He said Washington had earlier warned Kyiv about the blocking of intelligence if it did not stop strikes on Russian energy sites.
“This is, I think, the problem. And when it goes together with Starlink's decision, which is 100% the decision of American side … I think that (it is) not (about) military people. I think it's about SpaceX. So together it makes huge problems,” Zelenskyy added.
Zelenskyy said he told Trump that Ukraine will "destroy" Russia's ballistic missile launchers if Starlink opens on Russian territory.
He argued that if a diesel deal, such as the one announced over the weekend, forces Ukraine to be silent on the battlefield, then questions will arise concerning "when the next deal will be," which would "definitely" concern Russian gas.
The Ukraine leader said he does not want to interfere in "diesel deals," but Ukraine will respond to Russian strikes.
"The question (is): can you give me missiles for Patriot (systems), because when I will not attack them because you asked me not attack them, they will attack me. It's fair if you will give me with what to defend.
"It's the minimum what I ask. No? I think yes. And when I'm asking this, your answer is blocking Starlink," he added.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a freelance adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said on Wednesday that speed restrictions were implemented on Starlink satellites in Ukraine, limiting their speed to 100 mph (161 kph).
"Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," Beskrestnov added.
US billionaire Elon Musk said Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government," and decisions on speed or usage restrictions are made by the US military and ultimately the president.
Separately, Zelenskyy told British journalist Piers Morgan that he felt "betrayed" over the diesel agreement between Russia and the US.
He said he is "sure that they knew what they did," commenting on a question on whether the speed restrictions on Starlink satellites were implemented deliberately.

articles.title: Russian nuclear submarine conducts live-fire drill in Pacific (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russian nuclear submarine conducts live-fire drill in Pacific (VIDEO)
The Russian Navy has successfully conducted a live-fire exercise in the Pacific, using a nuclear-powered submarine to strike sea and land targets with cruise missiles.
The Yasen M-class attack submarine Novosibirsk launched the weapons while submerged during a scheduled drill, the Russian Defense Ministry announced on Wednesday.
According to the report, an Onyx cruise missile struck a simulated enemy warship at a distance of 170 km.
A Kalibr cruise missile was used to hit a land target at the Kura testing range on Kamchatka Peninsula, more than 1,200 km from the launch position.
The 130-meter-long Novosibirsk is the first submarine of the upgraded Yasen-M class to be built in series production.
Construction began in 2013, and the vessel was launched in 2019. It joined Russia’s Pacific Fleet in 2022 alongside the Knyaz Oleg nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine.

articles.title: The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink's operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
articles.body:
The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink's operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
Kyiv • UNN
SpaceX has restricted the speed of Starshield terminals, causing drones to lose connection in flight. The Ministry of Defense has appealed to the United States, SpaceX, and NATO.
On the night of October 14, SpaceX imposed restrictions without warning on the Starshield military satellite communications system, causing Ukrainian drones to begin losing connectivity during flights. Some Ukrainian Armed Forces units have already had to cancel some combat missions. Defense Express reports this, citing sources in the military and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, SpaceX set a speed limit for Starshield terminals at 160 km/h. After this threshold is exceeded, the terminal loses connectivity. At the same time, the military is recording disruptions even at significantly lower speeds—approximately 72 to 161 km/h.
In particular, when drones fly at speeds of 110–120 km/h, the connection may disappear for 10–20 seconds. Although the drones continue moving, such interruptions significantly complicate controlling them.
The restrictions threaten attack drones and interceptors
The greatest problems arise with high-speed drones, in particular Middle Strike-type drones, which need to reach high speed immediately after launch. Due to the unstable connection, some aircraft may lose the ability to carry out their missions.
The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones. At the same time, the forced reduction in flight speed makes Ukrainian UAVs more vulnerable to Russian countermeasures.
According to a Defense Express source, on October 14 alone, one of the unmanned systems units was forced to cancel some missions because of problems with Starlink.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to journalists that the restrictions had been introduced and said it was already in contact with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners. The American company has so far provided no official explanations for the reasons behind the changes.

articles.title: Ukraine Says Missile Strike Destroyed 6 Russian Warplanes at Voronezh Airfield
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Navy said Thursday that it destroyed six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers in an overnight missile strike on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in southwestern Russia’s Voronezh region.
The Navy said the attack was carried out using its Neptune coastal missile system. It also reported damage to equipment supporting flight operations, a fire and secondary explosions.
Ukrainian monitoring channels published satellite images purportedly showing damage to an aircraft parking area. The reported destruction of the six warplanes could not be independently verified.
Russian authorities did not acknowledge a strike on the airfield.
Voronezh region Governor Alexander Gusev said air defenses intercepted 33 drones and “several jet-powered aerial targets.” Falling debris damaged outbuildings at several private homes and a car in the regional capital, Voronezh, he said.
Residents of Borisoglebsk reported explosions and a large fire, with smoke visible from several parts of the city.
The military airfield lies about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) east of Borisoglebsk.
Russia uses Su-34 fighter-bombers to launch guided glide bombs at Ukrainian positions and populated areas. The Su-34M is an upgraded version of the aircraft.
In September, Ukraine’s military said it had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet near the Millerovo airfield in the Rostov region and a Ka-27 helicopter near the Yeysk airfield in the Krasnodar region.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces had previously reported striking four aircraft at the Shagol airfield in the Chelyabinsk region: two Su-57 fighters, a Su-34 and another Sukhoi aircraft of an unidentified model. Those targets were about 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

articles.title: Bloomberg: UK provides Ukraine with additional long-range Storm Shadow missiles
articles.body:
Bloomberg: UK provides Ukraine with additional long-range Storm Shadow missiles
The UK is sending Ukraine more long-range Storm Shadow missiles so it can disrupt Russian military operations targeting its civilian infrastructure before the winter.
Source: Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the sources, the resupply of the British-made cruise missiles was discussed by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy when the Ukrainian leader visited London on Wednesday 14 October.
The sources noted that the UK considers Ukraine's use of long-range weapons to target Russian sites involved in attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure to be defensive.
They said Russia has ramped up production of jet-powered drones and missiles in recent weeks in order to escalate its attacks on Ukraine, and it is important that Kyiv is able to counter those efforts.
They also noted that the UK does not believe Ukraine should halt its strikes on Russia while Moscow refuses to do the same.
The UK government declined to comment. It hasn't said how many Storm Shadow missiles it has given Ukraine during the war and doesn't regularly announce transfers.
Background:
- It emerged previously that the UK and Ukraine had agreed to speed up the delivery of British air defence systems.
- At the start of the meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham assured the Ukrainian president that his country's support for Ukraine "will not change". Ahead of the talks, the UK prime minister had pledged that Zelenskyy would not leave London "empty handed".
- It is worth noting that during his visit to Kyiv on 24 August, Burnham announced that the UK would share blueprints for long-range missiles with Kyiv so it could assemble them in Ukraine.

articles.title: ACC Mulls Commercial Counter-Drone Services for Air Base Defense
articles.body:
Air Combat Command is looking for defense firms capable of providing a private counter-drone service, complete with the personnel to operate it, for defending air bases across the Air Force.
ACC, which oversees the service’s Point Defense Task Force, is conducting a market survey to identify companies specializing in counter-small unmanned aerial systems defense technology that can provide “C-sUAS as a Service,” according to an Oct. 13 solicitation.
According to the solicitation, the intent of the service model is to:
- Provide organic, resilient, sustainable, and agile Point Defense capabilities across Department of the Air Force installations
- Implement a flexible, scalable architecture allowing installations to scale operational capacity up or down based on dynamic threat levels
- Leverage mature, commercially available or rapidly adaptable systems rather than initiating high-risk developmental programs
The market survey comes as the Air Force races to develop an arsenal of capabilities to defend its installations against drone threat.
“The Government envisions an initial prototype deployment at two designated Continental United States Air Force installations, with option mechanisms to scale across additional ACC installations upon proven performance,” the document states.
Interested firms have until Oct. 31 to respond to the solicitation. ACC is interested in companies that can provide technology for detecting, tracking, and identifying drones—ranging from small quadcopters to larger, Group 3 systems like the Iranian Shahed one-way attack drones that weight up to 1,320 pounds—at distances of up to five miles from a base perimeter, the document states.
Firms should also be capable of incorporating “government-approved kinetic and/or nonkinetic” effectors that range from radio frequency jamming to directed-energy such as lasers and high-powered microwave systems, the document states. Interested defense firms would also have to show they would continuously refresh software and hardware “within a multiyear service contract without frequent contract modifications,” according to the document.
ACC would also want a commercial capability to have the built-in logistical support to be self-sufficient for up to 96 hours, the document states.
The concept would require the contractor to “provide a complete, integrated, turn-key service solution covering materiel, personnel, training, sustainment, and ongoing modernization,” the solicitation states.
It’s unclear how this commercial service would align with the service’s intent to create a new point defense career field for enlisted Airmen, training and equipping them to defend air bases from drone and missile attack. The Air Force is slated to start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. As a short-term fix, the service has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Currently, the Air Force is equipping installations with the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
The service is also acquiring additional counter-drone systems through the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. In the future, counter-drone technology will fall under the “point defense weapon system,” a classification to manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and non-kinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.

articles.title: Britain funds Chornobyl repairs after Russian drone hit
articles.body:
Britain is putting £17 million towards repairing the protective shelter over the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, which was punctured by a Russian drone strike last year, according to the government.
The money forms part of an international programme coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development alongside the Ukrainian government and G7 donors, and will pay for work to restore the structure’s confinement and ventilation functions and protect its intended lifespan. Corrosion threatens to undermine decades of international investment and create longer term environmental and safety risks if the damage is left.
John Healey, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, said: “As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable. We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks.”
Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, said: “Our message to Putin is clear, we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail. Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine’s security, raising the cost of Russia’s aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace.”
The structure in question is the New Safe Confinement, the arch built over the remains of reactor four and the Soviet-era sarcophagus around it, which was slid into position in 2016 and handed over in 2019 after an international effort costing around €1.5 billion. It was designed to hold for a century while the reactor underneath is dismantled, and its outer skin and ventilation system are what keep moisture out of the space where that work has to happen. A drone strike that breaches it turns a sealed structure into one that corrodes.
Attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have continued through the autumn at a heavy rate. Between 5 and 11 October Russia carried out more than two hundred strikes on electricity infrastructure and a further seventeen on oil and gas facilities, six of them after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. On 13 October Russia fired thirty-nine ballistic missiles at Ukraine in one of the largest such attacks of the war, much of it aimed at energy targets, leaving six hundred thousand civilians without power.
Britain has been involved in nuclear safety at the site for years. It was a founding donor to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account in 2020, when that account took over responsibility for safety in the exclusion zone, and has given €8 million to it, making it the third largest individual donor behind Norway and France.
The Foreign Secretary visited Kyiv last week for the first time since taking office and announced £54 million of winter support, including £20 million in energy funding. The Prime Minister hosted President Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, where he set out a further package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles built by Thales in Belfast.

articles.title: Ukrainian troops lost Starlink access for a day. Elon Musk and the Trump White House both deny responsibility.
articles.body:
Ukrainian troops lost Starlink access for a day. Elon Musk and the Trump White House both deny responsibility.
On the morning of October 14, Ukrainian soldiers began reporting restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite network that is essential for maintaining contact with drones moving at high speed. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, said “this action can’t be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” referring to the conflict between Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump. On the morning of October 15, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said the system was working again. At the same time, no one in the United States has taken responsibility for the outage. Here is a brief summary of the various versions of what happened.
Volodymyr Zelensky, president of Ukraine. It’s their decision. It’s a big mistake. This decision will bring a lot of human losses. People will die if the attacks continue and Starlink doesn’t work. I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe a huge technical problem. We’re asking them to turn it back on. That would be fair.
Elon Musk, head of SpaceX (the satellite operator behind Starlink). Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
The White House, anonymously. The U.S. presidential administration has nothing to do with the disruptions to Starlink’s operation.
The White House, officially. Declined to answer questions about Starlink. The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Thom Tillis, U.S. senator. I’m not holding my breath for Defense Secretary Hegseth to offer transparency, so we’ll be asking the DOD Inspector General to initiate an investigation and report back to Congress and the American People. At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscience decision to clear the field for a Russian attack.
