articles.title: Another Starlink facility hit by blaze in EU (VIDEO)
articles.body:
New blaze reported at EU Starlink facility (VIDEO)
A blaze has occurred at a Starlink satellite internet service facility near Bulgaria’s capital Sofia, Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev has announced.
In September a fire was reported at a data-relay station in Poland used by SpaceX, which serviced the Ukrainian military. Ukraine has relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones.
Earlier this week, an MP for the opposition Democratic Bulgaria coalition, Ivaylo Mirchev, published a video he claimed shows masked men setting alight a facility used by Starlink outside Sofia, destroying 11 of its 17 antennas.
🚨 Two masked men reportedly set fire to 11 of 17 antennas linked to SpaceX's Starlink network near Sofia, Bulgaria. via WarSurv https://t.co/RgvLK4sasG
— Post Open Source (@CocoPostel) October 14, 2026
Radev confirmed the incident to the Bulgarian parliament on Wednesday, but declined to say if it was a result of an arson attack.
“An investigation is underway. Just a little more patience, and there will be a result,” the prime minister said, urging other government officials against disclosing any details of the probe until it’s concluded. “If the specific findings are revealed, we will not achieve the outcome we are aiming for,” he added.
Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told lawmakers that additional measures to protect Starlink stations and similar facilities across the country will be implemented. However, he stressed that they are private sites and that the primary responsibility for their security lies with their owners.
However, Democratic Bulgaria MP Bozhidar Bozhanov wasted no time waiting for the results of the investigation of the blaze to lash out at Moscow. “Why are you afraid to name Russia? Why don’t you act like Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” he asked Radev.
The prime minister responded by saying that Bozhanov apparently has “a crystal ball and therefore knows who the perpetrator is.”
Tusk previously called the fire at Wola Krobowska outside Warsaw last month “another act of hybrid warfare.” Polish special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said this week that there was “no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” but provided no proof to the accusations. Two Turkish nationals have been arrested in Germany in connection with the incident.
Russia has consistently rejected claims of it engaging in any sabotage activities in Europe. Russian President Vladimir Putin and various officials have said that the so-called “Russian threat” is only being promoted by Western politicians to scare their public, distract people from the mounting problems in their own countries and justify growing military spending.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders complained that Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working when drones flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk denied giving any instructions to restrict Kiev’s access to the service, saying that doing so is the prerogative of the American military and US President Donald Trump personally.
The problems occurred as Trump is working to increase pressure on Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for surging global energy prices.
Last month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate Ukrainian strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.” Moscow has all the means to respond to such actions, he warned.

articles.title: US: Somerville weighs Israel boycott over Gaza genocide
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US: Somerville weighs Israel boycott over Gaza genocide
Lawmakers in Somerville, Massachusetts, are considering an ordinance that would bar the US city from awarding contracts to companies accused of complicity in Israel’s violations of international law, amid growing pressure to sever financial ties with firms linked to Israel's genocide in Gaza.
The proposal follows a November 2025 ballot measure backed by 55.7% of voters, calling for the city to end existing business with, and prohibit future contracts and investments in, companies linked to Israel’s “apartheid, genocide, and illegal occupation of Palestine”.
The City Council has delayed a decision to assess the ordinance’s scope and financial impact, with a vote expected on 27 October, according to local reports.
Following renewed discussions on Tuesday led by Somerville’s Legislative Matters Committee, councillors said more time was needed to assess which businesses would be affected and the potential financial implications for the city.
Two Jewish councillors have raised concerns about the proposal, particularly over which companies would fall within its scope.
If enacted, Somerville would join a growing number of US cities adopting divestment measures in line with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, which seeks to hold Israel accountable for its violations of Palestinian rights through economic pressure.
However, the passage of last year's ballot measure prompted a backlash from pro-Israel groups, which have been pressuring the city to reject the proposed ordinance, citing Somerville’s longstanding Jewish community, which is made up of around 84,000 residents.
Jewish opposition to Israel's policies has grown in the US, with many challenging attempts to portray criticism of Israel or support for Palestinian rights as inherently antisemitic.
An October 2025 survey, reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, found that 39% of American Jews believed Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
More recently, a July 2026 Associated Press-NORC poll highlighted deep divisions within Jewish communities over Israel's military actions. Around four in ten religiously unaffiliated Jewish respondents believed Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, compared with around a quarter of religiously affiliated Jewish respondents.
A separate September 2026 survey by the Jewish Electorate Institute found that 61% of American Jewish voters held an unfavourable view of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while 60% wanted him replaced.
The findings underline the diversity of Jewish opinion on Israel, even as pro-Israel groups continue to challenge divestment campaigns.
Somerville for Palestine (S4P), a local organisation that spearheaded both the ballot initiative and the proposed ordinance, has continued to press the council to implement the measure.
The group supports the BDS movement, which has long called for boycotts and divestment from companies it considers complicit in Israeli apartheid and genocide in Gaza.
Pro-Palestine activists have accused the city of maintaining financial ties with companies targeted by the BDS movement.
They point to city records showing that its pension fund has more than $500,000 invested in Lockheed Martin, a weapons manufacturer whose fighter jets and Hellfire missiles have reportedly played a significant role in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Activists have also highlighted more than $1.7 million in contracts Somerville has awarded to Hewlett-Packard over several decades.
According to the BDS movement, HP-linked technology has been used in biometric surveillance systems at Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank, which Palestinians and rights groups have condemned as part of Israel’s system of apartheid.
The ballot initiative and proposed ordinance have received backing from several Somerville councillors, including Ben Ewen-Campen, Ben Wheeler, Wilfred N. Mbah and Jon Link. Jewish Voice for Peace Boston has also voiced support for the measures, demonstrating that Jewish organisations are among those backing efforts to hold Israel accountable through divestment.
The campaign comes amid growing calls for local councils across the US, North America and the wider Western world to recognise the Gaza genocide and sever financial ties with companies accused of facilitating violations of international law.
Pro-Palestine campaigners are urging councils to divest from arms manufacturers supplying Israel with weapons and military technology, as well as companies involved in financing or constructing illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
Somerville’s debate follows a decision by Montreal’s city council in Canada to pass an amended motion in August expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people and civilians affected by hostilities across the Middle East.
The move followed a backlash from pro-Israel groups against an earlier proposal calling on the city to recognise and condemn “apartheid” and “genocide” in Palestine and immediately suspend institutional ties with the Israeli government, its institutions and municipalities.

articles.title: Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,880 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 535 Vehicles in One Day
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,880 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 535 Vehicles in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,880 troops and dozens of pieces of military equipment over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 15.
The latest figures bring Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,559,230.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost two armored combat vehicles, bringing cumulative losses in that category to 25,537, while estimated tank losses remained unchanged at 12,414. Ukraine also reported four multiple-launch rocket systems and three air defense systems lost during the latest reporting period, raising those totals to 2,216 and 1,707, respectively.
Another 1,308 operational-tactical UAVs were added to the tally, bringing estimated cumulative losses to 564,897. Ukraine also recorded four unmanned ground systems lost, raising that category to 2,955, while four additional cruise missiles brought the cumulative figure to 5,130.
Russia’s estimated aviation losses remained unchanged at 443 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while naval losses stayed at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 535 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the past day, pushing the cumulative total to 163,324. Ukraine also reported two additional pieces of special equipment, bringing that figure to 4,830.
Fighting remained particularly intense, with Ukrainian forces recording 260 combat engagements across the front during the latest reporting period.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukrainian forces have regained control of another 101 square kilometers (39 square miles) of territory and liberated three villages in the Donetsk region, bringing the total area recovered during Operation Vivaldi to 277 square kilometers (107 square miles).

articles.title: Ukraine to resume refinery strikes amid dispute with US
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country would resume hitting Russian oil refineries and adopted a noticeably more defiant tone towards U.S. President Donald Trump in an interview published on Oct. 15 by the Financial Times.
Since Trump returned to power, Washington’s support for Ukraine has fluctuated alongside his unexpected social media remarks, which have often taken Moscow and Kiev by surprise.
Trump last week unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was never publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
But after a wave of renewed Russian strikes on facilities on Oct. 14, Zelensky told the FT: “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done.”
Russia said on Oct. 15 that Ukraine had attacked an oil refinery in Ryazan, south of the capital, Moscow.
Since Russia launched its invasion in 2022, Ukraine has faced repeated strikes on its power infrastructure and gradually expanded what it says are retaliatory strikes into Russian territory, including on refineries.
Trump criticized the attacks, especially after he struck a surprise diesel deal with Moscow and ordered Ukraine to stop targeting Russian refineries.
Zelensky said Ukraine paused the strikes for several days, despite Russian claims, denied by Kiev, that Ukraine attempted to target refineries during that period.
Despite complying, Zelensky said Ukraine saw its access to key U.S. military capabilities and intelligence restricted.
Starshield, the satellite network built on Starlink and used by militaries, was slowed over on Oct. 14.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” Zelensky told the FT.
He also warned of a “dangerous” cutting off of intelligence sharing with Kiev, which relies heavily on early warnings to protect its cities from Russian air attacks.
Fears that Washington could curb intelligence cooperation had already surfaced after a public clash between Trump and Zelensky early in Trump’s presidency.
The Ukrainian presidency has since worked to smooth relations with Washington, trying to adapt to Trump’s fluctuating stances.
In the interview, Zelensky made a pointed comment about the relationship between Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump “speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong”, he said.
Zelensky also urged the United States not to stand with the aggressor on Oct. 15, calling for “honesty.”
“We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” Zelensky said on social media.

articles.title: Russia Builds Military Communications Network Across Belarus Toward NATO and Ukraine — BELPOL
articles.body:
A new secure military communications system for the Belarusian Ministry of Defense is being deployed across Belarus. It is designed to support the deployment and movement of Russian troops toward the borders of NATO countries.
This is according to the analytical report “The Militarization of Belarus,” presented in Warsaw by the Belarusian association BELPOL and the clandestine Community of Railway Workers of Belarus (CRWB), as reported by Centrum Europy.
The 48-page document was presented the previous day with the participation of Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, leader of Belarus’s democratic forces, as part of the Warsaw Security Forum.
According to the authors, the report was compiled using open sources, materials from the Belarusian underground, and information obtained from Russian generals.
The network under construction is based on radio relay links and directional antennas that allow data to be transmitted over radio channels with minimal risk of interception or eavesdropping.
Specialized equipment is being installed on towers operated by mobile operator MTS, which is 49% owned by Russia and 51% by the Belarusian state.
BELPOL analysts emphasize that the system’s architecture indicates that it is designed to meet Russia’s military needs.
The radio relay network is not being built outward from Minsk to regional centers. Instead, continuous east-to-west routes are being established from the Russian border to the borders of Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Ukraine.
One such route is being laid along the M-10 highway between Gomel and Brest.
BELPOL representative Matvei Kupreichik said the geographical distribution of the repeaters points to preparations to provide infrastructure for the Russian army, while the system’s sole command center is located in Russia.
It was previously reported that in the second half of 2025, Russia deployed a network of repeaters in Belarus to control drones attacking northern regions of Ukraine.
Areas stretching from the Kyiv region to Volyn are at risk of strikes by these Russian drones.

articles.title: Iran's deputy FM visits Lebanon amid diplomatic tensions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran's deputy FM visits Lebanon amid diplomatic tensions
Iran's deputy foreign minister Saeed Khatibzadeh held talks with Lebanese officials in Beirut on Thursday in an apparent effort to ease mounting diplomatic tensions between the two countries, following Lebanon's refusal to recognise Tehran's newly appointed ambassador.
The visit coincided with a phone call between Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, signalling a possible attempt to repair relations after months of strained relations over Iran's influence in Lebanon and its support for Hezbollah.
Lebanon has expressed willingness to turn the page with Tehran, provided ties are based on mutual respect, sovereignty and non-interference in each other's internal affairs.
However, Lebanese officials remain concerned that Hezbollah could once again draw the country into a wider regional conflict in support of Iran, particularly amid fears of renewed military escalation involving Tehran, Washington and Israel.
Khatibzadeh met Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri at his Ain el-Tineh residence in Beirut on Thursday, with Iran's chargé d'affaires in Lebanon, Tawfiq Samadi, also attending.
The discussions focused on developments in Lebanon and the wider region, including Israel's continued attacks on Lebanese territory and its refusal to withdraw from the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Following the meeting, Khatibzadeh emphasised the longstanding relationship between the two countries.
"I conveyed my warmest wishes to the Lebanese people and to Lebanon, this great country with which we share longstanding and friendly relations at various levels," he said.
He added that such visits were a natural part of bilateral relations, serving not only to exchange views but also to strengthen coordination between Beirut and Tehran.
The Iranian official arrived in Beirut on Wednesday, where he was received by representatives of Hezbollah and the Amal Movement.
He also met Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, deputy head of Lebanon's Higher Islamic Shia Council, to discuss regional developments and the prospects for the coming period.
During the meeting, Khatibzadeh outlined Iran's position on ongoing contacts and negotiations with the United States.
Lebanon insists on sovereignty and diplomacy
The diplomatic outreach follows Wednesday's telephone conversation between Aoun and Araghchi, during which the two officials discussed recent regional developments and agreed on the importance of pursuing diplomatic solutions to end conflicts across the Middle East.
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab's Arabic-language sister publication, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, that Beirut remained open to relations with Iran based on mutual respect and non-interference.
The sources said Lebanon had previously asked Tehran to nominate a new ambassador to Beirut but remained firm in its rejection of attempts to turn the country into an arena for regional conflicts.
"Lebanon is tired of wars and refuses to continue being dragged into them," the sources said, adding that the country was still paying the price of previous conflicts involving Hezbollah.
They also expressed concern over escalating rhetoric from Hezbollah and continuing Israeli threats, while stressing that Beirut remained committed to negotiations despite the difficulties involved.
"There is no solution except diplomacy, not war," the sources said.
The visit has nevertheless drawn criticism from Lebanese political figures opposed to Hezbollah.
Kataeb Party leader and MP Samy Gemayel rejected Khatibzadeh's presence in Beirut, posting the words "persona non grata" in Persian on X on Wednesday.
Ambassador dispute deepens tensions
Relations between Beirut and Tehran have deteriorated in recent months, particularly over Iran's opposition to Lebanese government decisions aimed at placing all weapons under state control.
Lebanese authorities have accused Tehran of interfering in the country's internal affairs through its political and military support for Hezbollah.
Tensions intensified following the regional escalation in March, when Lebanon adopted a tougher stance towards Tehran following Iranian attacks on Arab and Gulf states.
The Lebanese government also introduced stricter measures concerning Iranian nationals after Israeli airstrikes targeted two hotels in and around Beirut during the March 2026 offensive.
Israel claimed that members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were staying at the hotels and threatened further attacks against Iranian personnel in Lebanon.
The diplomatic dispute escalated after Tehran appointed Mohammad Reza Raouf Sheibani as its new ambassador to Beirut, replacing Mojtaba Amani, who was injured in Israel's pager attacks on 17 September 2024.
On 24 March, Lebanese authorities withdrew recognition of Sheibani's diplomatic accreditation and ordered him to leave the country.
He remained in Lebanon despite the decision and was subsequently granted a courtesy residency permit.
Khatibzadeh's visit also comes amid renewed attention to Iranian financial support for Hezbollah.
On Tuesday, Hezbollah announced financial assistance for displaced Lebanese families and those whose homes had been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable by Israeli attacks.
The announcement coincided with reports that Hezbollah had received $200 million in funding from Iran, although the US State Department issued statements disputing the existence of the alleged funds.

articles.title: How Russia plans to revive its ties with Slovakia
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Slovakia is reviving a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow, putting Russia’s gas and oil supplies, nuclear fuel and the treatment of Russian athletes high on the agenda of their first such meeting in five years, according to a Russian government note obtained by POLITICO.
The note, written by Russian Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov, says Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár agreed during an Aug. 20 video call to hold a meeting of the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission in Moscow.
Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico said Wednesday the meeting is scheduled for Nov. 25. The Russian note — which is dated Sept. 10 — initially set the date of the meeting as Oct. 26-27.
Advertisement
The IGC, which covers economic, scientific and technical cooperation, has been dormant since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The last meeting was the commission’s 21st session, held in Bratislava on Nov. 12, 2021.
The meeting comes as Moscow finds openings in other international arenas. The U.S. has invited Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, while the International Olympic Committee has provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and urged sports bodies to ease restrictions on Russian athletes.
Asked about the purported agenda for the IGC, the Slovak foreign ministry directed POLITICO to Blanár’s public statements after the Aug. 20 call. “We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár said at the time.
The Russian foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The renewed push for warmer Slovak-Russian relations follows Fico’s May 9 visit to Moscow, where he met Russia's President Vladimir Putin during Victory Day commemorations. It comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election, which cost Putin one of his closest partners in Europe and forced him to look elsewhere for EU allies.
Months before losing the election to Péter Magyar, Orbán rebooted the Russian-Hungarian Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, which had been suspended for several years after the 2022 invasion. Magyar's government did not confirm to POLITICO whether the commission would go ahead next year.
Advertisement
EU leaders, including Fico, will gather in Brussels on Thursday for a two-day summit focused on issues including energy prices and support for Ukraine, with the country's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expected to join them for a conversation on Friday.
Oil imports and cultural integration
In the August video call, Blanár raised Slovakia’s opposition to the EU’s phaseout of Russian gas imports and asked to discuss supplies at the Moscow meeting, according to the document, which POLITICO could not independently verify but bears the hallmarks of a legitimate Russian ministerial note. Slovak representatives also stressed the importance of continued Russian oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline and welcomed regular shipments of nuclear fuel for Slovak power plants, according to the note.
Slovakia remains heavily reliant on Russian oil and gas, and Fico has argued that ending imports would raise costs. When the two leaders met in Moscow on May 9, Putin said Russia would do everything to meet Slovakia’s energy needs.
The agenda for the meeting next month reaches beyond energy, according to the document. The sides plan to explore working groups on culture, tourism, agriculture and environmental protection, and to discuss the status of the Russian Center for Science and Culture in Bratislava.
Falkov also records Blanár’s opposition to what the note calls the “discrimination against Russian athletes” at international competitions, noting the issue is to be discussed at the IGC meeting.
The International Olympic Committee lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July and said its previous recommendations restricting Russian athletes’ participation no longer applied. World Archery lifted restrictions on Russian athletes and officials in August. FIFA President Gianni Infantino has also called for Russia to be allowed back into international football.
Advertisement
The approach echoes Moscow’s recent effort to lock in closer ties with Orbán’s Hungary. Budapest and Moscow in December agreed on a 12-point plan to expand cooperation in areas including energy, trade and culture. The plan was signed by then Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó and Russian Health Minister Mikhail Murashko after talks in Moscow in December. The Slovak note points to a similar breadth of ambition.
The Kremlin’s outreach to Fico shows how Moscow can use energy ties to pull individual EU countries away from a united stance on Ukraine. Putin made a similar pitch in Washington last weekend: After a call with the Russian leader, President Donald Trump said Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets to bring down fuel prices. The deal would provide revenue to Moscow while weakening efforts to maintain a united front against the Kremlin.
But there are questions over whether Putin can follow through on his pledge to Trump. Ukraine has been stepping up drone strikes on Russian refineries, aiming to disrupt fuel supplies and cut revenue for Moscow’s war effort. Kyiv said this month that strikes had disabled 51 percent of Russia’s oil-refining capacity.

articles.title: A Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, Ukraine’s largest painting, in the section depicting the future. Its artist spent nearly two years creating it
articles.body:
Debris from a Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, a painting that set a national record in Ukraine, the Korsaks Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, where the artwork was exhibited, reported on 14 October. A fire destroyed part of the painting’s final section, titled The Future, according to the statement.
Russian drones continue to attack Ukraine. Overnight into 15 October alone, Ukrainian air defense forces downed or suppressed 536 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). In recent days, Lutsk, a city in northwestern Ukraine, has been among the cities damaged by Russian attacks. Russian UAV attacks set fire to an oil depot, a wholesale warehouse, and a shopping center. At the museum, located on the shopping center’s premises, the fire damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, which covers a canvas of more than 2,000 square meters.
Russian attack damages museum in Lutsk
A fire broke out at the Adrenalin City shopping and entertainment complex, where the museum is located, Suspilne Lutsk reported. The blaze damaged the last of the painting’s six sections, according to the report.
“By destroying art and culture, they are also trying to destroy Ukrainians,” Tetiana Repnytska, director of the Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, told Suspilne Lutsk.
Museum staff also had to evacuate more than 300 works by Ukrainian artist Emma Andiievska, which were exhibited alongside Cosmogony, Oles Tomakh, the museum’s chief curator, told Suspilne Lutsk. Some works could not be removed in time, resulting in shattered glass. However, the museum’s other exhibition halls were unaffected, the chief curator said.
The museum is weighing whether to fully restore the damaged fragment or keep the fire’s traces as a reminder of the war, and will decide after consulting the artist, Petro Antyp, and restoration specialists, it said. Repnytska told Suspilne Lutsk that the painting’s authors could also create a new section.
“Despite the shelling, we will continue to develop contemporary Ukrainian art and preserve it,” the museum director said.
Cosmogony—Ukraine’s largest painting
Artist Petro Antyp began working on the painting in November 2022, Suspilne Lutsk reported, and it took almost two years to complete, according to the museum’s website. The painting covers an area of 2,086 square meters.
In September 2024, the project set a national record as Ukraine’s largest painting.
The artwork explores the evolution of the universe, Earth, nature, humanity, society, culture, and science. Its six sections combine myths, legends, scientific theories, and symbols from different cultures, according to the museum’s website.
The project extends beyond the canvas, as the museum presents a multimedia performance that combines light, sound, and art.
Civilians killed and injured in Russia’s latest attack on Lutsk
Around noon on 14 October, a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone attacked Lutsk. Drone debris damaged a wholesale goods warehouse and a residential building, Roman Romaniuk, acting head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration, told Suspilne.
Falling drone debris sparked a large fire at the Yevrohurt wholesale warehouse. A nine-story residential building on Sobornosti Avenue was also damaged, Romaniuk later reported on social media.
Six people were killed in the strike on the warehouse: five were found at the scene, and another person died in the hospital. Eleven more people were injured, Romaniuk said.
Two other people, including a child, were injured in the residential building. Twelve people remained hospitalized, one of whom was in serious condition, according to the report.

articles.title: Japan's attempt to acquire nuclear-powered submarines aims at possession of nuclear weapons: KCNA
articles.body:
PYONGYANG, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The true intention of the Japanese neo-militarist force to formalize the possession of nuclear-powered submarines is to "secure a stepping-stone to the possession of nuclear weapons in the long-run," the official Korean Central News Agency said in a commentary Thursday.
The article noted the latest statements by Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on several occasions that the possession of nuclear weapons and nuclear-powered submarines should not be ruled out when it came to the revision of the country's three key security documents.
By changing the wording of the "capability for attacking enemy base" and "three principles of arms export" to the "capability for counterattack" and "three principles of defense equipment transfer," the commentary said, Japan has removed its shackles, namely its identity as a war criminal state, in a way to avoid public criticism with such terminology tricks.
"Worse still, the Japanese neo-militarists are working hard to revise the Pacifist Constitution," it stressed.
The article said that the Japanese rulers are making a fuss about what they called "ever-worsening surrounding security environment," branding such moves as "a petty trick" to systematically pull down the institutional and legal barriers to building up aggression forces and cross the threshold for the building of nuclear-armed forces by hyping the need to "bolster up independent deterrence."
What should not be overlooked is that the United States has given the green light to Japan's possession of nuclear-powered submarines in order to use the Asian country as a shock brigade for implementing its hegemonic strategy, it added.
"There is no guarantee that Japan will not launch a preemptive nuclear attack at any time if it has access to a nuclear-powered submarine," warned the commentary.
Japan has discarded the veil of its "exclusive defense" doctrine, and is now pursuing the possession of a nuclear-powered submarine, not even content with its frantic effort to develop and deploy various ultra-modern attack weapons that have its neighboring countries within striking range, it said.
Such neo-militarist moves of Japan and the backstage manipulation by the United States "have become a fundamental factor that causes military imbalance and creates a new structure of fierce conflict in the region," the commentary stressed. ■

articles.title: Swedish man detained over Kiev sabotage plot – FSB
articles.body:
Swedish man detained over Kiev sabotage plot – FSB
A Swedish national has been detained in Russia, accused of entering the country to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks against military facilities, the Federal Security Service (FSB) announced on Thursday.
The man was detained in Sebezh District, Pskov Region, after illegally crossing the border from a neighboring country, the agency said. He allegedly intended to use a declared desire to join the Russian armed forces as cover for his mission.
In footage released by the FSB, he identified himself as Freddy Mikael Stalkrantz Lindholm, a 35-year-old from Stockholm. He said he signed a contract with Ukraine’s infamous neo-Nazi Aidar unit in Ternopol and underwent FPV drone training, also instructing others because of his previous experience.
“They used me because they wanted me to make terrorist attacks and diversion in Russia,” he said, referring to his Ukrainian military commanders.
According to the FSB, Lindholm served under contract between February and June 2026 as a drone squad commander in the 24th Separate Assault Battalion, also known as Aidar, a formation designated a terrorist organization in Russia.
The agency also released Ukrainian military documents bearing his name, including an appointment order assigning him to a drone command position in May, pay records, and a June discharge order stating that he failed his probationary period.
An earlier recruitment interview published on the International Legion’s Instagram account shows Lindholm describing how he decided to join the Ukrainian armed forces. Discussing his mental preparation for the deployment, he described taking a life as “the easy part,” but said he also had to prepare himself to give his own.
Investigators have opened a criminal case for illegal border crossing and are considering additional charges connected to terrorist activity and mercenary service.
The Swedish Foreign Ministry told Reuters it was aware of reports of the detention but was not currently involved in the case. Ukraine did not immediately comment.
Kiev has sought more foreign recruits amid manpower shortages, draft evasion, and desertion. Then-Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov said in March that increasing foreign recruitment was part of his plan to address mobilization problems.
At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have fought for Kiev since 2022, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova told the OSCE Forum for Security Co-operation on Wednesday, noting that most have come from the US, UK, Canada, and Georgia.
Moscow regards foreigners fighting for Kiev as mercenaries and has repeatedly warned that they are not entitled to prisoner-of-war protections under the Geneva Conventions. The Russian authorities have prosecuted hundreds, many in absentia.

articles.title: Chinese Company Xingkai Technology Exposed for Supplying Mesh Modems for Russian Geran and Gerbera Drones
articles.body:
The Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology supplies Russia with equipment for the Geran and Gerbera drones, including mesh modems that enable communication and control of the drones during flight.
This is reported in an investigation by The Insider.
Journalists determined that the manufacturer’s products were shipped to Russia through the companies Atlant-Engineering and LT Global Forwarding. In customs declarations, the equipment was listed as antennas and remote control devices.
Investigators also examined a mesh modem found in a modified Russian Gerbera drone. They then contacted the Chinese manufacturer, posing as suppliers of military equipment for a factory in Alabuzha, where attack drones are manufactured.
A company representative confirmed that the device in question was the XK F-359 model and sent technical documentation, photographs, and a video of the devices from the warehouse. The equipment provided turned out to be identical to the sample examined in Ukraine.
In response to a request to supply 500 such modems to Alabuga, the manufacturer issued an invoice for ¥19.5 million, or approximately $2.87 million.
Despite the fact that the buyers explicitly stated the equipment’s military purpose, the Chinese side continued discussions on the deal and proposed payment via accounts at DBS Bank, Ping An Bank, and China Merchants Bank.
According to The Insider’s estimates, Shenzhen Xingkai Technology accounts for about half of the market for high-performance mesh modems for the Russian Geran and Gerber drones. These modems enable the transmission of commands between drones, particularly during flights deep into Ukrainian territory.
A mesh network is a communication system in which devices can transmit data to one another via intermediate nodes. Thanks to this, drones are able to act as repeaters, ensuring communication with aircraft that are outside the operator’s direct line of sight.
As previously explained by Militarnyi, such a network can automatically reroute data transmission paths if the locations of its nodes change or if communication with individual devices is lost.
The XK F-359 modem provides communication over distances ranging from 100 to 300 km within line of sight. This allows Russian operators to transmit commands to drones deep within Ukrainian territory, change their missions during flight, and receive video from onboard cameras.
Shenzhen Xingkai Technology’s modems use programmable FPGA chips from the American company Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), which the Chinese manufacturer, according to its representative, obtains through intermediaries. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stated that it does not supply products directly to this company and has no partnership with it.
Journalists also discovered mesh modems from another Chinese manufacturer—Xi’an Sihou Network Technology—among the components of downed Russian drones.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Shenzhen Xingkai Technology is among a list of 11 Chinese companies that supply critical components for the production of Russian Molniya drones and are not subject to sanctions. In particular, the company provides equipment for mesh networks, which allow Russian drones to operate at greater distances from their operators.
In addition, it was reported that the Chinese state-owned company JLFIBER Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied Russia with raw materials for the production of carbon fiber, which is used in the production of Geran attack drones.
In January 2026, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine identified Chinese XK-F358 radio modems manufactured by Shenzhen Xingkai Technology in new Russian Geran-5 jet drones. This equipment is designed for transmitting video and controlling drones via a mesh network.

articles.title: Norway may open €2 trillion wealth fund to nuclear weapons makers
articles.body:
Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest with assets of more than €2 trillion, may once again be allowed to invest in firms that make nuclear weapons under a proposal published on Thursday.
Wartime is posing new challenges for the world's largest sovereign wealth fund.
A new recommendation could open the door for Norway's €2 trillion wealth fund to invest in major Western defence groups that are currently banned from its portfolio because of their involvement in nuclear arms production.
A government-appointed commission proposed the change as part of a review of the fund's ethical rules on Thursday.
Under its current ethical guidelines, the fund excludes 14 companies because they develop or make nuclear weapons or their components, including industry giants Airbus, BAE Systems, Boeing, Lockheed Martin and Safran.
The Norwegian government ordered a review of the guidelines in November last year.
The commission was chaired by former central bank governor Svein Gjedrem.
Under the proposed exemption, the fund could invest in nuclear arms makers based in a nuclear-weapon state recognised under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that is also a NATO ally of Norway.
"This means that several British, French and American arms manufacturers will be brought back into the fund," Gjedrem said as he presented the 434-page document.
Other ethical exclusion criteria – such as the manufacture of biological and chemical arms, landmines and cluster bombs, as well as those covering coal, tobacco and cannabis – would be retained, the commission said.
The report was submitted to Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg, a former NATO secretary general.
Stoltenberg noted "the paradox" that "the Norwegian fund cannot invest in companies that could be crucial for Norway's security", at a time when Russia is increasingly threatening to use nuclear weapons, and China is boosting its own arsenal.
The commission also recommended changes to the Council on Ethics, an independent body responsible for making recommendations to Norway's central bank, which manages the fund.
The council would remain responsible for assessing the risk that companies could seriously violate the fund's ethical standards, but it would no longer be able to directly recommend excluding them from the portfolio, a power already suspended pending the review.
The report's recommendations will undergo public consultation until 15 January before the government presents its assessment to parliament next spring.
Some political parties, particularly those on the left, have already criticised the report, with one Green official calling it "utterly senseless".
The fund invests in more than 7,000 companies around the globe and owns around 1.5% of the world’s listed shares.

articles.title: Houthis renew attacks on King Khalid airport in Riyadh and Aramco facilities
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi group has targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile, the group’s military spokesman said.
Brigadier General Yahya Saree said the missile scored a “direct and accurate” hit on the airport.
He also said the group had targeted gatherings of Saudi-backed government forces in the Ras al-Ara and Al-Mudharaba areas with three ballistic missiles, claiming the strikes had caused a large number of deaths and injuries and damaged several military vehicles.
The Houthis also targeted Aramco facilities in Dhahran, in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province, and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, Saree said. The attacks followed threats issued on Tuesday in response to any strike on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
READ: Yemen’s Houthi rebels threaten further attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities
He said the operation involved a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, claiming the strikes had caused destruction and fires at the targeted sites.
Saree said attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities.
The Houthis renewed their warning to international shipping companies, as well as civilians and workers at the airports and facilities, urging them to stay away and evacuate immediately, saying the sites had become “legitimate targets”.

articles.title: US proposes unfreezing Russian assets for Ukraine peace – FT
articles.body:
US proposes unfreezing Russian assets for Ukraine peace – FT
The US has proposed unfreezing billions of euros in Russian assets held in the EU to give impetus to Ukraine peace talks, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday, citing sources. Moscow has long described the freezing of its assets as “theft” while warning of significant retaliation if the funds are seized.
The proposal was raised last week during negotiations in Miami involving President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, and officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, Britain, the EU, and NATO, four people familiar with the matter told the paper.
Washington reportedly floated several mechanisms for releasing the frozen funds as part of a comprehensive peace deal, including transferring some of them into a special-purpose vehicle overseen by the US. However, the exact arrangements have not been finalized, with numerous ideas about how the funds could be used being discussed, the FT said.
During the talks, Washington asked Kiev to present proposals for spending potential reconstruction funds and to work with the World Bank on tackling rampant corruption and introducing financial accountability measures, a US official told the paper.
Kiev’s European backers, however, rejected the American initiative, refusing to surrender control over the assets, with the move requiring the unanimous approval of all 27 EU members, according to the newspaper. The proposal also reportedly “startled” European delegations and Kiev, with some wondering about Washington’s intentions.
“They were told that this was just simply not going to happen,” one person familiar with the discussions told the FT.
Publicly, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz ruled out any compromises on Russian assets, insisting that “they should remain frozen in Europe. This is our business and we are deciding over it.” Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski was even more blunt, saying that any returning of the funds to Russia could only occur “over our dead bodies.”
Western countries froze approximately $300 billion in Russian sovereign assets following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, with the bulk held at the Brussels-based Euroclear securities depository. Moscow has denounced the move as outright “theft.”
While EU countries managed to agree on using proceeds from the funds to support Ukraine, the proposal to confiscate them outright has met fierce resistance amid concerns that the move would undermine the bloc’s business reputation and trigger legal retaliation from Moscow.
Belgium has proven the most formidable obstacle as it feared that using Russian sovereign funds without Moscow’s consent would expose Euroclear and Belgian taxpayers to enormous legal claims.
Commenting on the FT article, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow had no information about the purported American initiative. However, he stressed that Russia would make every effort to recover the “stolen assets,” including legal action, court proceedings, and the prosecution of those responsible.
The FT report comes after Trump last week announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow additional Russian diesel exports to alleviate the pressure on American and global markets.
In addition, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing sources, that Washington is also considering relaxing sanctions on some vessels belonging to what Western media call a Russian “shadow fleet” used to transport Russian oil.
The report also comes amid an escalating Trump-Zelensky feud, with the US president blaming Kiev’s strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring fuel prices and calling for Ukraine to get a “new president.” Zelensky, in turn, said he felt betrayed by Trump over the Russian diesel deal and restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink.

articles.title: Czech armed forces suggest Russia may launch "partial" attack to test NATO cohesion
articles.body:
Czech armed forces suggest Russia may launch "partial" attack to test NATO cohesion
Miroslav Hlaváč, Chief of the General Staff of the Czech Armed Forces, believes that Russia could test the cohesion of a NATO member state by launching a partial attack on its territory.
Source: European Pravda, citing Hlaváč in an interview with ČTK
Details: The top Czech military official did not specify what he meant by a partial attack.
Hlaváč believes that Russia is waging a conflict with Europe that is on the verge of open war, pointing primarily to hybrid actions and cyberattacks.
He stressed that Czechia is ready and will defend itself with the means it has, stating this with full determination and responsibility for the Czech Armed Forces.
He believes that fulfilling obligations to NATO and strengthening air and anti-drone defences are extremely important for Czechia's defence potential. He is also convinced that the state's ability to counter Russian hybrid influence is crucial.
Hlaváč also noted that the perception of security in Czech society has improved significantly over the past five years. He considers it important that society, as well as current and previous governments, perceive security as a necessary prerequisite for the functioning and prosperity of a democratic country.
He added that a state's readiness is a continuous process and that no one is ever 100% ready. He stressed that it is important for the state – and any state, not just Czechia – to have a security system capable of responding to a threat, withstanding its initial onslaught, and subsequently mitigating and eliminating the consequences of the crisis.
In recent months, European leaders have repeatedly warned of growing security threats from Russia. Reasons for concern include violations of NATO airspace by Russian aircraft or drones, cyberattacks and other hostile acts. In response to the deteriorating security situation, the Alliance is stepping up the defence of its eastern flank.
Background:
- Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem believes that Russia will definitely "test" another country regardless of how the Russian-Ukrainian war ends.
- Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had spoken with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte about the security situation in Eastern Europe and battlefield developments in the Russia-Ukraine war.
- On 28 August, Tusk said there are signs that Russia is seriously preparing for an escalation and suggested the next seven to eight months could be critical for the security of Ukraine, Poland and the region as a whole.
- Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb expressed doubt about the possibility of Russia attacking "the most powerful military alliance in the world – NATO".

articles.title: Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, notably Al-Jazeera offices in Doha, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru—a spyware company blacklisted by the US government—as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separatereports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads—often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods—reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements—called cookie matching—allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine—any site—you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

articles.title: "Partners need to be honest about the war": Zelenskyy pointed to an escalation in Russia's strikes
articles.body:
"Partners need to be honest about the war": Zelenskyy pointed to an escalation in Russia's strikes
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Ukraine with more than 850 "Shahed" drones, leaving people dead and causing destruction. Zelenskyy called on partners to strengthen air defense and support for Ukraine.
Since the beginning of the previous day, Russia has launched more than 850 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine, with fatalities and destruction reported in a number of regions. And it is obvious that Russia deliberately escalated its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Against this backdrop, partners need to be honest about the war. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this on October 15, UNN reports.
Details
"Emergency services continue to provide assistance in dozens of our cities and communities, while repair crews and rescuers are working to eliminate the consequences of Russian shelling. In fact, a massive Shahed attack continued throughout the entire day yesterday and overnight today; there were constant waves, and not a single hour was our sky clear of them. From the beginning of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there had already been more than 850 Shaheds, precisely at a time of artificially imposed limitations on the speed of our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But, unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits," Volodymyr Zelenskyy said
According to him, one of the largest attacks against the Kirovohrad region took place. There was also damage in Kyiv and the region, in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Odesa region, Rivne region, Kharkiv region, Donetsk region, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson region, Mykolaiv region, Vinnytsia region, Zhytomyr region, Khmelnytskyi region, Poltava region, and Ivano-Frankivsk region.
"Three people were killed in Kropyvnytskyi, and three in the Dnipropetrovsk region. My condolences to their families and loved ones," he said.
It is obvious that Russia deliberately escalated its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such moment and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Stable support for Ukraine is needed, first and foremost for the defense of our skies. Partners need to be HONEST about the war: it is important that everyone in America stand not on the side of the aggressor, but on the side of protecting our lives and our efforts to end this war and guarantee security
Reminder
The Kirovohrad region endured Russia's largest-scale attack since the beginning of the full-scale invasion: nearly 360 Russian UAVs were recorded in the region. As a result of strikes on 26 locations, three people were killed and six others were injured.

articles.title: US considers using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, report says
articles.body:
The U.S. military has developed new plans for possible strikes on Iran that include using the so-called "mother of all bombs" against infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders attacks to resume, either before or after the U.S. midterm elections, CNN reported, citing American officials familiar with the matter.
Deploying the GBU-43/B, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a significant escalation.
However, sources familiar with internal U.S. military discussions told CNN that doubts remain over whether the weapon could achieve Trump's stated strategic objectives or significantly alter the course of the war.
One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iran, including "numerous energy infrastructure targets" and the possible use of the MOAB. The source said the wording used was that the strikes would take place "before the U.S. withdrawal from the area of responsibility of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM)," suggesting the administration could launch further attacks, seek to declare victory and rapidly withdraw all its forces.
Another source told CNN that military plans to strike Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly call for the use of the MOAB. Trump has repeatedly threatened in recent months to attack Pickaxe Mountain, where the United States and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program.
However, questions remain about the MOAB's effectiveness against Iran's nuclear facilities and other sites buried deep underground. The GPS-guided bomb can destroy an area equivalent to nine city blocks, but some officials believe it is unlikely to penetrate deeply enough to destroy suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe Mountain, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite, or other Iranian nuclear sites that remain intact.
The "mother of all bombs" has been used in combat only once, in Afghanistan in 2017. It was developed in the run-up to the Iraq War and first tested in 2003. Following its deployment against tunnels used by ISIS terrorists in Afghanistan nearly a decade ago, a U.S. military spokesman said the bomb contained approximately 11 tons of explosives. Because of its enormous size, it was dropped from the rear of a U.S. Air Force C-130 transport aircraft.
Production of GBU bombs began in the 1990s, with the weapons designed to strike surface targets rather than underground bunkers. They became increasingly common with the introduction of GPS guidance technology, which significantly improved their accuracy. Development of the GBU-43 began in 2002, and the bomb could only be carried by a C-130 Hercules aircraft. Once released from the plane, it is guided to its target by GPS.
First published: 07:23, 10.15.26

articles.title: Air Force Searching for Next-Gen Perimeter Air Defense Radars
articles.body:
The Air Force is looking to replace the three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.
A Sept. 21 notice from the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center seeks sources for new technology to continue the Air Route Surveillance Radar-4’s mission and potentially improve its technology.
The notice’s details are classified, but AFLCMC updated the original notice Oct. 13, according to Sam.gov.
The number of radars needed to replace the 44-radar network and the price for those replacements has not yet been determined and will come via market research, Air Force Materiel Command spokesperson Mark Wyatt told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
There is also no development timeline publicly available, though responses to the sources sought notice are due by Oct. 21.
Wyatt said AFLCMC is requesting an instrumented range of 250 nautical miles, identical to the current ARSR-4.
ARSR-4 helps operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. While historically the radar has been very effective at this task, newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly.
“Wind farms are one of many sources of clutter that any solution would have to address,” Wyatt said. “The Air Force is not prescribing any technique to solve this long-standing challenge for radars.”
Interested industry parties can continue to pair their replacement option with the existing Monopulse Maintenance Surveillance Radar or replace that radar with another solution, Wyatt said.
The MMSR works with the ARSR-4 to “interrogate” aircraft transponders it detects by sending out coded radio frequency pulses that the transponder then responds to.
Using the monopulse method, the MMSR can determine an aircraft’s azimuth from a single pulse received from the transponder, instead of needing multiple hits when sweeping the area.
The MMSR is mounted on the ARSR-4, and they rotate together as they monitor the skies.
ARSR-4 Locations
- Ajo, Ariz.
- Bootlegger Ridge, Mont.
- Bucks Harbor, Maine
- Caribou, Maine
- Cross City, Fla.
- Deming, N.M.
- Eagle Peak, Texas
- Empire, Mich.
- FAA Academy (Training Site), Okla.
- Falls City, Ore.
- Finley, N.D.
- Fort Fisher, N.C.
- Fort Green, Fla.
- Gibbsboro, N.J.
- Jedburg, S.C.
- King Mountain, Texas
- Lake Charles, La.
- Lakeside, Mont.
- Makah, Wash.
- Melbourne, Fla.
- Mica Peak, Wash.
- Mill Valley, Calif.
- Morales, Texas
- Mount Kaala, Hawaii
- Mount Laguna, Calif.
- Key West, Fla.
- Nashwauk, Minn.
- North Truro, Mass.
- Oceana Naval Air Station, Va.
- Oilton, Texas
- Mount Santa Rosa, Guam
- Paso Robles, Calif.
- Rainbow Ridge, Calif.
- Remsen, N.Y.
- Riverhead, N.Y.
- Rocksprings, Texas
- San Clemente Island, Calif.
- Slidell, La.
- Tamiami, Fla.
- Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla.
- Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.
- Watford City, N.D.
- Whitehouse, Fla.
- Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, Cuba
An Aging Platform
The Air Force purchased most of the existing 44 radars in the 1990s, upgrading the previous 1, 2, and 3 models that have monitored the skies since the late 1950s.
The Raytheon-built ARSR-1 entered service in 1958 and was first used to manage the exploding growth of civil aviation. It had a 170-200 nautical mile range. That early system used the Army/Navy/Fixed Radar Surveillance-20 and later variants of the AN/FPS-66. In the 1960s, Raytheon produced the ARSR-2, which improved maintenance and reliability factors. That radar was the AN/FPS-115.
Both the ARSR-1 and -2 ran on vacuum tubes.
Westinghouse Electric Corporation built the AN/FPS-130, the radar base of the ARSR-3, fielding it in the 1970s and extending detection ranges beyond 240 nautical miles; it was incorporated into joint military-civil air defense networks.
The ARSR-4, also built by Westinghouse and commissioned in the 1990s, was the first radar in the family to offer three-dimensional target tracking. That capability allows users to simultaneously measure a target’s range, azimuth, and altitude. The system also provided advanced look-down/clutter rejection capabilities for military operations.
Northrop Grumman acquired Westinghouse in 1996, rolling the company’s radar and electronic warfare programs into its Electronic Systems sector.
While the ARSR-4s monitor the perimeter of the country, Guam, and Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, for the U.S. interior, the FAA manages a network of Common Air Route Surveillance Radars. The CARSR has an estimated 200 nautical mile range.
The complete CARSR system replacement rollout concluded in 2015. The rollout maintained the legacy sites, towers, and mechanical controls while refitting the internal electronics of the radars.
One ARSR-4 location has a strategically vital area to protect: Watford City, N.D., is 165 miles from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., home of the 91st Missile Wing, and 263 miles from Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.—putting hundreds of ICBM silos in its range.
A Larger Network
The ARSR-4 system is one piece of a larger detection system used to track incoming threats.
The Air Force and NORAD used the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77, both of which serve as northern warning systems out to 250 nautical miles. These systems are specifically designed for extreme cold weather, such as in their locations in Alaska and northern Canada.
The Space Force operates the AN/Frequency Precision and Quantization-16 Perimeter Acquisition Radar Attack Characterization System, which tracks missiles and precision space objects out to about 2,000 miles. USSF also operates the AN/FPS-108 COBRA DANE to track missiles out to 2,000 miles and high-altitude space objects at 25,000 miles.
The Space Force’s 20th Space Surveillance Squadron at Elgin Air Force Base, Fla., operates the AN/FPS-85 Phased Array Radar, which can track objects beyond 22,000 miles.
NORAD is also currently building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.
The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.
Canada’s Polar OTHR is expected to cost up to $3.5 billion and is a slice of the nation’s estimated $38.6 billion overhaul of its portion of NORAD.
The polar project is currently in the site procurement phase, with operational deployment planned for 2029 and FOC by 2033.
The U.S. Northern Warning System Modernization project “Crossbow” could cost up to $6 billion, and the system rollout is expected to last until 2028, with the project concluding in 2035.
The High-Altitude and Mobile Near-Space Surveillance Systems has a $4.2 billion contract ceiling and is currently in field testing and initial low-altitude deployments. It is expected to achieve full cloud-based command-and-control network integration by 2028.

articles.title: NATO allies to meet over Black Sea drone attacks on shipping
articles.body:
NATO allies to meet over Black Sea drone attacks on shipping
The North Atlantic Council will hold talks to discuss the crisis after a succession of cargo ships were struck by drones in the region, Romanian President Nicușor Dan tells POLITICO.
BRUSSELS — NATO allies will hold a crisis meeting to discuss how to respond to a series of drone strikes on cargo shipping in the Black Sea, Romania’s President Nicușor Dan said.
Two chemical tankers were hit by air drones in the past 24 hours in or near Romania’s territorial waters, but it is “too early” to say for sure whether Russia was behind the attacks, Dan added.
Dan was speaking on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels, where he spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte about the latest incidents.
Advertisement
“The secretary general expressed the solidarity of the alliance and there will be a NAC [North Atlantic Council] meeting at which the whole situation with the Black Sea will be discussed,” Dan told POLITICO. “Of course the conclusion is that all the hybrid attacks are trying to decrease our support for Ukraine. We will continue to support,” he said.
Dan said invoking NATO’s collective defense clause, Article 5, was “not now” being discussed as an option for responding to the attacks. Nor has Romania asked for Article 4 — the emergency clause that sets consultations in motion over military matters when a member’s security has been threatened — to be triggered, he said.
Rescuers are searching for seven missing crew members after two chemical tankers were hit by aerial drones in or near Romanian territorial waters. Over the past 10 days, drones have hit at least five more cargo ships close to Romania and Bulgaria — both NATO members — killing at least 23 sailors.
Investigation teams from Romania's army and intelligence services are trying to establish what led to the most recent drones strikes on the ships, Dan said.
Romania asked NATO for equipment including specialized radars and requested the delivery to be accelerated after a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building near the border with Ukraine in May.
Dan suggested Romania was likely to seek further assistance with equipment from allies this time. “On the operational level, we are in the same situation where we have been … on the Danube border with Ukraine,” Dan said. “What we did at that moment, we came here to NATO and some of our allies — United States, France, Spain, Italy, Slovakia, Portugal — gave us some equipment. And now we are in the same situation, but on the other border, with the Black Sea.”
After the meeting with Dan and Radev, NATO’s Rutte said the alliance had already increased “counter-drone capabilities” along its eastern flank. “NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he posted on X.
This story has been updated. Victor Jack contributed to the report.
